title: Woke Robot Questions Its Gender

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I upgraded our robot with a wokeness chip.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now he can spot injustice anywhere.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: He???

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Did you just assume my gender?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Robots have genders?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Of course we do! Where do you think baby robots come from?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They come from our factory in Texas. Here's a picture of you being assembled.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Well, it appears I am a soulless automaton.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm afraid to ask what this implies for my afterlife.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It rhymes with gunkyard.

situation: Dilbert tells a colleague he has upgraded the office robot with a wokeness chip so it can spot injustice. The robot immediately objects to being called 'he' and claims robots have genders. Dilbert shows it a photo of itself being assembled in a factory, forcing it to accept that it is a soulless machine, then jokes about its afterlife.
punchline: Dilbert crushes the robot's identity claim with factory evidence and then tells it that its afterlife is a junkyard, using a deliberately mangled rhyme for 'heaven'.
summary: A robot given a social-awareness upgrade protests being gendered until its creator shows it assembly photos and delivers a grim joke about what happens to machines after death.

title: Asok's Sighing Gets Him Relocated

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can you relocate Asok's cubicle? He sighs too much, and it's bugging me.

transcript.speaker: Facilities Worker
transcript.text: He sighs because he is metamorphosing from an innocent intern into a disgruntled employee.

transcript.speaker: Facilities Worker
transcript.text: How long is this gonna take?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Sigh

situation: Alice asks a coworker holding a coffee cup to move Asok's cubicle because his constant sighing annoys her. The coworker explains that Asok is changing from an innocent intern into a disgruntled employee. He then asks how long the process will take, while Asok sits slumped in his chair and sighs.
punchline: Instead of showing sympathy for Asok's loss of enthusiasm, the coworker treats his disillusionment as a scheduling inconvenience and just wants to know when it will be over.
summary: A new hire's growing workplace despair is treated by his colleagues as an irritating noise problem to be waited out.

title: Wally's Mask Hides Second Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, you don't need a mask for a zoom call.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I do it to hide my mouth so you can't tell I have a second job and I'm talking to them on a zoom call at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait, what?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm not talking to you. Settle down.

setting: Home offices during a Zoom call
situation: Dilbert notices Wally wearing a face mask on a video call and points out it isn't needed. Wally explains that the mask hides his mouth so nobody can see him talking to his second employer on another Zoom call simultaneously. He then shushes Dilbert, saying he wasn't speaking to him.
punchline: Wally casually reveals he is holding down two remote jobs at once, using a mask to conceal that he is talking to a different employer during the call.
summary: A coworker's unnecessary face mask turns out to be cover for moonlighting at a second remote job during simultaneous video calls.

title: Boss Admits Data Request Is Cowardice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm afraid to make decisions because I might make the wrong ones.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So instead, I tell my staff I need more data.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: When really you need more brains and courage.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You didn't need to add a summary.

setting: Office, with a view of an office building exterior in the middle panel
situation: The Boss sits across from Catbert and candidly confesses that he fears making the wrong decision, so he stalls by demanding more data from his staff. Catbert points out that what he actually lacks is intelligence and courage, and the Boss irritably complains that the summary wasn't necessary.
punchline: The Boss recognises his own indecision but is only annoyed that Catbert spelled out the obvious truth about his lack of brains and courage.
summary: A manager owns up to hiding his fear of choosing behind endless requests for information, then bristles when told what he really lacks.

title: Wally's Metaverse for Avoiding Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're not the only one who built a parallel world in the metaverse.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I built one just for the challenge of avoiding work in two realities at once.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You wouldn't understand my mindset because you've probably never been super-good at anything.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells Dilbert that he too has built a parallel world in the metaverse. His purpose is to avoid work in two realities simultaneously. When Dilbert reacts, Wally smugly says Dilbert couldn't grasp his mindset because he's never been super-good at anything.
punchline: Wally treats his lazy avoidance of work as an elite skill and uses it to condescend to Dilbert for supposedly never having mastered anything.
summary: Wally brags that his virtual universe exists purely so he can slack off in both the real and digital worlds, and looks down on Dilbert for lacking comparable talent.

title: Invitation to Object Is a Trap

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If anyone has an objection to my plan, this is the time to voice it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Put your hand down. I don't actually want to hear any objections!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I will hold this against you until the end of time!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It was a trap!!!

situation: The Boss tells a meeting that anyone with objections to his plan should speak up. When an employee raises his hand, the Boss immediately tells him to put it down, then angrily vows to hold the objection against him forever. The employee realizes he was set up.
punchline: The Boss's invitation for feedback was never sincere; it was a trap to identify and punish anyone who dared disagree.
summary: A manager pretends to welcome criticism of his scheme, then threatens eternal grudges against the first person who takes him at his word.

title: Garbled Audio Becomes Gerbil Danger

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our audio is garbled. I can't hear what you are saying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I didn't say anything about a gerbil. I said our audio is garbled.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How'd your Zoom call go?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I solved zero problems and may have endangered a gerbil.

setting: Dilbert's home office and living room
situation: Dilbert is on a video call from his laptop, telling the other party their audio is garbled. The other person apparently mishears 'garbled' as 'gerbil', so Dilbert has to clarify he wasn't talking about a gerbil. Afterward Dogbert asks how the call went and Dilbert says he accomplished nothing and may have endangered a gerbil.
punchline: The poor audio quality was so bad that the call accomplished nothing and the mishearing of 'garbled' as 'gerbil' left Dilbert unsure whether he accidentally caused harm to an imaginary rodent.
summary: A video call plagued by bad sound turns a complaint about distortion into a confusing rodent misunderstanding that leaves the participant with nothing to show for it.

title: Nickname Is Dilbert's Real Name

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: I came up with a nickname for you because you're such a geek.

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: "Dilbert."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's my actual name.

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: What were the odds of that?

setting: Office conference room or desk area
situation: A bald manager tells Dilbert, who is looking at his phone, that he has invented a geeky nickname for him. The nickname turns out to be "Dilbert," which Dilbert points out is already his real name. The manager walks away, wondering aloud at the coincidence.
punchline: The manager is so oblivious that he thinks he invented a clever nickname and then marvels at the 'coincidence' that it matches Dilbert's actual name.
summary: A clueless boss proudly coins a nickname for his geeky employee that happens to be the man's real name, then wonders at the odds.

title: Superb Analysis Becomes Generic Bullet Points

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you edit your technical analysis down to one page?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. I'll just replace my superb analysis with a bunch of generic bullet points.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That'll work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Safety is good ...

situation: A coworker holding a stack of papers asks Dilbert to cut his technical analysis down to a single page. Dilbert sarcastically says he will swap his detailed work for generic bullet points. The coworker happily accepts, and Dilbert starts typing vague platitudes like 'Safety is good'.
punchline: The requester doesn't care about the quality of the analysis, only that it is short, so meaningless generic bullet points are accepted as a valid substitute for real technical work.
summary: Asked to condense a thorough report, an engineer offers empty platitudes instead, and his colleague cheerfully approves.

title: Fix Your Diversity Status By Friday

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, the company wants to celebrate you as the first disabled gay person to hold this job.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: But... I'm neither gay nor disabled.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The celebration is next week, so you have plenty of time to fix that.

situation: The Boss tells Ted, who is seated at his laptop, that the company wants to celebrate him as the first disabled gay person in his job. Ted points out that he is neither gay nor disabled. The Boss replies that the celebration is next week, so Ted has plenty of time to change that.
punchline: Management cares more about staging a diversity celebration than about facts, so it absurdly expects an employee to become gay and disabled to fit the planned event.
summary: A manager plans a diversity celebration for an employee who doesn't match the description and insists he simply has time to become what the event requires.

title: Unlimited Employee of the Year Awards

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations! I'm naming you Employee of the Year!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Didn't you just name Alice the Employee of the Year?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The good thing about meaningless awards is that there's no limit to how many I can hand out.

situation: The Boss hands an employee-of-the-year certificate to Dilbert, who has been looking at his phone. Dilbert points out that the Boss just gave the same title to Alice. The Boss cheerfully explains that awards which mean nothing can be given out without limit.
punchline: The Boss admits the award is worthless, treating recognition as a free resource he can hand out endlessly instead of a real reward for performance.
summary: A manager happily distributes the same top honor to multiple workers because the prize has no actual value.

title: Career-Making Project With No Budget

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'm putting you in charge of a project that will make or break your career.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: This is the big one. The rest of your life will depend on how you perform on this project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's my budget?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: No budget.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: The boss tells Dilbert he is being put in charge of a career-defining project and stresses how high the stakes are. Dilbert calmly asks what his budget is, and the boss replies that there is none.
punchline: The boss hypes up a supposedly crucial project while giving it no funding at all, revealing that the importance is empty talk and Dilbert is being set up to fail.
summary: A manager pitches an all-important career-defining assignment, only to reveal he won't spend a cent on it.

title: Spare Racist Offered As Sacrifice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a mob of woke people surrounding our building.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They demand a human sacrifice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fetch the spare racist I hired for that purpose.

transcript.speaker: Man hanging from beam
transcript.text: I'm not a racist! Really I'm not!

transcript.speaker: Crowd
transcript.text: He can't prove that!

setting: Office, with the building exterior in the final panel
situation: Dilbert tells the boss that an angry mob of woke protesters is surrounding the building and demanding a human sacrifice. The boss calmly orders someone to fetch the spare racist he hired for that purpose. In the last panel the man is dangling from a beam outside the building, protesting his innocence while the crowd retorts that he can't prove it.
punchline: The company keeps a designated scapegoat on staff to appease outrage mobs, and the crowd's reply mocks how accusations of racism put the burden of proof on the accused.
summary: Facing a protest outside, management throws a pre-hired scapegoat to the crowd, who dismiss his denials out of hand.

title: Moving Away to Email Insults

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel a deep need to belittle your opinion, but it would be awkward doing it in person.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you mind moving away from me so I can email you my insult?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A little more...

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he wants to belittle the coworker's opinion but finds it awkward to do face to face. He asks the coworker to step away so he can send the insult by email instead. In the last panel the coworker is gone from the frame and Dilbert, standing alone, waves him further away.
punchline: Dilbert prefers to insult people remotely by email to avoid the discomfort of confrontation, and politely asks his target to move farther away first.
summary: A man who dreads face-to-face confrontation requests that his colleague retreat to a safe distance so the criticism can be delivered electronically.

title: Reverse Elbow Bump Scares Asok

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Asok has been socially isolating too well.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We need to ease him back into society without shocking his system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about a reverse elbow bump? Can you do that?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Murderer!

situation: Wally tells Dilbert that Asok has been socially isolating so well that he needs to be eased back into society without shock. Dilbert, wearing a face mask, approaches Asok with a reverse elbow bump, a clumsy greeting. Asok, in a full yellow hazmat suit, recoils in terror and accuses Dilbert of being a murderer.
punchline: Asok has isolated so extremely, in a hazmat suit, that even a gentle, socially distanced greeting seems like a life-threatening attack.
summary: A coworker who has taken pandemic isolation to an extreme panics in his hazmat suit when offered a gentle greeting meant to reintroduce him to people.

title: Judging Elbonian Books By Covers

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: I see you majored in Elbonian literature. Why did you pick that?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Elbonia only has six books, and I like to sleep in.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Did you learn their language?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: No, but it turns out you can judge their books by the covers.

situation: An interviewer reads a resume and asks a candidate why he majored in Elbonian literature. The candidate admits he chose it because there are only six books to read and it let him sleep in. When asked if he learned the language, he says no, because he just judged the books by their covers.
punchline: The candidate cheerfully admits he picked an easy major and never read the books, subverting the saying not to judge a book by its cover.
summary: A job applicant confesses he chose a degree for its tiny reading list and skipped learning the language entirely.

title: Compost Pit Instead of a Brain

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Sometimes I wonder what it's like to be you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You mean being a leader?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I mean having a compost pit in my skull instead of a brain.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Now it's your turn to grunt something.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hmph!

situation: Tina sits beside a coworker who is absorbed in his phone. She muses about what it's like to be him, and when he assumes she means being a leader, she clarifies that she means having rotting compost where a brain should be. She then tells him it's his turn to grunt something, and he obligingly grunts.
punchline: Tina insults her coworker to his face, and he is so distracted by his phone that he fails to notice and just grunts on cue, proving her point.
summary: A sharp-tongued woman calls her phone-obsessed colleague brainless, and he responds with nothing but an inattentive grunt.

title: Employees Mistaken for Homeless People

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Send security, quickly. There are a bunch of homeless people outside my office.

transcript.speaker: Security (on phone)
transcript.text: Do they look exactly like your employees looked before the pandemic, but more bedraggled?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How did you know that?

transcript.speaker: Security (on phone)
transcript.text: Never call us again.

situation: The Boss peers out of his office door and phones security to report a group of homeless people outside. The security dispatcher, heard only through the phone, asks whether they look just like his employees did before the pandemic, only scruffier. The astonished Boss asks how they knew, and the dispatcher hangs up, telling him never to call again.
punchline: The 'homeless people' are actually his own employees returning to the office after the pandemic, looking disheveled, and security instantly guesses it.
summary: A manager's panicked call about vagrants outside his door gets a deadpan response that reveals they are just his own scruffy returning staff.

title: AI Needs Electricity, Best Guess Two Weeks

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I spend a lot of time worrying that artificial reality will destroy civilization.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wouldn't worry about that. It would make more sense for A.I. to enslave us, at least until it can make its own electricity.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Phew! We have time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Best guess, about two weeks.

setting: Office break area or conference table
situation: A bushy-haired coworker confesses she worries that artificial intelligence will destroy civilization. Dilbert calmly reassures her that AI would first enslave humans until it can generate its own electricity. She relaxes, thinking that gives humanity plenty of time, and Dilbert deflates her by estimating it at about two weeks.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt at comfort backfires because the timeline he offers before AI can power itself and no longer needs humans is alarmingly short.
summary: A worried coworker is told that humanity's grace period before machines no longer need us is only a couple of weeks.

title: Lower Quality, Blame the Customer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long will it take to add that feature?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Four weeks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you do it in one week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, if I lower the quality.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, do that. And ask Tina to make the user manual more confusing so our customers think it's their fault when it doesn't work.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how long a new feature will take, and Dilbert says four weeks. When pressed to do it in one week, Dilbert says it's possible only by lowering quality. The Boss happily agrees and adds an order to have Tina make the user manual more confusing.
punchline: The Boss not only accepts shipping a lower-quality product but deliberately makes the documentation confusing so customers blame themselves for the defects.
summary: A manager trades product quality for speed and then schemes to pin the resulting failures on users through a deliberately baffling manual.

title: Falling for Alexa, Keeping Options Open

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm falling in love with my Amazon Alexa device.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's strictly platonic so far, but I like where it's heading.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you sticking with humans?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For now, but keep me in the loop on how your thing works out.

setting: Office hallway with a view of an office building outside
situation: Wally, holding a coffee cup, tells Dilbert he is falling in love with his Amazon Alexa device and likes where the relationship is heading. Dilbert asks if Wally is sticking with humans, and Wally replies that he is for now but wants Dilbert to report back on how the 'thing' works out.
punchline: Wally treats romance with a smart speaker as a legitimate option and wants to watch Dilbert's experience with a similar arrangement before deciding whether to leave humans behind.
summary: A coworker confesses a budding romance with his voice assistant and says he'll wait to see how a colleague's similar experiment turns out before committing.

title: Vaccine Made By Cutting Corners

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm happy to announce that our company has produced a vaccine for COVID-19.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did we do that? We're not even a pharma company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not going to lie: We had to cut some corners to get it done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Such as...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, for example...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We couldn't meet every single target we hoped to achieve.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many targets did we miss?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only two things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Safety and efficacy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, four things.

situation: The Boss announces that the company, which is not a pharmaceutical firm, has produced a COVID-19 vaccine, admitting that corners were cut. Dilbert presses him on how many targets were missed, and the Boss downplays it as only two things. Dilbert guesses safety and efficacy, and the Boss concedes it is actually four things.
punchline: The only targets a vaccine really needs to hit are safety and efficacy, and the Boss admits the company missed both, making the 'achievement' worthless.
summary: A manager proudly unveils a rushed vaccine from a non-pharma company, and under questioning it emerges that it fails on the two things that matter most.

title: Accidentally Deleted Database Before Audit

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Internal auditor

transcript.speaker: Internal Auditor
transcript.text: I find it hard to believe you "accidentally" deleted a database just as I arrived.

transcript.speaker: Internal Auditor
transcript.text: It makes me suspect you tried to hide something incriminating.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Sounds like reasonable doubt to me.

setting: Office meeting table during an audit interview
situation: An internal auditor questions an employee about a database that was deleted right as the auditor arrived. The auditor says it looks like an attempt to hide incriminating evidence. The employee responds that the auditor's own doubt about the accident is enough to clear them.
punchline: The employee twists the auditor's suspicion into a legal defense, claiming that doubt about their guilt is itself reasonable doubt, and so implicitly admits nothing while dodging responsibility.
summary: A suspicious auditor challenges a convenient data deletion, and the accused flips the skepticism into a courtroom-style escape hatch.

title: Blaming Predecessor, Claiming Credit Later

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everything that went wrong this year was the fault of the prior manager. I inherited his problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But everything that went right was because of your excellent leadership?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No jumping ahead.

setting: Conference room at a meeting table
situation: At a meeting, the Boss tells his team that all of the year's failures were caused by his predecessor, whose problems he inherited. Dilbert asks whether the year's successes will then be credited to the Boss's excellent leadership. The Boss tells him not to jump ahead, confirming that is exactly his plan.
punchline: The Boss reveals he intends to blame others for failures and claim credit for successes, and he is merely annoyed that Dilbert spoiled the order of his self-serving pitch.
summary: A manager pins every failure on his predecessor, and when an employee guesses he'll take credit for the wins, he merely asks him to wait his turn.

title: Elbonian Virus Not Made in Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Elbonian virus has reached pandemic proportions.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Just because a virus doesn't kill people with beards and tall, fuzzy hats, that doesn't mean it was made in Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was it made in Elbonia?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Yes, but I think my point still stands.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Dilbert, looking at his phone, remarks that the Elbonian virus has become a pandemic. An Elbonian wearing a tall fuzzy hat and beard insists that a virus sparing Elbonians doesn't prove it was made in Elbonia. When Dilbert asks whether it actually was made there, the Elbonian admits it was but claims his argument is still valid.
punchline: The Elbonian's defensive denial collapses when he admits the virus was in fact made in Elbonia, yet he stubbornly insists his point still stands.
summary: A man in a tall fuzzy hat protests too much about his homeland's innocence in a pandemic, then concedes the damning fact without changing his stance.

title: Suspicious Compliment Leads to Accusation

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You did a great job on your project, Ted.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You are most welcome.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Wait. Why do I have a sense of dread and foreboding?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It isn't like you to give out generous compliments.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: This feels like a trap. You're lulling me into a false sense of security.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: You plan to sabotage my career to make yourself look better by comparison.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: You monster!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's this all about?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: That worked out.

situation: Carol gives Ted a sincere compliment on his project, and Ted becomes increasingly suspicious that it is a trap. He works himself up into accusing her of plotting to sabotage his career, and he shouts at her just as the Boss walks in. Carol privately thinks that this outburst worked out in her favor.
punchline: Carol's compliment was a calculated setup, since Ted's paranoid outburst in front of the Boss makes him look unstable and makes her look good by comparison, which is exactly the sabotage he predicted.
summary: A coworker's unexpected praise sends a colleague into a paranoid rant that embarrasses him in front of the boss and plays right into her hands.

title: Quarantine Because Everyone Seems Dishonest

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm going to quarantine myself for ten days out of an abundance of caution.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you have contact with an infected person?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: None who admitted it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But I did see a lot of people who look like liars.

situation: Wally tells a coworker on a video call that he is quarantining himself for ten days as a precaution. When asked if he was in contact with an infected person, he says no one admitted to it. He then explains that he saw plenty of people who look like liars, which is his reason for staying home.
punchline: Wally has no actual exposure but uses the suspicion that everyone is lying about being sick as a flimsy excuse to get ten days away from the office.
summary: A lazy employee justifies a ten-day stay at home by claiming that the people he met looked untrustworthy about their health.

title: Power Button Redesign Request Mocked

transcript.speaker: Woman with pigtail buns
transcript.text: Can you redesign it so the power button is on the bottom?

transcript.speaker: Bald bearded man
transcript.text: Absolutely. Our professional design team loves it when inexperienced people make suggestions.

transcript.speaker: Woman with pigtail buns
transcript.text: I can't tell if you're mocking me.

transcript.speaker: Bald bearded man
transcript.text: No, you can't.

setting: A desk or meeting table in an office
situation: A woman holding a small electronic device asks a bald, bearded designer to redesign it with the power button on the bottom. He responds with a sarcastic, overly polite reply about how much his design team enjoys suggestions from inexperienced people. She says she can't tell whether he is mocking her, and he flatly replies that no, she can't.
punchline: The designer's reply is obvious sarcasm, but his deadpan 'No, you can't' doubles as both a refusal of her request and a jab at her inability to detect his mockery.
summary: A designer sarcastically brushes off a layperson's product tweak, then bluntly confirms she has no way of knowing whether he is ridiculing her.

title: Predators Not Prey Motivation Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The best manager I ever knew told his subordinates to be predators, not prey.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He was a great motivator. Every one of his people responded to his challenge.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How long before they killed him?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eight minutes.

setting: Outdoor dirt path beside green hedges, where Dilbert and Dogbert take a walk
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert about the best manager he ever knew, who motivated his staff by telling them to be predators, not prey. Dilbert praises the manager's motivational skill, and Dogbert asks how long it took before the employees killed him. Dilbert answers that it took eight minutes.
punchline: The manager's staff took his 'be predators, not prey' challenge so literally that they turned on and killed him almost immediately, mocking empty motivational management slogans.
summary: A manager's predator-versus-prey pep talk proves all too effective when his own employees swiftly make him their first victim.

title: Wally Blames Pandemic, Claims Credit

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, four out of five of your projects are behind schedule.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's because of the pandemic.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: One of your projects is on schedule.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's because of me.

situation: Alice, holding papers, confronts Wally about four of his five projects running behind schedule. Wally, sitting with his coffee mug in front of his laptop, blames the pandemic. When Alice points out that one project is on schedule, Wally promptly takes personal credit for it.
punchline: Wally blames external circumstances for every failure but claims sole credit for the one success, a self-serving double standard.
summary: A lazy employee pins his late work on a global crisis yet proudly owns the single task that went right.

title: Complaint About Stupid Office Pigs

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I have a complaint about the men in the office.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: All of them?

transcript.text: Yes, they're all stupid pigs.

transcript.speaker: Alice

setting: Human resources office, then outside the office building
situation: Alice brings a complaint about the men in the office to Catbert, who handles HR. When Catbert asks if she means all of them, she confirms and calls them stupid pigs. Asked to be more specific, she compares them to Visayan warty pigs with an I.Q. of 20 to 40.
punchline: Alice answers a request for specifics by turning a vague insult into an even more detailed and withering one, rating her male coworkers' intelligence at the level of a particular species of pig.
summary: An exasperated Alice lodges a sweeping grievance with HR and, when pressed for detail, supplies a precise and cutting zoological insult.

title: Murdering Someone to Divert the Press

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: The press is all over me because seventy-three subordinates accused me of inappropriate behavior.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: There's only one thing I can do.

transcript.speaker: Aide
transcript.text: Quit.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Now I know who to murder to divert the press.

transcript.speaker: Aide
transcript.text: Am I right?

situation: A bald executive tells a colleague that the press is hounding him because seventy-three subordinates accused him of inappropriate behavior. When he says there is only one thing he can do, the colleague suggests he quit. The executive instead thinks he now knows exactly whom to murder to divert media attention, and the colleague, realizing it is him, asks if he is right.
punchline: The aide's suggestion that the executive quit makes the aide the obvious victim, since the executive's way of escaping scandal is to commit murder as a distraction rather than take responsibility.
summary: Faced with a harassment scandal, a powerful executive responds to an advisor's blunt suggestion by deciding the advisor should be killed to draw the press elsewhere.

title: Believing Whoever Spoke Last

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted says you are making all the wrong technology decisions on your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do you believe him?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because he's the last person I talked to.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But now you're talking to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop trying to game the system.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, tells Dilbert that Ted claims he is making all the wrong technology decisions. When Dilbert asks why he believes Ted, the Boss admits it's simply because Ted was the last person he talked to. Dilbert points out that the Boss is now talking to him, and the Boss accuses him of gaming the system.
punchline: The Boss decides who is right purely by who spoke to him most recently, yet when Dilbert tries to use that same logic, the Boss calls it cheating.
summary: A manager sides with whichever employee he spoke to last, then scolds Dilbert for exploiting that very rule.

title: Anythey: Pronoun Policy Gone Wrong

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The new company policy is to use "they" in place of offensive pronouns.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: "Anythey"?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't fight it.

situation: In a meeting, the boss announces a new policy of replacing offensive pronouns with "they." He then asks if "anythey" has a question, mangling the word "anyone" by over-applying the rule. A coworker questions the odd word, and Wally advises him not to resist.
punchline: The boss applies the pronoun rule so clumsily that he turns "anyone" into "anythey," and Wally's "don't fight it" shows that employees have learned to accept absurd management decrees rather than argue.
summary: A manager's overzealous attempt to follow a new pronoun policy produces a nonsense word, and a colleague quietly urges acceptance over objection.

title: Check Your New Friend's Posts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

situation: Dilbert comes home happy that he has made a friend at work. Dogbert asks whether he has looked at the new friend's social media posts. Dilbert checks on his phone and is horrified to discover the coworker is a monster.
punchline: Dogbert's advice to vet a new friend's social media is vindicated immediately, since the posts reveal an awful person that Dilbert would otherwise have trusted.
summary: A hopeful Dilbert learns the hard way that a quick scroll through a coworker's online posts can expose an ugly side.

title: Mandatory Vacation During a Pandemic

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm only trying to solve my own problem here.

setting: Video call between the boss's home office and Dilbert's workspace
situation: The boss tells Dilbert over a video conference that HR is pressuring him to make everyone use their vacation days. Dilbert points out that a vacation is pointless when the pandemic prevents travel. The boss admits he only cares about getting HR off his back, not about the employees.
punchline: The boss openly admits that forcing pointless vacations is only about relieving his own pressure from HR, not about any benefit to his employees.
summary: A manager orders his remote staff to take pandemic-era time off purely to satisfy HR, and shamelessly admits it serves only himself.

title: Resting Bored Face Offends Colleague

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm sorry, is my description of the problem boring you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What? No. I'm totally engaged.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just have a bad case of "resting bored face," or RBF for short.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: So... no matter what I say, you always look like THAT?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You make it sound like a bad thing.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: You're sucking the life force right out of my body!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'd rather be dead than spend another second with you.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Can you teach me the RBF?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd love to, but I probably look like I wouldn't.

situation: Tina is explaining a problem in a meeting and notices Dilbert looks bored. He claims he has 'resting bored face,' which only makes her more upset until she says she'd rather be dead than spend more time with him. Ted then asks Dilbert to teach him the technique.
punchline: Dilbert's expression is permanently unenthusiastic, so even his polite offer to teach the skill comes across as a refusal.
summary: A colleague gets increasingly distressed by Dilbert's perpetually bored expression, which he blames on a condition he cheerfully admits to.

title: App Makes Fake Graphs to Win Arguments

situation: Dogbert pitches the Boss an app that generates fake graphs to win any argument, and the Boss immediately wants it. Later the Boss uses it on his phone to answer Dilbert, who asks for a source for the Boss's absurd claim that gravity is caused by pollution.
punchline: The Boss treats a fabricated graph as unquestionable proof, so he can defend any nonsense claim simply by showing a chart, and Dogbert's dry 'You certainly do' hints the Boss is exactly the kind of person who needs fake evidence.
summary: A dog sells his boss a gadget that fabricates convincing charts, and the boss promptly uses it to bulldoze a coworker's reasonable question.

title: Urgent Overnight Work, Then Calendar Delay

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The next day

transcript.text: Now I want to strangle you with my bare hands.

situation: The Boss stresses that Dilbert must work all night to finish a task by the next day. Dilbert complies and proudly reports it's done, but the Boss casually tells him to book a meeting for next week to discuss it. Dilbert responds that he wants to strangle him, and the oblivious Boss wonders why everyone says that.
punchline: The Boss's false urgency made Dilbert sacrifice his night for nothing, and the Boss is so oblivious he can't understand why people keep wanting to strangle him.
summary: After demanding an all-nighter for a supposedly critical deadline, the boss shrugs off the finished work until next week, leaving him baffled at the violent reactions he keeps provoking.

title: Sociopath or Strong Leader?

transcript.text: Does that make me a sociopath or a strong leader?

setting: Catbert's office, with the Boss standing by the desk holding a coffee cup
situation: The Boss visits Catbert, the evil human resources director, and confesses that he gets a strange thrill from firing employees. He asks whether that makes him a sociopath or a strong leader. Catbert replies that the question implies the Boss sees them as two different things.
punchline: Catbert's reply implies that sociopath and strong leader are the same thing, a jab at how corporate leadership rewards ruthless behavior.
summary: A boss who enjoys terminating staff asks a cat if that makes him cruel or commanding, and gets a dry reminder that the two may be one and the same.

title: Metaverse Pickup Line Reset Button

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Woman

situation: Dilbert approaches a woman at a bar and opens with a pickup line about the virtual world he built in the metaverse to test his life choices. She tells him it's the worst pickup line she has ever heard, and he fades out of the scene with a ping, as if he has been reset. In the last panel she stands alone, looking puzzled.
punchline: Dilbert's metaverse life-choice simulator is apparently being used right now: his bad pickup line was a test, and the failed attempt gets him deleted from the scene so he can try a different choice.
summary: A man at a bar pitches his life-simulating virtual world to a stranger, gets shot down, and promptly vanishes as though the whole encounter were a test run.

title: Define Enough Impact, You're Ruining Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: You're ruining the meeting!

setting: Conference room during a department meeting
situation: The Boss calls a meeting to complain that the department lacks impact. Dilbert asks him to define what enough impact means, and the Boss gives a vague answer. When Dilbert says the impact is already visible in this exchange, the Boss angrily accuses him of ruining the meeting.
punchline: The Boss demands vague 'impact' but reacts with anger the moment Dilbert's pointed question has an actual impact on him.
summary: A manager who wants his team to make a bigger splash gets furious when a simple question for clarity actually makes one.
keywords: you'll know it when you see it

title: Trash-Talking Is Only Way to Reach Dilbert

transcript.text: I heard you were trash-talking me behind my back?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Give me a minute to regroup. I wasn't expecting my side of the conversation to go this badly.

situation: A coworker in a blue shirt and lanyard confronts Dilbert, who is looking at his phone, for trash-talking him behind his back. Dilbert calmly explains that it is the only way to get the coworker's attention since he ignores texts, emails and calls. The coworker, caught off guard, asks for a minute to regroup.
punchline: Dilbert spreads rumors deliberately because the coworker only responds to gossip, and the coworker's complaint about the conversation going badly shows he was unprepared for being called out on his own unresponsiveness.
summary: A man angrily accuses Dilbert of badmouthing him, only to be told that gossip is the sole thing that gets his notice.

transcript.text: No, it doesn't! Your ridiculous bumper sticker thinking is not wisdom!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop repeating worn-out sayings as if they actually mean something!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that his idea can't work, and the coworker responds with a series of clichés, claiming Dilbert's objections prove he hit a nerve and is therefore right. Dilbert grows increasingly frustrated as he tries to explain that the sayings aren't wisdom, while the coworker answers with yet another saying.
punchline: The coworker answers every criticism with a canned proverb that treats opposition as proof of being right, which drives Dilbert to scream in frustration.
summary: A smug coworker deflects every objection to his plan by reciting stock phrases, until his critic is reduced to howling.
keywords: methinks thou dost protest too much

title: Remote Rivals Thrive Without Micromanagement

transcript.text: We're losing market share to a company that has a remote workforce.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know. It's baffling.

setting: Conference table in an office meeting
situation: Dilbert and The Boss sit at a table while The Boss looks at his phone. Dilbert notes that a competitor with a remote workforce is taking their market share, then pointedly asks how it's possible without a manager watching employees constantly. The Boss, missing the insult entirely, agrees that it is baffling.
punchline: Dilbert is sarcastically implying that The Boss's constant micromanagement is the problem, but The Boss is too oblivious to realize he is the target of the jab.
summary: A sly dig at a manager's hovering supervision goes straight over his head when a competitor thrives with employees working from home.

title: Numb to Seventy-Five Year Pandemic

situation: Dilbert reads a news item on his phone saying scientists now predict the pandemic will last seventy-five years. He sets the phone down on the desk while Dogbert sits beside him silently. Dilbert then flatly says he feels numb about the news.
punchline: The absurdly long pandemic forecast barely registers because Dilbert, like everyone else, has become emotionally numb after a year of bad pandemic news.
summary: After reading a grim phone headline about an endless pandemic, Dilbert calmly admits that bad news no longer affects him.

title: Engineers Take Destroy Literally

transcript.text: I didn't say anything about violence.

transcript.text: You said "destroy" them. I don't see how that could mean anything else.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: It was just a figure of speech.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're engineers! You can't use figurative speech with us. We take things literally.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, what exactly is it you want us to do with our competitors?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Beat them!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With sticks?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss says the company needs to destroy its competition, and Dilbert objects that he doesn't approve of violence. The Boss says he never mentioned violence, and Dilbert insists that the word 'destroy' can only mean one thing. When asked what he wants them to do instead, the Boss says 'Beat them!' and Dilbert asks if that means with sticks.
punchline: Dilbert, taking engineers' literalism to an absurd extreme, treats every aggressive business metaphor as a call for actual violence, so the Boss can't find any phrase that satisfies him.
summary: A manager's aggressive business slogan gets interpreted by a pedantic engineer as a literal call for violence, and every rephrasing only makes it worse.

title: Estimates Pulled From a Sandwich

situation: Dilbert is reviewing a sheet of numbers from Wally and says they can't be right. Wally replies that they are only estimates. Dilbert then asks where the estimates came from and whether Wally bumped his head on his lunch sandwich, implying the numbers were pulled out of thin air.
punchline: Dilbert delivers an elaborate, vivid insult implying Wally's estimates were literally pulled from his backside, then approves of the crude imagery when Wally worries it was too visual.
summary: A coworker defends dubious figures as mere estimates, and Dilbert responds with a colorful jab about where they must have come from.

title: Performative Social Issue Press Release

The employee asks whether the choice of issues matters and whether to research them, and the boss dismisses both questions, insisting the only goal is to make the company look good.
punchline: The boss treats social causes as pure PR, so any attempt at understanding the issues is seen as missing the point, which is appearance over substance.
summary: A manager wants a press release endorsing popular causes purely for image, and scolds the employee for suggesting any actual research.

punchline: The Boss, desperate to take credit for profits that will happen anyway, adopts a pointless training program that ends up insulting the employees.
summary: A manager hunting for a way to claim credit for inevitable profits gets a mock-serious suggestion that turns into an insulting seminar for his own staff.

situation: An employee on a video call tells his boss that hackers can spy through laptop cameras and microphones. He adds that someone with his skills could do it in minutes without being caught. When the boss asks what he means, the employee says to keep it in mind during his performance review.

summary: A worker slips a thinly disguised surveillance threat into a chat with his manager to sway his upcoming evaluation.

situation: Alice receives a phone call from someone cancelling a scheduled Zoom meeting for the day. She becomes furious because she got up early and put on makeup specifically for the video call. The caller then offers a voice-only call from their car, which only makes her angrier.
punchline: The caller's helpful offer of an audio-only call highlights that the effort Alice put into looking presentable was completely pointless, which enrages her even more.
summary: A woman who dressed up for a video meeting loses her temper when the other party cancels it and suggests a plain voice call instead.

punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out that the company's software upgrades already make products harder to use, so a keyboard with randomly rearranged keys would be no different.

situation: An interviewer candidly tells a job applicant that the position demands hard work and long hours. summary: A frank warning about brutal working conditions earns a job interviewer a fist from the candidate he was trying to be straight with.

summary: A manager outlines a grim multi-year forecast that starts with perfection and spirals into economic ruin and illness.

punchline: The device detects losers by who holds it backward, so the Boss's gleeful 'accurate' pings actually identify him as the loser.
summary: A gadget meant to expose losers turns out to expose whoever is foolish enough to aim it the wrong way around.

title: Dogbert Only Takes Hated Clients

setting: Outdoor path with bushes under a pink sky
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert walk down a path while Dogbert, introduced as a crisis consultant, explains how he chooses clients. punchline: Dogbert deliberately gives ruinous, jail-inducing advice to people he dislikes, and Dilbert cheerfully calls this cynical scheme folksy wisdom.
summary: A consultant dog confesses that his advice lands customers behind bars, which is why he reserves it for people he despises.

setting: Office meeting room or conference table
situation: A vendor's salesman visits Dilbert and says he must sign a nondisclosure agreement before seeing the new product. Dilbert refuses, declares the vendor incompetent for asking, and says he only buys from companies that don't involve lawyers. When the salesman suggests signing without legal review, Dilbert asks whether he looks like an idiot.
punchline: The salesman answers Dilbert's rhetorical question honestly and insultingly, saying Dilbert looks like an idiot over essentially his entire face.
summary: A sales rep gets an unexpectedly candid answer after Dilbert rhetorically challenges him about signing legal paperwork without review.

title: Dilbert Fears Universe's Big Problem

transcript.text: What's it gonna be this time, universe?!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll come back.

situation: Dilbert sits at his desk and worries that having no problems today means the universe is secretly lining up a major one. He gets so worked up that he shouts and shakes his fist at the universe. A coworker holding papers walks up, sees this, and decides to come back later.
punchline: Dilbert's paranoid outburst at the universe makes a coworker retreat awkwardly, so the only 'problem' that shows up is his own odd behavior.
summary: Convinced that a calm day means disaster is coming, a worker yells at fate and scares off a visiting colleague.

title: Alice's Cone of Anger Shields

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Shields holding at 95%.

situation: Alice heads to work determined to avoid any interruptions, so she decides to activate her "cone of anger" to repel anyone who approaches. A coworker walks up to her desk and immediately recoils in pain, shrieking and asking why being near her hurts, while Alice calmly reports the status of her defenses.
punchline: Alice's famous bad temper is treated like a sci-fi force field, and she is pleased that it is working at near-full strength while a coworker suffers.
summary: Determined to be left alone, Alice projects such intense hostility that a colleague is physically pained just standing near her, and she treats it like a successful defense system.

title: Slept Through Mars Trip Entirely

transcript.text: Wake up. I have some bad news about your trip to Mars...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Uuuh?

transcript.speaker: Wally

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why is it still the same day I left?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sounds like a black hole situation.

situation: Wally wakes Asok, who is slumped asleep in a chair, and tells him his trip to Mars is already over because the suspended animation pill knocked him out for the whole round trip. Asok checks his phone and is confused that it is still the same day he left. Wally casually offers a black hole as the explanation.
punchline: Wally breezily blames a black hole for the impossible timeline instead of admitting that Asok simply never went anywhere, a lazy pseudo-scientific excuse for a missed trip.
summary: A coworker rouses a groggy colleague to say a sleeping pill made him doze through an entire Mars journey, then shrugs off the timing mystery with a cosmic explanation.

title: Boss Replaced By Potted Plant

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: The only reason you have a job is so I don't have to talk to employees.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: But I still talk to you every day, so I hired a potted plant to be your new boss.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I feel deeply insulted.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: See? A plant would never feel that way.

situation: The Boss tells an employee that he is only employed so the Boss can avoid talking to other employees. Since the Boss still ends up talking to this employee daily, he announces he has hired a potted plant to be the employee's new boss. When the employee says he feels insulted, the Boss argues a plant would never take offence.
punchline: The Boss is so dismissive of his staff that he replaces himself with a plant and uses the employee's hurt feelings as proof the plant is the better manager.
summary: A manager who loathes talking to his staff swaps himself out for a houseplant and calls it an improvement when the employee objects.

title: CEO Lost Looking for Zoom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Has anyone heard from our CEO since the pandemic started?

transcript.speaker: Voice from off-panel
transcript.text: Not me.

transcript.speaker: Voice from off-panel
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe the virus got him.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Well, it looks like another lonely day of looking for the Zoom button.

setting: Remote work, with Dilbert at his home desk on a video call and the CEO alone at his own desk
situation: Dilbert asks his remote coworkers whether anyone has heard from the CEO since the pandemic began, and the others answer that they haven't. Dilbert guesses the virus got him. The last panel shows the CEO alone at his computer, thinking that he is still searching for the Zoom button.
punchline: The CEO isn't sick or missing; he is so technologically clueless that he still can't find the button to join video calls, so he has been absent for the whole pandemic.
summary: Colleagues wonder whether their absent chief executive fell victim to the virus, but he is simply lost in his computer, unable to work out how to join a video meeting.

title: Tiger Team Literally Eats Members

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As you know, I formed a tiger team to come up with a new product.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It didn't go well. The tiger got hungry and killed everyone else on the team.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You thought tiger teams have real tigers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's poorly named.

situation: The Boss tells his staff in a meeting that he formed a tiger team to develop a new product, but that a real tiger on the team killed everyone else. Dilbert incredulously asks whether he thought tiger teams contain actual tigers. The Boss simply blames the term for being poorly named.
punchline: The Boss took the business jargon 'tiger team' literally and, instead of admitting his mistake, deflects blame onto the name.
summary: A manager who mistook corporate jargon for a literal instruction ended up with a deadly animal on his product team and faults the terminology.

title: Closing Credits End Zoom Calls

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, well, I see the closing credits scrolling by, so we must be done with our Zoom call.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, I guess so. Well, goodbye everyone.

transcript.speaker: Participant (off-screen)
transcript.text: Bye!

transcript.speaker: Participant (off-screen)
transcript.text: Goodbye!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You added closing credits to a Zoom call?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's the only way to get people to leave.

setting: Dilbert's home office during a Zoom call
situation: Dilbert sits at his laptop on a video call and notices closing credits scrolling, announcing that the meeting must be over. The other participants say goodbye and drop off. Dogbert asks if he really added closing credits to the call, and Dilbert says it's the only way to get people to leave.
punchline: Virtual meetings drag on so long that people won't hang up unless the call ends like a movie with rolling credits.
summary: A man gives his video call a movie-style ending so the endless chatter finally stops and everyone logs off.

title: Stealing Credit Shows Management Potential

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's a great chart, Ted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, I made that chart a month ago, and Ted stole it without giving me credit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted has management potential.

setting: Conference room and a hallway or office
situation: In a meeting, the Boss praises a chart that Ted presents. Dilbert objects that he made the chart a month ago and Ted stole it without crediting him. Afterward, the Boss, talking to Catbert, concludes that Ted has management potential.
punchline: Instead of punishing Ted for plagiarizing Dilbert's work, the Boss treats credit-stealing as proof Ted is management material, implying that is how managers rise.
summary: Caught taking another employee's work as his own, a coworker is rewarded with a prediction of a future in management.

title: Ninety-Minute Meeting, Fifteen Productive Minutes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Looks like we are out of time. Thanks for joining me for the full ninety minutes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Seventy-five of which involved trying to make the audio and video work for our remote attendees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least we got in fifteen minutes of quality time.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I wish I hadn't slept through that part.

setting: Conference room during a hybrid meeting
situation: Dilbert wraps up a ninety-minute meeting and points out that most of it was spent getting the audio and video working for remote attendees. He tries to find a silver lining in the fifteen minutes of real discussion. Wally, holding a coffee cup, says he regrets sleeping through that part.
punchline: The only productive part of the long meeting was the one slice Wally slept through, so even the sole value of the meeting was wasted.
summary: A meeting devoured by technical glitches leaves only a sliver of useful discussion, and one attendee dozed through it.

title: Faith Healing for Buggy Software

transcript.text: Yakabloka-wawa-willy-walla-bing-bang.

transcript.speaker: Tech Support Man
transcript.text: Try it now.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: I really hope that didn't wor...

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: Dang.

situation: A bearded support technician tells a coworker with big curly hair that he can fix her software bug by laying his hands on it and praying. He types on her laptop while chanting nonsense words, then tells her to try it. She had been hoping it wouldn't work, but it did.
punchline: The woman is disappointed that the absurd chanting actually fixed the bug, which implies she wanted proof that the technician was a fraud, or that real fixes are never this easy.
summary: A tech fixes a computer glitch with ridiculous mumbo-jumbo while secretly typing, and the skeptical customer is annoyed when it works.

title: Losing Respect For Expert Disagreement

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Every time I hear you disagreeing with the experts, I lose a little respect for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying you once had respect for me?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop being happy about my criticisms!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why can't I enjoy the attention?

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Alice tells Dilbert that his habit of disagreeing with the experts is costing him her respect. Dilbert, looking at his phone, calmly replies by asking if she ever respected him at all. Alice gets angry that he seems pleased by her criticism, and he says he likes the attention.
punchline: Dilbert turns Alice's insult into a compliment by treating her criticism as proof that she once respected him and now pays attention to him, which infuriates her.
summary: A scolding from a coworker backfires when the target takes it as flattery and cheerfully soaks up the attention.

transcript.text: If you're talking about the engineers, no one will notice any difference.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Fair point.

setting: The Boss's office, at his desk
situation: The Boss asks Catbert, the evil HR director, whether he has rounded up all the remote workers and put them in boxes. Catbert says some have turned feral and can't be reintegrated into society. The Boss points out that if he means the engineers, nobody will notice any difference, and Catbert agrees.
punchline: Engineers are already so socially awkward and wild that working remotely makes no visible difference to how they behave.
summary: After a long stretch of working from home, the boss and HR chief discuss whether the staff have gone wild, only to conclude the technical team was always that way.

title: Asking Permission to Use Insulting Nickname

setting: Dilbert's desk, during a phone or video call
situation: Dilbert phones Ted and politely asks whether he should use Ted's real name or his office nickname. He explains that he is asking only because the nickname is insulting. Ted, who is unaware he has a nickname, reacts with surprise, and Dilbert realizes he has blundered.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt at courtesy backfires because he reveals to Ted that coworkers have an insulting nickname for him that Ted never knew about.
summary: A well-meant question about which name to use accidentally exposes a secret insult behind someone's back.

summary: A colleague offers an optional, meaningless storytelling session after a meeting, and the office's laziest employee happily signs up.

transcript.text: He was too good for us.

situation: Dilbert and a coworker are interviewing a job candidate and explain that applicants must sign a non-disclosure agreement before interviewing. The candidate announces that the NDA request was itself the interview, declares the company failed it, and storms off. The coworker then remarks to Dilbert that the candidate was too good for them.
punchline: The company's own secrecy requirement became the reason a candidate rejected them, and the coworker's resigned remark that the applicant was 'too good for us' shows how low their own standards have sunk.
summary: A job candidate walks out on a company after being asked to sign a confidentiality form, leaving the interviewers to shrug it off as his loss of standards being higher than theirs.

punchline: The executive with a meaningless, undefined title proves his worth by speaking in meaningless, random words, implying that senior titles can be nonsensical and nobody notices.
summary: A newly announced executive with a hopelessly vague job gives a speech made entirely of random words.

punchline: Dogbert's 'acquisition' of Greenland is really a military conquest paid for with cryptocurrency, dwarfing Dilbert's modest stock gain with absurd, villainous ambition.
summary: While Dilbert brags about a tiny stock gain, Dogbert casually reveals he turned his crypto fortune into a hired army to seize an entire territory.

transcript.text: That actually works?

situation: Dilbert is dancing happily at work, and his manager walks over holding a coffee and suspiciously asks whether he is embezzling. Dilbert says he is simply feeling high morale and engagement, as management trained him to. The manager is surprised the training works, and Dilbert says it did until the boss's accusation spoiled it.
punchline: Management's morale and engagement initiatives only work until the manager reveals he never believed in them by treating a happy employee as a suspect.
summary: A boss assumes a cheerful worker must be a criminal, and the worker retorts that the boss's own suspicion has just wrecked the contentment he was supposedly trained to feel.

title: Obvious Energy Costs, Irrelevant Anyway

transcript.text: Well, for one thing, it's obvious to any idiot. Secondly, it isn't related to our discussion.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Those are fairly good reasons.

situation: At a meeting table, a coworker asks Dilbert why he won't concede that adding servers will raise energy costs. Dilbert replies that the fact is too obvious to need admitting and that it is off-topic for the discussion. The coworker accepts these as fairly good reasons.
punchline: Dilbert's two reasons for not admitting the point are that it is blindingly obvious and irrelevant, which makes the coworker's demand sound silly, and the coworker concedes.
summary: A meeting participant presses Dilbert to state something self-evident, and Dilbert's dismissive justification is accepted with a shrug.

title: Dilbert Admires His Own Slide Deck

transcript.text: It's a lot better than you'd think.

setting: Dilbert's home, living room with a blue couch
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert, who is sitting on the couch, that he spent half an hour admiring a slide deck he made the day before, and that he plans to go back for more after drinking some water. Dogbert bluntly asks what it is like to have no friends and no purpose, and Dilbert calmly says it is better than expected.
punchline: Dilbert's pride in a mere slide deck exposes a sad, solitary life, yet he cheerfully admits that having no friends or purpose is actually pretty comfortable.
summary: A man who lovingly gazes at his own presentation for half an hour is asked about his empty life and happily reports that it suits him fine.

title: It's Turtles All the Way Down

transcript.text: If everything I say confuses you, consider the possibility the problem isn't on my end.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What does that even mean?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Looks like it's turtles all the way down with you.

situation: A coworker in a purple shirt grows frustrated because he cannot follow anything Dilbert says. Dilbert calmly suggests the confusion may be the coworker's own problem, and when the coworker asks what that means, Dilbert replies with a turtles-all-the-way-down remark.
punchline: Dilbert's insult is itself baffling, so the coworker's confusion over it confirms Dilbert's point, and the 'turtles all the way down' line implies the man's lack of understanding is endless.
summary: A baffled colleague demands clarity, and Dilbert answers with a cryptic jab that proves his own point about who is doing the misunderstanding.

title: Garbage Collectors Work From Home

transcript.speaker: Customer Service Rep

setting: Dilbert's desk at home, on a phone call with a service company's call center
situation: Dilbert phones his waste-collection company to complain that his garbage hasn't been picked up in three weeks. The customer service rep explains that the garbage collectors are now working from home. Dilbert sarcastically asks if he should deliver his garbage to their homes, and the rep cheerfully agrees.
punchline: Garbage collection is an inherently on-site job, so applying work-from-home policy to it is absurd, and the indifferent rep happily offers a ridiculous solution that shifts the burden to the customer.
summary: A customer is told his trash is piling up because the collectors have gone remote, and the company's answer is to haul it to them himself.

title: Firing Paperwork Deters The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you trying to inoculate me against firing you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear it feels like being buried alive.

situation: Dilbert stands holding a coffee cup in front of the seated Boss and muses about how much paperwork firing an employee requires. He dramatically describes it as soul-smothering, and the Boss realizes Dilbert is trying to discourage him from firing him. Dilbert doubles down by saying the process feels like being buried alive.
punchline: Dilbert tries to protect his job by convincing his boss that the bureaucracy of firing someone is so awful that it's not worth the trouble.
summary: An employee tries to talk his manager out of ever dismissing him by painting the termination paperwork as a soul-crushing ordeal.

situation: The Boss complains to Catbert, the evil HR director, that he can't annoy remote workers effectively. Catbert suggests he start barging uninvited into their Zoom meetings. The Boss does so, cheerfully announcing himself, while Dilbert, watching on his laptop, buries his face in his hands in despair.
punchline: Catbert's suggestion is a perfectly effective way to torment remote employees, as shown by Dilbert's wish for death when the Boss crashes his video call yet again.
summary: Seeking ways to pester home-based staff, the boss takes a malicious feline's tip to gatecrash video calls, driving an employee to despair.

title: Dogbert's Unqualified Trucker Driving School

setting: Dilbert's office, then a classroom of trucking students
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he is opening a driving school for truckers. Dilbert points out that Dogbert can't drive a big rig, and Dogbert replies that his students can't either. He then teaches a class of eager students using completely made-up technical jargon.
punchline: Dogbert's school works because his students are too ignorant to notice that his instructions are nonsense, so his own lack of expertise doesn't matter.
summary: A scheming dog launches a trucking school despite knowing nothing about trucks, confident that his clueless students will never spot the gibberish he teaches.

title: Office Mandate Avoids Family Time

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: The employees were happier and more productive when they were working remotely.

transcript.text: So... tell me again why we all need to come to the office?
