transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Okay. I can respect that.

situation: A coworker with a coffee cup points out that employees were happier and more productive working remotely, then asks why everyone must return to the office. The manager answers that the real reason is so he can spend less time with his family, and she accepts that reasoning.
punchline: The return-to-office mandate has nothing to do with business benefits; the manager simply wants to escape his family, and the coworker finds that more understandable than any corporate justification.
summary: Pressed on why staff must leave remote work, a manager admits his own reason is avoiding his household, and the questioner shrugs and accepts it.

title: Suppressing a Cough Looks Worse

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, no... I feel a non-covid cough coming on.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must... control it... to avoid... looking infected.

transcript.speaker: Bystander
transcript.text: What's up with him?

transcript.speaker: Bystander
transcript.text: He looks infected.

situation: Dilbert, wearing a face mask, feels a cough coming on and worries it will make people think he has covid. He tries to suppress it, shaking and convulsing, and ends up falling over on the sidewalk. Two masked passersby watch and conclude he looks infected.
punchline: Dilbert's frantic effort to hide a harmless cough makes him look far more sick than simply coughing would have.
summary: A masked man's desperate attempt to hold back an ordinary cough turns into a bizarre fit that convinces onlookers he is contagious.

title: Sarcasm Or Sincere Dumb Idea

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was your suggestion meant to be sarcasm, or are you so dumb you think it is a good idea?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I think it's a good idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have no further questions.

setting: Office meeting table with coffee cups
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker whether his suggestion was meant as sarcasm or whether he sincerely believes it is a good idea. The coworker enthusiastically gives a thumbs up and says he thinks it's a good idea. Dilbert, now satisfied that the idea really is stupid, says he has nothing more to ask and drinks his coffee.
punchline: The coworker's sincere confidence confirms the worst possibility, that he is genuinely dumb enough to think the bad idea is good, leaving Dilbert with nothing left to ask.
summary: A blunt question about whether a proposal was a joke or a sincere blunder gets the most damning possible answer.

title: Choose Your Poison: Focus or Quality

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you prefer that I focus on one of my projects at the expense of all the others...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...or should I spread my attention across all of my projects and do low-quality work on all of them?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And your answer cannot involve magic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can I hear the choices again?

setting: Office, with a brief exterior shot of an office building
situation: Dilbert asks his boss to choose between two bad options for handling his overloaded project list: focus on one project and neglect the rest, or spread his effort thin and produce poor work on all of them. He adds that the boss cannot pick a magical solution. The boss, unable to grasp the dilemma, asks to hear the choices again.
punchline: The boss is so unwilling or unable to accept the trade-off between workload and quality that he can't even process the choices, forcing Dilbert to repeat the problem.
summary: Dilbert lays out an impossible tradeoff to his boss about too many projects, and the boss responds by asking him to start over.

title: Frequent Victims Club Loyalty Program

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Would you like to join our frequent victims club?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I just want to buy this beverage.

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: You could save a dollar if you join now. It only takes a minute.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want you tracking my purchases and selling my data.

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: If you don't sign up, my colleagues and I will pester you to do it every time you try to buy something.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll take my business elsewhere!

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: No, you won't.

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Because other stores are just as bad as we are.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am not a victim!

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Tell that to the customer survey I'm about to pester you into doing.

setting: Checkout counter of a retail store
situation: A store cashier repeatedly pushes Dilbert to join a loyalty program called the frequent victims club while he just wants to buy a beverage. Dilbert objects that the store would track his purchases and sell his data, and the cashier admits they will keep pestering him and that every other store is equally bad. The cashier then hits him with a customer survey request as well.
punchline: The store openly admits its loyalty program exploits customers' data and that customers have no alternative, then piles on a survey request, proving Dilbert is exactly the victim he denies being.
summary: A shopper trying to buy a drink is hounded by a cashier to join a data-harvesting rewards club and then a survey, with the cashier cheerfully admitting that every competitor does the same.

title: Cartoonist Creator Is In It For Money

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I have a report that you were watching a cartoonist doing a live stream when you should have been working.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm practicing my religion. I believe a cartoonist is our creator, and reality is some kind of simulation.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Does the creator love us?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, he's in it for the money.

situation: A coworker with dark pointed hair confronts Dilbert about watching a cartoonist's live stream during work hours. Dilbert claims he was practicing his religion, which holds that a cartoonist created us and reality is a simulation. The coworker asks if the creator loves us, and Dilbert deflates the idea.
punchline: Dilbert's cynical answer reveals that the cartoonist-creator is motivated by profit rather than love, a self-referential jab at the strip's own creator.
summary: Caught slacking off to watch an artist's online broadcast, Dilbert excuses it as worship of a cartoonist deity who made us purely for profit.

title: Casual Day for Remote Workers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tomorrow is casual day for remote workers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Most of you already dress like roadkill, but see if you can take it down another level.

transcript.speaker: Remote Worker (off-screen)
transcript.text: Why are you doing this to us?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hear it builds morale.

setting: Video call between a manager's desk and remote employees' laptops
situation: The Boss addresses his remote staff over a video call and announces a casual day for remote workers. He then insults them by saying they already dress like roadkill and tells them to dress even worse. When an employee asks why he is doing this, he says he has heard it builds morale.
punchline: The Boss insults his staff's appearance and orders them to dress worse, then justifies the pointless exercise by claiming it boosts morale, which it clearly won't.
summary: A manager orders his work-from-home staff to look even scruffier for a pointless casual day, insisting without evidence that this lifts spirits.

title: Two Theories of Personal Problems

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker
transcript.text: All of my problems are caused by people intentionally being jerks to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All of my problems are caused by insecure people who interpret every situation in the worst possible way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker
transcript.text: Was that about me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would it matter?

setting: Office break area table with coffee cups
situation: A coworker with a black bob haircut declares that everyone else is deliberately being a jerk to her. Dilbert, looking at his phone, replies with his own theory that insecure people interpret everything in the worst way. She immediately asks if that was about her, and he deflects.
punchline: Her instant assumption that his comment was aimed at her proves his point about insecure people reading the worst into everything.
summary: A woman blames her troubles on deliberate meanness, and when Dilbert describes people who assume the worst, she promptly takes it personally.

title: Banning Politics Because Employees Are Brainwashed

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our CEO has banned political talk on all employee messaging platforms.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's just as well because you're all brainwashed and underinformed, so your opinions are not worth the spittle that comes with them.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: We hope this change will improve internal harmony.

setting: Conference room, with an exterior shot of the office building in the last panel
situation: Catbert, acting as the HR voice, announces at a meeting that the CEO has banned political talk on employee messaging platforms. He then insults the employees, calling them brainwashed and underinformed. A final caption shows the office building and states the hope that the change will improve internal harmony.
punchline: The announcement of a policy meant to promote harmony is delivered with a blunt insult, which undercuts the stated goal and shows how little respect management has for employees' opinions.
summary: HR informs the staff that political chatter is now off-limits at work, then insults their intelligence while claiming the rule will bring everyone closer together.

title: Go Cheap on Rocket Reentry

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO wants to join the billionaire space club. He asked us to build him a rocket.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We might need to cut some corners on the rocket design, for budget reasons.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Any ideas?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd go cheap on reentry.

situation: The Boss tells his team that the CEO wants to join the billionaire space club and has asked them to build him a rocket. He warns that corners will have to be cut for budget reasons and asks for ideas. Dilbert suggests skimping on the reentry part of the design.
punchline: Dilbert is quietly suggesting the CEO's rocket be built so that its return to Earth is deadly, since a cheap reentry system would likely kill him.
summary: Told to build a budget-friendly rocket for the boss of the company, an engineer proposes the one cost-saving measure that would be fatal to the passenger.

title: Autobiography Help Costs Royalties

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm writing my autobiography, and I wondered if you could take a look at the first three chapters.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Sure! What percentage of the royalties do I get for doing that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um...

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Is there a chapter about how to take advantage of your subordinates?

situation: The boss asks a subordinate to review the first three chapters of his autobiography. The employee cheerfully agrees but asks what share of the royalties she will receive for the work. When the boss hesitates, she asks whether his book includes a chapter on exploiting subordinates.
punchline: The employee points out that the boss's request for free work is itself an example of taking advantage of subordinates, which his book would presumably teach.
summary: A manager wants free editing help on his memoir, and his employee turns the request into a dig at his exploitative habits.

title: Idiots Are the Target Market

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our researchers have invented a technology that turns idiots into smart people.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Only an idiot would believe that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I prefer calling them the "target market."

situation: Dilbert announces at a meeting that researchers have invented a technology that turns idiots into smart people. Wally scoffs that only an idiot would believe such a claim. Dogbert, seated at the table, says he would rather call those gullible people the target market.
punchline: Dogbert cynically points out that the idiots who would believe the miracle technology are exactly the customers the product would be sold to.
summary: A boast about a brain-boosting invention is met with the observation that the gullible folks who'd buy it are the ideal customers.

title: He Said You'd Say That

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I just talked to Ted, and he says your project plan is not feasible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think you mean he mischaracterized my plan and then stabbed me in the back when I wasn't there to defend it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: He said you'd say that.

setting: Office, over a video call on a laptop
situation: A coworker (Asok, on a video call) tells Dilbert that Ted claims Dilbert's project plan is not feasible. Dilbert replies that Ted misrepresented the plan and backstabbed him behind his back. The coworker answers that Ted predicted this exact response.
punchline: Ted has already anticipated and pre-empted Dilbert's defense, so any rebuttal can be dismissed as just what a guilty party would say, making the backstabbing unanswerable.
summary: A colleague relays a rival's criticism of Dilbert's plan and learns the rival has already discredited Dilbert's objection in advance.

title: Consultant Stayed For The Donut

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: The reason I'm here is to help you look at the big picture.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll need a fact-check on that. I think you stayed over from the last meeting to finish your donut.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: It seems you beat me to the big picture.

situation: A bald consultant in a green shirt tells the meeting attendees he is there to help them see the big picture. Dilbert doubts this, pointing out that the consultant simply lingered after the previous meeting to finish his donut, which sits on the table in front of him. The consultant concedes that Dilbert has grasped the big picture before he did.
punchline: Dilbert sees through the consultant's lofty pretext and reveals the real reason he is in the room is a leftover donut, and the consultant sheepishly admits it.
summary: A consultant who claims to offer strategic insight is caught having hung around merely to finish his pastry.

title: They Said It Couldn't Be Done

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They said it couldn't be done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But you did it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, it turns out they're usually right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who are "they," and why am I just learning this?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You sound like me last week.

situation: Wally walks up to the Boss holding a coffee mug and announces that people said something couldn't be done. The Boss assumes Wally defied the doubters, but Wally admits the doubters were right. The Boss reacts with confusion and annoyance at only now hearing this, and Wally notes that the Boss sounds just as he did a week earlier.
punchline: The clichéd 'they said it couldn't be done' triumph story is deflated when Wally admits the naysayers were simply correct, and he only learned this himself recently.
summary: A lazy employee reveals that the conventional wisdom about impossible tasks usually holds true, leaving his boss as surprised as he once was.
keywords: they said it couldn't be done

title: Karen Demands Dilbert Be Fired

transcript.speaker: Karen
transcript.text: Dilbert called me "Karen." You need to fire him immediately.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe he called you Karen because that's your actual name.

transcript.speaker: Karen
transcript.text: I thought about that, but it doesn't fit my low opinion of him.

situation: A woman named Karen storms into the Boss's office and demands that he fire Dilbert for calling her "Karen." The Boss points out that it is her actual name. She admits she considered that, but dismisses it because it doesn't fit her low opinion of Dilbert.
punchline: Karen would rather assume Dilbert meant the insult than accept the innocent explanation that it is simply her name, because she already dislikes him.
summary: A coworker named Karen wants someone fired for using her own name, and she rejects the obvious explanation because it conflicts with how little she thinks of him.

title: Lazy Efficiency and Useless Assignments

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They say the laziest employees are the best because they know how to be efficient.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't think I get enough credit for all of my efficiency.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Efficiency only matters if you are doing something useful.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're the one who gives me my assignments.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't ask you to do anything useful because you are too lazy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are the useful projects generally harder than the useless ones?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then I'd say the system is working.

situation: Wally tells the Boss that lazy employees are the most efficient and that he deserves credit for it. The Boss replies that efficiency only counts on useful work, but admits he only gives Wally useless assignments because Wally is lazy. Wally concludes that since useful projects are harder, the arrangement suits everyone.
punchline: Wally's laziness and the Boss's habit of assigning him only pointless work reinforce each other, so Wally can claim the broken system is working perfectly for him.
summary: A slacker and his manager discover that dodging hard, worthwhile tasks is exactly how their arrangement is meant to function.

title: Cake for a Disliked Coworker

transcript.text: I don't like Ted.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No one does. We didn't invite him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why are we having an event for him?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We like cake?

setting: Office cubicle area (middle panel shows an office building exterior)
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert that the office is having cake in the conference room for Ted's birthday. Dilbert says he doesn't like Ted, and Wally replies that nobody does and Ted wasn't even invited. When Dilbert asks why the event is happening at all, Wally admits it's simply because they like cake.
punchline: The office birthday celebration has nothing to do with the honoree; coworkers will hold a party for someone they dislike and exclude him, purely as an excuse to eat cake.
summary: Coworkers throw an office birthday party for a man nobody likes and didn't invite, just so they can enjoy free dessert.

title: Video Call Love Declaration Mix-Up

transcript.speaker: Off-screen voice
transcript.text: I love you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You do?

transcript.speaker: Off-screen voice
transcript.text: No, not you. I was talking to my wife, who is off camera.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one loves you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This was my longest relation-ship.

setting: Dilbert's home, sitting in a chair with a laptop during a video call
situation: During a video call, the Boss's voice says 'I love you' and Dilbert, surprised, asks 'You do?' The Boss clarifies he was speaking to his wife off camera. Dilbert then tells the Boss that no one loves him, and the Boss replies that this was his longest relationship.
punchline: The Boss's longest relationship is with Dilbert, a coworker who merely tolerates him, which pathetically underlines how unloved and lonely he is.
summary: A boss's misdirected affection on a video call reveals that his work connection with an employee is the closest relationship he has ever had.

title: Profiting From Pandemic Without Guilt

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks to the pandemic, our sales are at an all-time high.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shouldn't we feel guilty for profiting from a deadly virus?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think if we were going to feel that, it would have kicked in by now.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that pandemic-driven demand has pushed sales to a record high. Dilbert asks whether the company should feel guilty about profiting from a deadly virus. The Boss calmly replies that any guilt would have shown up already.
punchline: The Boss treats his own lack of conscience as proof that guilt isn't warranted, openly admitting the company is incapable of feeling bad about profiting from a tragedy.
summary: A manager cheerfully shrugs off the moral question of cashing in on a global health crisis by noting that his remorse is evidently absent.

title: Video Call Insults Escalate Quickly

transcript.speaker: Caller (via laptop)
transcript.text: What's that behind you on the shelf? Can't you make your background more attractive?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we're being that way, who cuts your hair? Your lawn mower?

transcript.speaker: Caller (via laptop)
transcript.text: Did your gym go out of business?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I already miss our last shred of human decency.

setting: Dilbert's home workspace during a video call
situation: Dilbert is on a video call at his laptop when the person on the other end criticizes the shelf visible in his background. Dilbert retaliates by mocking the caller's haircut, who then jabs at Dilbert's physique. Dilbert concludes that the exchange has destroyed their civility.
punchline: Once a petty criticism of his background is answered in kind, the two trade increasingly personal insults, and Dilbert sarcastically laments how quickly basic decency was lost.
summary: A nitpicky comment about a tacky backdrop on a remote meeting spirals into a swapping of grooming and fitness barbs.

title: Remote Work Ends Dilbert's Mating Odds

transcript.text: Your best chance of reproduction has always been to wear down a co-worker over several years.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We should have a goodbye party for your genes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe next time we could walk and not talk.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe.

setting: Grassy outdoor field where Dilbert and Dogbert are on a walk
situation: While out walking, Dogbert tells Dilbert that working from home has destroyed his chances of meeting a mate at work. He adds that dating apps won't help because they depend on looks, and that Dilbert's only hope was always to slowly wear down a co-worker. Dilbert, sitting glumly on a rock, suggests they walk without talking next time.
punchline: Dogbert insults Dilbert's looks and love life so thoroughly that he proposes a goodbye party for Dilbert's genes, leaving Dilbert wishing for a silent walk.
summary: A stroll turns into a brutal dissection of Dilbert's hopeless romantic prospects now that the office is no longer available as a hunting ground.

transcript.text: It's not fair.

transcript.text: You already said that.

transcript.text: You should do something to make it more fair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why?

situation: Dilbert complains to his boss by video call that Alice gets all the best projects. The boss keeps asking what his point is, and Dilbert can only repeat that it's not fair. When Dilbert asks the boss to fix it because it's unfair, the boss asks if he bumped his head.
punchline: The boss treats fairness as a meaningless argument in the workplace and suggests that anyone who expects it must have suffered a head injury.
summary: An employee appeals to fairness to get better assignments, but his manager dismisses the idea as something only a concussion could explain.

title: Spot the Interruption Pattern

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Dilbert is always interrupting me because I'm a woman.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe he doesn't interrupt me because I make sense when I talk.

transcript.text: Whereas you're more of a babbling nincompoop and a notorious ruiner of meetings.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well, I certainly don't know where you...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let's head back now.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You interrupted me!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Try to spot the pattern.

situation: Two women walk together through the office while a coworker complains that Dilbert always interrupts her because she is a woman. Alice says Dilbert doesn't interrupt her, and the coworker insists that makes no sense. Alice replies that it's because she makes sense when she talks, then insults the coworker as a babbling nincompoop and meeting-ruiner, and finally interrupts her.
punchline: The coworker's real problem is that she babbles and is hard to listen to, not her gender, and Alice drives it home by interrupting her and telling her to spot the pattern.
summary: Alice blames a coworker's rambling, rather than sexism, for why people cut her off, then proves the point by cutting her off herself.

title: Zoom Lunch Meeting Etiquette Rules

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If you chew louder than a beaver making a dam out of bubble wrap, please turn off your microphone.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And if you are an ugly eater. . .

transcript.speaker: Laptop
transcript.text: We get it. Video off.

setting: Alice's home workspace, at a desk with a laptop during a video call
situation: Alice hosts the company's first Zoom lunch meeting and sets ground rules for the participants. She tells noisy chewers to mute their microphones, then starts to add that ugly eaters should do something too. The laptop cuts in with the voice of the attendees, saying they get it and will turn their video off.
punchline: Alice's pointed etiquette rules make it clear that everyone's eating is disgusting, so the participants hastily agree to hide from view.
summary: A host's blunt warnings about loud and unsightly chewing send her virtual lunch guests scrambling to switch off their mics and cameras.

title: Sleeping Wally Yoga Pose

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A yoga mat? When did you get into yoga?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was right after I convinced our Pointy-Haired Boss that there is a yoga position called "Sleeping Wally."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How long can you hold the pose?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My record is sixteen hours.

situation: Wally is carrying a rolled-up yoga mat and a coffee cup, and Dilbert asks when he got into yoga. Wally explains he tricked the Boss into believing that 'Sleeping Wally' is a real yoga position, which lets him nap at work. Dilbert asks how long he can hold the pose and Wally proudly reports sixteen hours.
punchline: Wally has disguised his habitual sleeping on the job as a yoga pose, and his 'record' is simply a very long sleep.
summary: Wally passes off his workplace napping as a legitimate yoga practice by fooling the boss with an invented pose.

title: Trick Employees Into Working Hard

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You've tried rewarding good performance and punishing bad.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But have you tried tricking employees into working hard?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. Can you teach me?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Remember, hard work is its own reward.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Is it?

situation: Catbert, acting as a management consultant, tells the Boss that rewarding good work and punishing bad work is the conventional approach, then offers to teach him how to trick employees into working hard. The Boss eagerly agrees, and Catbert then tells an employee that hard work is its own reward, which the employee doubts.
punchline: The trick is simply convincing employees that hard work is its own reward, a cheap way for management to avoid paying for it, and the skeptical employee sees through it.
summary: A scheming feline advisor shows management that the cheapest motivation is persuading staff that effort needs no payment.
keywords: hard work is its own reward

title: Vacationing in Your Head at Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Asok, there are two kinds of employees. One kind works hard and hopes for the best.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The other kind learns how to take vacations in his head while pretending to work.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Where are you right now?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm sipping coffee in a fjord.

situation: Wally walks with Asok, both holding coffee cups, and lectures him about the two types of employees: those who work hard and hope for the best, and those who mentally vacation while appearing to work. When Asok asks where Wally is mentally right now, Wally says he is sipping coffee in a fjord.
punchline: Wally is demonstrating the lazy approach in real time, mentally vacationing in a Norwegian fjord even while giving career advice.
summary: Wally coaches a young colleague on slacking off by daydreaming, then reveals he is currently doing exactly that.

transcript.text: Hmm, yes. I've heard about supply chain issues on the news.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you really have supply chain issues?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I might if I ever start the project.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Wally tells the group that his project is six months late because of pandemic-related supply chain problems. The Boss accepts this because he has heard about supply chain issues on the news. Dilbert asks whether Wally actually has such problems, and Wally admits he hasn't even started the project yet.
punchline: Wally uses a popular news-friendly excuse to explain delays on a project he never began, and the gullible Boss accepts it without question.
summary: A lazy employee hides behind a trendy excuse for his late work, which turns out to be a cover for never having started it.

transcript.text: I sometimes change my opinions when the facts change. How do you play it?

transcript.speaker: Laptop
transcript.text: Now you're moving the goalposts.

setting: Dilbert's desk, apparently on a video call via laptop
situation: Dilbert tells someone on a laptop video call that the project should be put on hold. The voice on the laptop laughs and points out that this contradicts what Dilbert said the previous week. Dilbert replies that he changes his opinions when facts change and asks how the other person handles it, and the voice accuses him of moving the goalposts.
punchline: Dilbert's reasonable defense of updating his views on new facts is dismissed by his critic with a sports cliché, showing that the critic reflexively attacks any change of position rather than engaging with the facts.
summary: A man defends reversing his stance on a project, only to have his remote colleague brush off his reasoning as a dishonest tactic.

title: Remote Work Was Never Your Idea

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Looks like my idea of remote work is being implemented by management all over the world.

transcript.text: I don't think that was "your idea" so much as totally obvious to every thinking person.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, maybe. But would they have implemented it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to talk to smart people now.

situation: The Boss, looking at his phone, boasts that his idea of remote work is being adopted by managers worldwide. Dilbert, holding a coffee cup, points out that it was simply obvious to anyone who thinks. When the Boss argues that obvious ideas still need someone to implement them, Dilbert walks away to find smarter conversation.
punchline: Dilbert implies the Boss is not smart, leaving him to go talk to intelligent people instead of someone who claims credit for the obvious.
summary: A boss takes credit for the global shift to working from home, and an unimpressed employee dismisses both the claim and the boss's intelligence.

title: Experts Only Know Old Ideas

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every expert in the world says your idea can't work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Experts only know about old ideas. If they knew about future ones, they would be entrepreneurs, not experts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, my entire worldview just collapsed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert, while holding a sheet of paper, that every expert says Dilbert's idea cannot work. Dilbert replies that experts only understand existing ideas, otherwise they would be entrepreneurs. The Boss is stunned, saying his worldview has collapsed, and Dilbert apologizes.
punchline: Dilbert's logic that experts only know the past is so disarming that it shatters the Boss's deference to expert opinion, leaving Dilbert mildly apologetic for the collateral damage.
summary: Faced with a manager citing unanimous expert doubt, an engineer argues that authorities only understand yesterday's thinking and accidentally topples his boss's whole outlook.

title: Boss Wins Meeting, Presenter Quits

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it a coincidence that the only part of your presentation I understand is also clearly wrong?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Well, you caught me. I'm actually a fraud. I offer my resignation, effective immediately. Goodbye.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is the first time I ever won a meeting. I have to say, it feels good.

situation: A presenter shows a chart on a whiteboard while the Boss challenges him, saying the only part he understood was wrong. The presenter dramatically confesses to being a fraud, resigns on the spot and throws his marker as he leaves. The Boss, sitting with Dilbert and Alice, is pleased to have finally won a meeting.
punchline: The Boss's accidental, clueless challenge is mistaken for a brilliant catch, and he gleefully takes credit for a victory that came purely from the presenter's overreaction.
summary: A presenter responds to a bewildered question by confessing fraud and quitting, handing the baffled manager his first-ever meeting triumph.

title: Lying Has Five-to-One ROI

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: I compared the R.O.I. for lying versus telling the truth.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: I regret to inform you that lying has a five-to-one advantage.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Is that true?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: I won't be taking questions.

situation: A bespectacled employee in a green shirt presents a slide comparing the return on investment of lying versus telling the truth. He announces that lying wins by five to one. When an audience member asks if that is true, he refuses to take questions.
punchline: By dodging the question about whether his claim is true, the presenter shows that he is actually lying, which proves his own conclusion about the advantage of dishonesty.
summary: A presenter's analysis concludes that dishonesty pays off handsomely, then he dodges scrutiny of his own findings in a way that quietly confirms them.

title: Wally's Strong Finisher Excuse

transcript.text: Wally, do you have a minute to talk about your total lack of accomplishments?

transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I just had the best idea of my career, and your interruption made me forget it!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But no accomplishments until now?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm a strong finisher.

situation: The Boss approaches Wally at his laptop to discuss his complete lack of accomplishments. Wally reacts with exaggerated alarm, claiming the interruption made him forget the best idea of his career. When the Boss points out he has accomplished nothing until now, Wally claims he is a strong finisher.
punchline: Wally deflects criticism of his lack of output by blaming the interruption for a supposedly brilliant lost idea, then excuses his history of doing nothing by calling himself a strong finisher.
summary: Wally dodges a performance critique by blaming his boss for scaring away a great idea and then boasting about finishing strong.

title: Canceled Project, Awkward High-Five

transcript.text: I'm happy to report that I met all of my deadlines before you canceled my project for no good reason.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In that one moment, you transformed my meaningful work into a tedious slog toward oblivion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And now I'm left to rot in this meeting.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I never know the right time for a high-five.

situation: Seated at a meeting table, Dilbert addresses a coworker who canceled his project even though he met every deadline. He explains that the cancellation turned his meaningful work into a pointless slog and left him stuck in a dull meeting. The coworker responds by raising a hand, wondering aloud if now is the time for a high-five.
punchline: The person who just destroyed Dilbert's worthwhile project responds with obliviously cheerful pride, wanting a high-five instead of acknowledging the harm.
summary: A worker tells off the colleague who killed his on-schedule project, only to be met with a clueless request for celebration.

title: Asok Becomes Co-CEO Via Diversity

transcript.text: I mentioned to the board of directors that there has never been any diversity in the CEO position, so they made me co-CEO.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I didn't even ask for the job. I just made an observation, and they panicked.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How's it feel to be my peer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It hurts all over!

situation: Asok tells a coworker that he pointed out the lack of diversity among CEOs to the board, and they promptly made him co-CEO. He then asks the Boss, now his equal, how it feels to be his peer, and the Boss reacts in visible agony.
punchline: Asok got promoted to the Boss's level simply by pointing out a diversity gap, and the Boss is physically pained by having to treat his lowly subordinate as an equal.
summary: A junior employee talks his way into a top executive title by highlighting a diversity gap, much to his former boss's distress.

title: Alice Sabotages Dilbert, Gets Praised

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try to be more like Alice. She gets things done.

setting: Conference room during a weekly status meeting
situation: At a meeting, Alice reports that she reorganized the lab and threw out all the old equipment. Dilbert then says he got nothing done because someone hid his cables and threw away his prototype. The Boss, oblivious to the connection, tells Dilbert to be more like Alice because she gets things done.
punchline: Alice's "accomplishment" is the very thing that sabotaged Dilbert's work, yet the clueless boss rewards her activity and criticizes Dilbert's lack of results.
summary: A coworker's tidy-up wrecks a colleague's project, but the manager only notices who looks productive.

title: Planning To Be Extra Early

transcript.speaker: Coworker with topknot
transcript.text: If you plan to be on time, you are planning to fail.

transcript.speaker: Coworker with topknot
transcript.text: Plan to be ten minutes early, so you will still be on time if something comes up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I plan to be fifteen minutes early because I'm better than you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker with topknot
transcript.text: Stop it.

setting: Office conference table, with coffee cups
situation: A coworker with a topknot hairstyle lectures Dilbert that planning to arrive exactly on time guarantees failure, and recommends arriving ten minutes early as a buffer. Dilbert responds by claiming he plans to arrive fifteen minutes early. The coworker, annoyed, tells him to stop.
punchline: Dilbert turns the coworker's punctuality advice into a one-upmanship contest, smugly boasting he is better because he will be even earlier, which irritates the lecturer.
summary: A smug lesson about arriving early gets trumped when Dilbert brags that he will arrive even earlier.

title: Making Up Data Improves Life 27.4%

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My life has been so much better since I started making up my own data for everything.

transcript.text: How much better?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wow! I should try that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You'll love it.

situation: A coworker holding a coffee cup tells a colleague at her desk that his life has improved since he began fabricating his own data for everything. When she asks how much, he gives a suspiciously precise figure of 27.4%, and she decides she should try it too.
punchline: The precise-sounding 27.4% improvement is itself made-up data, proving the claim by demonstrating it, and showing how easily fake statistics are accepted as credible.
summary: A smug coworker boasts that inventing his own numbers has transformed his life, backing it up with a conveniently exact invented percentage.

title: Third Thing I Like About You

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: That's the third thing I like about you.

situation: Tina, seated at her cubicle, tells the Boss she can't decide what she likes most about him, offering his management style or his physical fitness as candidates. The Boss, standing nearby, says he can't tell whether she is mocking him. She replies that his obliviousness is the third thing she likes about him.
punchline: Tina's reply confirms she is mocking him while praising his cluelessness, which she lists as a third quality she likes about him.
summary: A sarcastic employee showers her unsuspecting boss with backhanded compliments and then admires his inability to notice.

title: Wally's Uneventful Weekend Small Talk

situation: Alice makes polite small talk by asking Wally about his weekend. Wally describes in flat detail how he spent it idly on his couch playing with his phone. Alice says she has no follow-up questions, and Wally notes that nobody ever does.
punchline: Wally's weekend was so empty and dull that no one ever wants to hear more, and he is fully aware of it and unbothered.
summary: A coworker's routine weekend question gets a bleakly lazy answer that shuts down any further conversation.

title: Boss Defends Extortion for Hugs

transcript.text: You know that's a crime, right?

transcript.text: Maybe I shouldn't handle my own defense.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, tells the Boss that seventy-three employees have accused him of inappropriate behavior. The Boss earnestly asks what is wrong with threatening to ruin a subordinate's career unless he gets a hug. Catbert points out it is a crime, and the Boss concludes he should not act as his own defense.
punchline: The Boss so obliviously fails to see that coercing hugs by threatening careers is wrong that he only grasps he is in legal trouble when told it is a crime, and even then only worries about his defense.
summary: A clueless manager confronted by HR over dozens of complaints casually admits to blackmailing workers for hugs and only realizes he may need a lawyer.

title: Boss Asks If Software Is Blockchain

situation: Dilbert asks his boss to approve a software purchase, telling him up front that the boss is too clueless to understand why it's needed and should simply sign off without questions. The boss, unable to resist, asks whether it's blockchain, and Dilbert shuts him down.
punchline: The boss proves Dilbert's point by ignoring the instruction not to ask questions and responding with a trendy buzzword, showing he understands nothing about the purchase.
summary: A request to rubber-stamp a software buy is answered by a manager's reflexive jargon guess instead of silent approval.

setting: Video call between the Boss's home office and Wally's workspace
situation: The Boss, on a video call, scolds Wally for once again making no progress on any of his projects. Wally replies that choosing not to act is itself a decision, reframing his laziness as deliberate strategy. The Boss responds that he hates talking to Wally, and Wally mildly calls that harsh.
punchline: Wally dresses up his chronic laziness as a conscious decision, which is so exasperating that even the Boss snaps, while Wally remains unbothered and only mildly offended.
summary: A manager's complaint about stalled projects is met with a smug philosophical excuse that leaves him openly fed up.

transcript.text: And now I'm calling tech support as my only hope.

setting: Dilbert's phone conversation, with a table and coffee mug, then a tech support desk

punchline: After exhausting every broken self-service option, Dilbert's last hope, tech support, is closed, showing how companies make customers jump through hoops and then offer no real help.
summary: A customer runs through a gauntlet of malfunctioning sign-up methods, and the one human fallback he has left clocks out just as he reaches it.

punchline: The employee is so enraged by the bonus denial that his head literally explodes, and the boss responds with casual indifference by requesting paper towels.
summary: A manager's news about a withheld bonus is so infuriating that the recipient's head bursts, leaving the manager more concerned about the mess than the person.

punchline: The Boss's attempt at morale-boosting is a thinly veiled insult, and Alice retaliates by calling him "Adolph," comparing him to a tyrant.
summary: A boss tries to cheer up the team with nicknames but only manages to insult his angriest employee, who hits back with a far harsher label.

punchline: Wally openly admits he is exploiting an asymptomatic pandemic as a rare career opportunity to avoid work, treating it as a perk he refuses to waste.
summary: A lazy employee keeps calling in sick with a repeat illness and shamelessly justifies it as a once-in-a-career chance to skip work.

summary: A man turns down a coworker's friendly lunch offer because he dreads saying the wrong thing and being publicly shunned.

situation: The Boss opens a Zoom call and asks if everyone can hear him. Wally, relaxing in bed with his laptop, lies that the Boss's microphone is broken even though he can hear him fine. The Boss then decides to reschedule the call, and Wally approves of that plan.

situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that he sometimes needs time alone and insists it isn't personal. summary: A man's polite request for solitude gets a sarcastic guilt trip from his dog, then a clumsy reply that makes the insult worse.

summary: A mysterious phone caller delivers a doomsday robot prophecy and then hints that it is a machine itself, with a grim promise that it will outlive Dilbert.

situation: Dilbert sits at a laptop and complains aloud about how pointless the Zoom meeting is and how he hates dealing with imbeciles. A voice from the call informs him that his microphone is on, so everyone heard him. Dogbert, sitting beside him, remarks that it could have been worse.

summary: A man grumbles about a tedious video call, only to learn that everyone on it heard him, while his dog offers cold comfort.

setting: Office, at a desk or conference table
situation: A coworker named Dick introduces himself to Dilbert as his workplace nemesis. He then tells Dilbert that people are saying terrible things about him behind his back, but refuses to say who or what. When Dilbert asks why he bothered, Dick reveals he gets energy from other people's suffering.
punchline: Dick's vague, unactionable warning has no purpose except to upset Dilbert, because he literally feeds on his coworker's pain.
summary: A self-declared office nemesis delivers a deliberately useless rumor warning just to enjoy watching his target squirm.

title: Remote Work Injuries Blamed on Thieving Guard

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm proud to announce we reduced workplace injuries by 76% this past year.

transcript.speaker: Voice from laptop
transcript.text: We all worked from home this year. Shouldn't we have seen a 100% reduction?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our security guard kept hurting his back stealing office equipment.

setting: Home office, during a video conference call
situation: The Boss proudly announces on a video call that workplace injuries dropped 76% over the year. An attendee points out that since everyone worked from home, injuries should have fallen by 100%. The Boss explains that the remaining injuries came from the security guard hurting his back while stealing office equipment.
punchline: The Boss takes credit for a supposed safety improvement that is just a side effect of remote work, and his explanation for the leftover injuries reveals that the company's own security guard is a thief.
summary: A manager brags about a big drop in injuries, then reveals the leftover ones came from the building's own guard burgling the empty office.

title: Pay Raise Versus Inflation Standoff

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am confident you two can come up with a solution that makes everyone happy.

transcript.speaker: Manager

situation: Dilbert sits at a meeting table between an employee and a manager, with Ratbert nearby. The employee complains that his pay isn't keeping up with inflation. Dilbert, acting as mediator, optimistically says the two can find a solution, and the manager privately mocks him for implying that he could lower inflation.
punchline: The manager is exasperated because Dilbert's vague mediation misses that the only real solution is a raise, and instead sounds like he expects the manager to control the national economy.
summary: A mediator's cheerful call for a win-win solution to a pay dispute leaves the manager baffled, as he thinks he is being asked to fix the economy.

title: Her Calendar Is A Weather App

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I like her.

setting: A table at a coffee meeting, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert invites a woman to go on a hike, and she says she needs to check her calendar. He notices she is actually looking at a weather app. Later he tells Dogbert she schedules unwanted activities for days likely to be rained out, and Dogbert approves.
punchline: The woman politely avoids Dilbert's hike by choosing a rainy day, and Dogbert admires her clever way of dodging commitments.
summary: A date's calendar check turns out to be a weather forecast, revealing a sneaky strategy for getting out of plans.

title: Too Busy to Hire Help

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm working two jobs since Ted quit. Maybe you could hire a replacement for Ted.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That won't work because you're too busy to train a new person.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop making that death stare and get back to your two jobs.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has been doing two jobs since Ted quit and asks him to hire a replacement. The boss refuses, arguing that Dilbert is too busy covering both jobs to train a new person. When Dilbert glares at him, the boss tells him to stop the death stare and return to his double workload.
punchline: The boss creates a catch-22 where the overwork caused by the vacancy is the very reason he won't fill it, and he then scolds Dilbert for being visibly angry about it.
summary: A boss uses an employee's overload as the excuse for never hiring the help that would relieve it.

title: Self-Esteem Resentment Is Not Dilbert's Problem

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not my problem.

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was I supposed to hear that?

setting: Office desks, with Dilbert and Alice seated side by side
situation: Alice, seated at her desk, tells Dilbert that her low self-esteem makes her hate him because he is good at his job. Dilbert, absorbed in his phone, dismisses it as not his problem. Alice menacingly replies that it will be his problem, and Dilbert asks if he was meant to overhear that threat.
punchline: Dilbert's casual indifference to a coworker's open resentment backfires into a veiled threat, and he is left obliviously wondering whether he was supposed to hear it.
summary: A coworker admits her insecurity breeds hatred toward a competent colleague, shrugs off by him, then ominously promises he will soon share her problem.

title: Wally's Remote Work Success Story

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And by that you mean you went into the office and did not work remotely?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Okay, sure.

setting: A home office video call, and Wally's bed
situation: The Boss video-calls Wally and asks whether he has been successful on his projects while working from home. Wally answers "Not remotely," and the Boss, interpreting this charitably, assumes Wally went into the office instead. Wally agrees, though he is actually lying in bed with his laptop.
punchline: Wally's pun "not remotely" admits his failure, but the Boss misreads it as a claim of in-office work, and Wally lazily goes along with it from his bed.
summary: A clueless manager spins his slacking employee's confession of failure into a story about commuting, and the employee happily plays along from under the covers.

transcript.text: I... don't know how to process that.

situation: Alice, looking at her phone, tells Wally she has been tracking everything he said this year and all of it has been false. Wally shrugs it off, pointing out that they both still got paid. Alice is left speechless, and Wally turns her accusation around by saying she wouldn't believe him anyway.
punchline: Wally dodges the accusation of constant lying by noting that being paid is all that matters, then uses her stated distrust as an excuse to avoid ever explaining himself.
summary: A coworker catalogues a colleague's falsehoods, only to find that his paycheck and her disbelief leave her with no leverage at all.

In the final panel he sits at a desk with his feet up and his hands behind his head, pointing out that the CEO is grossly overpaid before announcing it's time for his second nap.
punchline: The co-CEO gleefully admits that the top executive role is easy, overpaid, and mostly spent napping, satirizing how little CEOs actually do for their huge compensation.
summary: A freshly minted co-executive happily brags that running the company is effortless and lavishly paid, then settles in for another snooze.

situation: Dilbert tells his team that a government contract requires a CO2 capture machine and invites ideas, promising there are no bad ideas. punchline: The 'no bad ideas' rule collapses when the team suggests ridiculous solutions, and the coworkers are oblivious to Dilbert's frustration, happily enjoying the meeting.
summary: A brainstorming session on carbon capture produces silly suggestions that push the engineer running it to storm off and do the work himself.

punchline: Dilbert's unnoticed week of vacation proves he is not essential, exposing the boss's claims about employee value and engagement as empty rhetoric.
summary: A worker's request for time off is met with praise about his importance, until he reveals that his previous absence went entirely unnoticed.

title: Cognitive Dissonance Over Canceled Meeting

transcript.text: Whatever you say next is likely to be an absurdity that allows you to be right when you are wrong.

punchline: Confronted with proof she is wrong, Alice escapes through an absurd, unrelated accusation so she can still claim victory, just as Dilbert predicted.
summary: Shown undeniable text evidence of her mistake, a coworker dodges admitting error by inventing a nonsensical argument about animals and declaring herself the victor.

title: Under-Valuing the Moron Option

He points out that a vendor demanding immediate payment would supply the same product at half the price. punchline: The boss, offered a sensible choice to break a pointless rule and save money, treats following the rule like a rigid policy as a better path, showing how management prizes foolish adherence to policy over common sense.
summary: A sensible engineer proposes bending a payment-terms rule to halve costs, but his manager would rather stay foolishly compliant.

summary: A consultant explains that a person's video call background can expose unflattering truths, then confirms that is precisely what a good backdrop should conceal.

Everyone nominated themselves on the first day and nobody has submitted anything since. He then admits that asking for nominations wasn't one of his best ideas.
punchline: The Boss blames the employees' idea for the failure of his own recognition program, when it was his request that invited self-nominations and then silence.

summary: A manager demands a free in-house replacement for costly business systems, dismisses the engineer's realistic estimate as laziness, and responds by threatening to lower his salary.

summary: An HR villain declares genetic screening will replace performance reviews, then condemns an employee for doubting it.

summary: A disturbing confession slips out in a meeting icebreaker because the speaker figured his coworkers were tuning out anyway.

transcript.text: Then I'd get a big raise?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We pay market rates.

situation: The Boss tells the team that the company can only succeed if employees take creative risks. Dilbert asks whether mistakes will be forgiven or rewarded, and the Boss says no. Dilbert concludes it is a suicide mission, and the Boss says success is possible but offers no raise beyond market rates.
punchline: The Boss demands bold risk-taking while offering no reward for success and punishment for failure, so employees bear all the downside with no upside.
summary: A manager urges staff to gamble on bold ideas but makes clear there is no payoff whether they win or lose.

title: Wrong Manual Shipped, No Refunds

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We won't meet our launch date because the user manual isn't done yet.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Stick a manual from a different model in the box and ship it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today I found out why we don't offer a money-back satisfaction guarantee.

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert the product will miss its launch date because the user manual isn't finished, then suggests shipping the manual from a different model instead. A shocked Dilbert later reflects at home, with Dogbert on the couch, that this explains the company's lack of a refund policy.
punchline: The company knowingly ships products with the wrong manual, so it can't afford to offer a money-back guarantee because customers would return everything.
summary: Pressure to hit a launch date leads a coworker to propose shipping mismatched instructions, which reveals why the company avoids refunds.

title: Remote Team Building With Self-Gifts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And buy a gift for yourself.

setting: Office, with the manager and Dilbert on a Zoom video call
situation: A manager (shown with his pointy hair in the recurring style) announces a Zoom team-building session on Friday. He encourages employees to drink heavily since they'll already be at home, and then adds that they should buy a gift for themselves. Dilbert, watching the call from his laptop, remarks that it couldn't get more absurd.
punchline: The manager's plan for remote team building is so hollow that it amounts to employees drinking alone and buying their own presents, which makes the whole exercise pointless.
summary: A manager's idea of a virtual bonding event turns out to be employees drinking alone at home and giving themselves gifts.

title: Dogbert's Zoom Slimming Tips

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's tips for Zoom calls

transcript.text: To make yourself look thinner on cam. . .

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try eating right and exercising.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When that doesn't work, adjust your camera so it only shows your forehead.

setting: Dogbert's desk, presented as a video call tip segment
situation: Dogbert, seated at his desk, offers tips for looking thinner on Zoom calls. He first suggests the honest approach of healthy eating and exercise, then admits that when that fails the real solution is to frame the camera so only his forehead is visible.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses real health effort as ineffective and jumps straight to the lazy cheat of cropping the camera to hide your body.
summary: Dogbert advises that if diet and exercise don't make you look slimmer on video calls, you can simply point the camera at your forehead.

title: Rumor Chain Predicts Company Bankruptcy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm planning to increase the budget for training by fifty percent next year.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: He didn't say anything about the other budgets.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He didn't say anything about the budget for research and development.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Sounds like he's phasing out research and development.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: He wouldn't phase out research and development unless he knows the company is failing.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: The company must be going bankrupt.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: The company is bankrupt.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I guess I don't need to increase the training budget.

situation: The Boss casually mentions he plans to raise the training budget by fifty percent. As the remark is passed from one coworker to the next, each person reads more into what he failed to say, and the speculation escalates from budgets to research cuts to the company failing. By the end, the rumor is treated as fact, and the Boss, hearing it, abandons his own training plan.
punchline: Employees infer something from what the boss didn't say, and the rumor snowballs so far that it becomes accepted fact and even changes the boss's original plan.
summary: A passing comment about training funds mutates through office gossip into a confirmed corporate collapse that undoes the original plan.

title: Eight Billion Dollar Woke Ad Loss

situation: At a board meeting, an executive announces that the company's deliberately 'woke' ad strategy cost it eight billion dollars in a quarter, then justifies it by saying you must offend some customers to make others loyal. After the meeting, a colleague asks how he kept a straight face while saying it.
punchline: The executive jokes that Botox keeps his face frozen, so he can deliver an absurd rationalization of a massive loss without showing any expression.
summary: A leader spins a multibillion-dollar advertising flop as a loyalty-building success, and later deflects a colleague's incredulity with a cosmetic-procedure quip.

title: Generic Feedback, Spelled Wrong

setting: Office break area with a table and coffee cups
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert whether he received his notes on improving a slide deck. Dilbert, looking at his phone, says the feedback was clearly just a web search for generic feedback with a typo. The coworker denies it, but Dilbert points out the first note literally told him to search for the misspelled term.
punchline: The coworker's lazy feedback was so obviously copied from a search that it still contained the instruction to search with the misspelled term, which disproves his denial.
summary: A reviewer's supposed critique of a presentation turns out to be a botched internet search, and the evidence is embarrassingly baked into his own note.

situation: Alice, seated at her desk, tells a coworker that she dreamed about him. When he asks what he was doing, she says he was screaming for her to stop hitting him. He asks if she stopped, and she replies that she didn't because it was a dream and not a nightmare.
punchline: Alice reveals that beating up her coworker in her dream was pleasant for her, showing how much she dislikes him.
summary: A woman casually recounts a dream in which she was beating up her coworker, and admits she enjoyed it.

title: Vaccinated Boss Taunts Unvaccinated Dilbert

situation: The Boss announces he has had the COVID-19 vaccination and feels safe. He then smugly says he pities unvaccinated people stewing in deadly viruses, apparently directing this at Dilbert. Dilbert responds with polite, deadpan thanks while the Boss childishly taunts him.
punchline: The Boss's smug pity is undercut by his childish 'neener-neener' taunt, while Dilbert's flat 'thank you for your concern' reads as dry sarcasm.
summary: A gloating manager fresh from his vaccine shot mocks his coworker's vulnerability with schoolyard-level taunting.

title: Career Plan: Die in Cubicle

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, asks a bald, bespectacled employee whether he has a career plan. The employee bleakly answers that he intends to drift between dead-end projects until he dies in his cubicle. Catbert approves, saying that was exactly what he was about to recommend.
punchline: The employee's hopeless career plan is exactly what the company's HR department wants for him, showing that HR has no interest in real career development.
summary: An HR chief quizzes a worker about his future, and the worker's grim resignation turns out to match the fate the company had in mind for him.

title: Stealing the CEO's Birthday Gift

situation: Dilbert asks Wally what to buy the CEO for his birthday, since the CEO already has everything. Wally suggests stealing something from the CEO, wrapping it, and presenting it as a replacement for the stolen item. When Dilbert worries the CEO would notice, Wally reveals he is doing exactly this with the CEO's office chair.
punchline: Wally's lazy, dishonest gift-giving scheme is not hypothetical advice but something he is already doing, using the CEO's own office chair as the present.
summary: Wally's solution to buying a gift for the man who has everything is to give him back something of his own.

title: Customers Alive When They Bought

setting: Office, with an exterior view of the company building in the final panel
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that activists claim the company inflated its customer list with dead people. The boss defends the company by insisting the customers were alive when they bought the products. Dilbert then asks whether they died while using the products, and the boss only hopes the activists don't ask that.
punchline: The boss's technically true defense accidentally raises the worse possibility that the company's products killed its customers, and he cares only about avoiding the question, not the answer.
summary: A boss rebuts an accusation of faking his customer list with a narrow technicality that hints his products may have been fatal.

title: Tricking Coworker Into Suspended Animation

Dilbert asks whether Wally plans to wake him up. Wally says it depends on how hard it is to get a feeding tube into the sleeping man.
punchline: Wally has drugged a coworker for his own convenience and is casually weighing whether waking him is worth less effort than keeping him fed through a tube.
summary: A scheming employee drugs a pesky colleague with a fake space-travel story and shrugs off the question of whether he'll ever revive him.

He calls out that she is only pretending to listen because she is thinking about the text, and kindly offers to let her check and reply. punchline: Instead of being embarrassed about being distracted, the coworker turns the offer into a rude ultimatum, implying that Dilbert's explanation is not worth more than a few seconds of her attention.
summary: A buzzing phone steals a listener's focus, and when the speaker graciously calls her out, she responds by setting a stopwatch on his talking.

The applicant explains he majored in Elbonian literature even though he can't speak Elbonian and none of the books are translated. Dilbert asks how he earned the degree without reading anything, and the applicant says he is a great test-taker.
punchline: The applicant admits he earned a degree without actually learning the material, implying that degrees reward test-taking skill rather than real knowledge or ability.
summary: A job candidate boasts of a degree in a literature he never read and couldn't read, crediting his exam-taking skill.

punchline: The CEO saves his own job by offering up a subordinate executive as a scapegoat and lying about the reason for the firing, showing how leaders shift blame and consequences onto others.
summary: Facing dismissal for his public remarks, a chief executive talks the board into accepting another executive's head instead of his own.

summary: A dog offers advice about dressing casually for video meetings, only to have his own furniture object to the arrangement.

summary: After the boss's gene experiment gives everyone tails, a worker says opinion is divided between gratitude and calls for execution, then asks for an extra tail.

situation: Dilbert and a coworker sit side by side at a table, each absorbed in a smartphone. Dilbert complains that technology leaves him feeling disconnected and alone ninety percent of the time. summary: A man grumbling about phone-induced isolation turns out to prefer total solitude, and asks his seatmate to help make it complete.

Dilbert angrily complains that he has already wasted twenty minutes waiting and asks why he wasn't told sooner. The caller replies that they expected him to be a jerk about it, so they deliberately made him wait as punishment, leaving Dilbert with nothing to say.

summary: A man learns that the delay notice he received was withheld on purpose to teach him a lesson about his own anger.

situation: Dilbert sits on his couch texting or messaging a female colleague, suggesting a Zoom call to discuss a work issue. situation: The Boss announces to the assembled team that the company's new strategy is to monetize virtual reality in simulated worlds called the metaverse. summary: A manager announces a trendy plan to sell virtual worlds, then reacts with alarm when an engineer wonders whether their own reality is a simulation.

summary: A young engineer's advancement for criticizing a lack of diversity prompts his boss to try buying his silence with an even bigger title.

Wally, who is sitting at the table, boasts that the robot will never replace him. A coworker tells him that he is actually the robot, and the real Wally is sitting across from him.

summary: A coworker's boast about being irreplaceable by a slacker robot collapses when he learns he is the machine himself.

title: Sentient Virus Defeated by Face Masks

situation: Dilbert sits at a table eating a donut and sipping coffee while a news broadcast on his laptop reports that the Epsilon variant virus has become sentient. summary: A calm man watches news of a virus that has gained consciousness and wants world domination, only to hear that the usual precaution will beat it.

title: Weekly One-on-Ones Become Boss Monologues

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he will hold weekly one-on-one meetings with each engineer. Dilbert asks whether he plans to spend them talking about himself. Afterward the Boss, holding a coffee cup, tells Catbert that the engineers are getting much better at predicting.
