summary: A manager takes it as a compliment when his staff correctly foresees that his new private meetings will be all about him.

title: Stealth Firing Via Fake Promotion

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm promoting you to Vice President of the Network Audit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this a stealth way of firing me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gotta go.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The audit will be done in three months.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I'll be the Vice President of nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can eliminate the entire function and never have to confront me about why you fired me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But first you'll make me fire all of my staff before you fire me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You tried to misdirect my attention from your treachery with a bogus promotion that comes with no extra pay!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In my defense, I didn't expect him to know any of that.

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss announces a promotion for Dilbert to Vice President of the Network Audit. Dilbert suspects it is a stealth firing and, while walking and talking with the Boss, works out that the job will vanish when the audit ends and that he will be forced to fire his own staff first. Dilbert storms off angry, and the Boss admits he didn't expect Dilbert to figure it out.
punchline: The Boss's only defense for his sneaky scheme is that he assumed Dilbert was too dim to see through the fake promotion.
summary: A boss tries to disguise a layoff as a promotion, only to be shocked when his employee sees through the whole plan.

title: Marriage Terms for Appearances and Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Before we get married, we need to talk about a few things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: First, I'm only marrying you to prove I'm not a bigot and to save my job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Second, neither of us is gay.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: They say marriage takes work.

situation: Dilbert sits across from a coworker with a tall purple head and lays out conditions before their planned marriage. He admits the marriage is only to prove he isn't a bigot and to protect his job, and adds that neither of them is gay. The coworker dryly replies that marriage takes work.
punchline: A sham marriage undertaken purely for workplace optics and job security is met with the deadpan observation that marriage takes work, implying this loveless arrangement will still be a burden.
summary: Two coworkers prepare for a marriage of convenience designed to satisfy corporate image concerns, and discover that even a fake union comes with effort.

title: Signed Away Your DNA

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: As you know, when you signed your employment documents, you agreed to let us manipulate your DNA.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Judging from the looks on your faces, none of you reviewed the documents before signing.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Roll up your sleeve so I can erase that disapproving look on your face.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells employees seated at a meeting table that their employment contracts let the company manipulate their DNA. When their shocked faces show they never read the paperwork, he pulls out a syringe and orders one to roll up a sleeve.
punchline: Employees who sign contracts without reading them can have unthinkable terms enforced on them, and Catbert will happily use them to genetically wipe away any disapproval.
summary: An HR cat reveals that unread employment paperwork permits genetic tampering and promptly reaches for a needle.

title: Social Media Brain Manipulation Profit Scheme

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a technology that will manipulate people's brains for our profit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shhh!!! You can't say that part out loud.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The technology will create civil strife and destroy relationships.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But we would make lots of money?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lots and lots.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I could finally afford the trophy wife I always wanted!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shhh!!! You can't say that part out loud.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: What is this miracle technology called?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "Social media."

setting: Office hallway and an office building exterior
situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has invented a technology that manipulates people's brains for profit. The boss shushes him at first, then gets enthusiastic when he learns it will cause civil strife and make lots of money. Each then shushes the other for saying the quiet part out loud, and the final panel reveals the technology is social media.
punchline: The strip satirizes social media companies as knowingly profiting from manipulating users and damaging society, with both men aware they shouldn't admit their motives publicly.
summary: Two coworkers gleefully plot a profitable mind-control gadget that wrecks society, only for the reveal to name it as an existing everyday platform.

title: Amazon Birthday Every Single Day

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yay! My package has arrived!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I buy one thing per day from Amazon and then forget what I ordered, so it feels like my birthday every day.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can't watch this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes! Dish soap! How did I know I wanted that?

setting: Outside Dilbert's front door, then inside his home on the couch
situation: Dilbert excitedly retrieves a package from his doorstep and explains that he orders one item from Amazon every day and forgets what it was. He opens the box on the couch and is thrilled to find dish soap, while Dogbert covers his eyes, unable to watch.
punchline: Dilbert's self-inflicted forgetfulness turns mundane household supplies into exciting surprises, which is a sad and pathetic way to feel joy, as Dogbert's embarrassment shows.
summary: A man gets giddy about a delivery he has no memory of ordering, treating a bottle of dish soap like a surprise gift while his dog cringes.

title: Pay Cut for Not Commuting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to reduce your pay because you no longer commute.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you pocket those savings, it is as if you are stealing from the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, it isn't like that at all.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everyone in prison says they're innocent too.

setting: Video call between Dilbert's home office and the Boss's desk
situation: Over a video call, the Boss announces he is cutting Dilbert's pay because Dilbert no longer commutes to work. He claims that keeping the commuting savings amounts to stealing from the company. When Dilbert objects, the Boss dismisses the objection by saying everyone in prison claims to be innocent.
punchline: The Boss treats Dilbert's protest as proof of guilt, using absurd logic to justify a pay cut for working from home.
summary: A manager slashes a remote worker's salary on the grounds that the money saved on commuting belongs to the company, then waves away any objection as a guilty person's excuse.

title: Hiding Incompetence Inside Successful Teams

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: You don't need to do any actual work in order to succeed here.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Just find a team that is already successful and burrow into it so deeply your incompetence goes unnoticed.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Won't the smart people notice?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Yes, but no one listens to them.

setting: Office hallway, with an exterior view of an office building
situation: A veteran coworker with a coffee cup advises a younger colleague that success at the company requires no real work. He suggests embedding yourself in an already-successful team so your incompetence is hidden. The newcomer asks whether smart people will notice, and the veteran says they will but are ignored.
punchline: Competent people may see through the freeloaders, but the company's culture ignores them, so incompetence is never punished.
summary: A seasoned slacker teaches a newcomer to coast on a high-performing team, noting that anyone who spots the scam gets ignored.

title: CEO Volunteered as Rocket Test Pilot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When will my rocket be ready for human flight?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're scheduled to fly in it next week to make sure it's safe for animal test flights later this month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did I hear that wrong?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You should have hired engineers who hate animals and love CEOs.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert when his rocket will be ready for human flight. Dilbert replies that the Boss himself is scheduled to fly it next week, as a safety check before animals are used for test flights. When the Boss questions what he heard, Dilbert says the engineers care more about animals than about CEOs.
punchline: The engineers have reversed the usual safety order and made the CEO the test subject, because they value animal welfare above his life, which Dilbert points out is the Boss's own hiring mistake.
summary: A boss eager to launch his rocket learns the engineers plan to test it on him before any animals.

title: Random Decisions Until Changing Jobs

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We need to think longer term about how all of these dynamics play out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds reasonable. What exactly were we doing before?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't speak for anyone else, but I was making random decisions and hoping I'd change jobs before anyone found out.

situation: At a meeting, a bearded coworker says the team should think longer term about how dynamics play out. Dilbert agrees and asks what they were doing before. The coworker candidly admits he was making random decisions and hoping to leave for another job before anyone noticed.
punchline: The coworker's admission reveals that his past decision-making was baseless guesswork, and his only long-term plan was to escape before the consequences caught up with him.
summary: A colleague calls for long-term thinking, then confesses his previous strategy was winging it and job-hopping to dodge accountability.

title: Interviewer Hopes Candidate Is Lying

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: You say you learned to code at the "Prestigious University of Elbonia."

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: I've never heard of that "prestigious" school. So either you are lying, or I'm an idiot.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I'm hoping it's both.

setting: Job interview at a conference table
situation: An interviewer with a topknot hairstyle reads the resume of a candidate who claims to have learned coding at the Prestigious University of Elbonia. She says she has never heard of the school, so either he is lying or she is an idiot. The candidate calmly answers that he hopes both are true.
punchline: The candidate admits he is probably lying on his resume and hopes the interviewer is also foolish enough to believe him anyway.
summary: A job seeker responds to doubts about his dubious degree by cheerfully wishing for the worst on both sides of the desk.

title: Wally Requests Unlimited Budget

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Wally, I need your budget requirements for next year.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Put me down for as much as I can get.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: You're not even trying to be helpful.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's start with a trillion dollars and see how far that goes.

situation: A manager with a notepad asks Wally for his budget requirements for next year. Wally, holding his coffee, says to put him down for as much as he can get, and when the manager complains he is not being helpful, Wally proposes starting at a trillion dollars.
punchline: Wally treats budgeting as a game of grabbing as much money as possible, and cheerfully suggests an absurd trillion dollars as an opening bid.
summary: Asked for a realistic budget, a lazy employee simply demands the biggest sum he can get and floats an outrageous starting figure.
keywords: as much as I can get

title: Promotion With a Pay Cut

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I'm promoting you to Category Manager.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The job duties are the same as your current position.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But with more pay?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A slight decrease.

situation: The boss tells Asok he is being promoted to Category Manager. He then explains the duties are identical to Asok's current job. When Asok hopefully asks about more pay, the boss admits it will actually be a slight decrease.
punchline: The 'promotion' is only a new title with no new responsibilities and actually comes with a pay cut, exposing how companies use fancy titles in place of real rewards.
summary: A manager hands out a grand new job title that changes nothing about the work and quietly reduces the salary.

title: Chipmunk Hearsay Science Trust Problem

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I listen to actual scientists, and they say your idea will never work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If a chipmunk listens to scientists, should I trust the chipmunk to understand what he heard?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I don't get your point.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And yet you do understand science?

situation: A woman seated across from Dilbert dismisses his idea, saying actual scientists told her it will never work. Dilbert responds with an analogy about trusting a chipmunk who overheard scientists. When she says she doesn't get his point, he sarcastically asks whether she really understands science.
punchline: Dilbert implies that the woman is like the chipmunk, merely repeating secondhand science she doesn't actually understand, and her failure to grasp his analogy proves it.
summary: A skeptic invoking unnamed scientists to reject an idea gets compared to an eavesdropping rodent who can't be trusted to grasp what it overheard.

title: Nobody Knows Why We Meet

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think you all know why we are gathered here today.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not really.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Nope.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Me neither, and I guess I won't be getting any clues from you idiots.

setting: A conference room meeting, with an office building shown in the middle panel
situation: The Boss opens a meeting by assuming everyone knows why they are gathered. The attendees each reply that they have no idea, and the Boss admits he does not know either. He then insults the group for failing to give him any hints.
punchline: The boss called the meeting without knowing its purpose, and then blames his employees for not supplying one.
summary: A manager convenes a meeting, discovers no one knows its purpose including himself, and complains that his staff is no help.

title: Nobody Cares Cures Social Anxiety

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What can I do to fix my social anxiety?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try keeping in mind that no one cares about you whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's working, but I think it might be creating a new problem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't care.

setting: Around a table with coffee mugs, apparently an office or meeting room
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert, acting as an advisor, how to fix his social anxiety. Dogbert tells him to remember that no one cares about him at all. Dilbert says the advice works but is causing a new problem, and Dogbert responds that he doesn't care.
punchline: Dogbert's blunt advice does cure the anxiety by making Dilbert feel worthless, and Dogbert then demonstrates the new problem by callously dismissing Dilbert's complaint.
summary: A man seeking relief from his social fears gets brutally honest counsel from his dog, which soothes one worry while creating another.

title: Written Up for Breathing Near Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I have to write you up for breathing on a co-worker.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I don't think you realize how many deadly pathogens come out of your toxic pie hole.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I stop breathing, or what?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Only until we can encase you in concrete.

setting: Office, Catbert's desk, with an exterior shot of the office building in the last panel
situation: Catbert, acting as human resources, tells Dilbert he must be disciplined for breathing on a co-worker. He lectures Dilbert about the deadly pathogens in his breath. When Dilbert asks if he should simply stop breathing, Catbert says that is only necessary until they can entomb him in concrete.
punchline: HR's pandemic-era germ paranoia is so extreme that its proposed solution to a person's breathing is to permanently encase him in concrete.
summary: Catbert disciplines Dilbert for exhaling near a colleague and calmly suggests burying him in concrete as the fix.

title: Ten-Year Projection Credibility Check

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Our financial model predicts slow sales for years, followed by a huge surge in year ten.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What causes that surge?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Why do you care? That's ten years away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I ask so I can judge the credibility of your model.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: I guarantee our model is as good as any other ten-year projection.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Has any ten-year projection ever been right?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: How would I know?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Don't you put in those earbuds! Dooon't!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please continue.

setting: Conference room during a financial presentation
situation: A presenter with pointy hair shows a financial model predicting years of slow sales followed by a huge surge in year ten. Dilbert asks what causes the surge and whether any ten-year projection has ever been right, and the presenter can't answer. When the presenter sees Dilbert reaching for earbuds, he panics and begs him not to tune out, and Dilbert politely tells him to continue.
punchline: The presenter's unfounded ten-year forecast collapses under basic questioning, and his desperation to keep the audience from tuning out shows he knows the model is meaningless.
summary: A presenter's wildly distant sales forecast unravels when a skeptical engineer asks why it should be believed.

title: Unknown Risks Versus Unknown Alternatives

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How did you decide to recommend Option B?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I compared the unknown risks and benefits of each plan to the unknown risks and benefits of the alternatives.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You mean you guessed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is such a cynical way to look at it.

setting: Office, at a desk during a one-on-one discussion
situation: A manager with pointy hair asks Dilbert how he arrived at his recommendation of Option B. Dilbert gives an elaborate, jargon-heavy explanation about comparing unknown risks and benefits. The manager translates it bluntly as guessing, and Dilbert protests that this is cynical.
punchline: Dilbert's impressive-sounding analysis is really just a guess dressed up in formal language, and he objects to having it described accurately.
summary: A recommendation justified with polished risk-analysis language turns out to be nothing more than a hunch.

title: Ransomed Ranking Database Is Worthless

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Elbonian hackers stole our employee performance ranking database, and now they demand a ransom payment to give it back.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They can keep it. We've been ranking employees solely on their haircuts for years, and no one has complained yet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We will speak of this no more.

situation: Dilbert reports to his boss that Elbonian hackers have stolen the employee performance ranking database and are demanding a ransom. The boss shrugs it off and admits that employees have been ranked only on their haircuts for years. Dilbert is stunned, and the boss shuts down the conversation.
punchline: The company's employee performance rankings are based on nothing but haircuts, so the stolen database has no real value and the ranking process is exposed as a sham.
summary: A ransomware threat falls flat when the boss reveals that the stolen rankings were never based on real performance.

title: Alice Rejects Lunch With Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you like to go to lunch with me?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No, I ate yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I should probably just walk away.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And I hate the restaurant you never mentioned.

situation: Dilbert approaches Alice at her desk and asks her to lunch. She curtly refuses, claiming she already ate yesterday. As Dilbert resigns himself to leaving, she piles on by saying she hates the restaurant he hadn't even named.
punchline: Alice rejects Dilbert so thoroughly that she dismisses not only the invitation but also a restaurant he never suggested, showing her contempt in advance.
summary: A hopeful coworker's lunch invitation is shot down with deadpan sarcasm and then a pre-emptive insult for good measure.

title: Management Retreat Lessons Misapplied

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How was the management retreat?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you learn lots of lessons you will now misapply?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm not allowed to argue with you intersectionals.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And there it is.

situation: A woman at her desk asks a returning coworker how the management retreat went, then sarcastically asks whether he learned lessons he will now misapply. He responds that he is not allowed to argue with 'intersectionals', and she remarks that this is exactly the kind of misapplied lesson she predicted.
punchline: The coworker immediately proves her sarcastic prediction right by misusing a buzzword from the retreat as an excuse to avoid arguing with her.
summary: A cynical office worker predicts that a colleague will misuse his retreat takeaways, and he promptly does so with a garbled bit of jargon.

title: New Guy Quits After Acronym Barrage

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, explain to the new guy what he needs to know about your project.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our PDR system is downstream from the QRD data and the BMR, so don't order a GREF or else the PLR will get boodled.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: I quit.

setting: Conference room, then outside an office building
situation: The Boss asks Wally to brief a new employee on his project. Wally replies with an incomprehensible string of acronyms and nonsense jargon, leaving the new hire sweating and horrified. In the last panel the new guy has leapt out of a high window of the office building, shouting that he quits.
punchline: Wally's jargon-filled onboarding is so baffling that the new hire would rather jump out a window than work on the project.
summary: A new hire gets a bewildering acronym-laden briefing from Wally and promptly flees the job by diving through a high-rise window.

title: Accused of Defensiveness Over Printer Paper

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you use the last of the printer paper and neglect to inform anyone to buy more?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I don't even use that printer. I use the one in the lab.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If you aren't guilty, why are you being so defensive?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not being defensive. I'm just telling you the facts.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And there you go again, being defensive. Why can't you admit you were wrong?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you teach me the proper way to behave when I know I'm right and you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And by any chance did you use the last of the paper and tell no one?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop moving the goal posts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And there it is.

situation: Alice accuses Dilbert of using up the last printer paper without telling anyone. When Dilbert truthfully denies it, she treats his denial as proof of guilt, calling him defensive. Dilbert finally turns the question on her, and she accuses him of moving the goal posts.
punchline: Alice's accusation was a trap where any denial counts as guilt, and when Dilbert asks the obvious question of whether she was the culprit, she reacts with the same deflection she condemned, revealing she did it.
summary: A coworker rigs an accusation so that every denial looks like guilt, then dodges the same question when it is turned back on her.

title: Compensating for Unskilled Employee With Vagueness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, you are just the right guy for this assignment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't have the proper skills to do it right, but I plan to compensate for that by being unclear in what I want.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Will that work?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Frankly, it's our best shot.

setting: Office, in the boss's meeting with Ted
situation: The Boss hands Ted an assignment and tells him he is the right person for it. He then admits Ted lacks the proper skills, and says he will make up for that by giving unclear instructions. Ted asks whether that will work, and the Boss concedes it is their best option.
punchline: The Boss's strategy for covering an employee's lack of skill is to be deliberately vague about requirements, and he admits it is the best plan they have.
summary: A manager gives a staffer a job he isn't qualified for and plans to offset that gap with murky instructions, which he concedes is the best chance they've got.

title: Employees Grew Tails, Nobody Minds

transcript.speaker: Catbert

transcript.text: Productivity is up 50%, and no one has complained.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is anyone bothered by the fact that we all grew tails?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No. Feels natural.

setting: Boss's office, an office building exterior, and a corridor
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, reports to the Boss that gain-of-function experiments on employees have succeeded and productivity is up 50%. An exterior shot of the office building underscores that the whole company is affected. Dilbert asks whether anyone minds that everyone grew tails, and Wally casually says it feels natural.
punchline: Employees have been mutated into tailed creatures by corporate experiments, yet they accept it without complaint as long as they are more productive, showing how passively workers tolerate absurd treatment.
summary: After the company secretly modifies its staff so they sprout tails, productivity soars and the workers shrug it off as perfectly normal.

transcript.text: It's a long flight, so you will be asleep for all of it.

situation: A coworker tells a man holding a phone that he has been selected for the first manned flight to Mars, even though he never applied. The coworker says he will sleep through the whole trip and then offers him a pill that he was asked to hand over. The strip ends with 'To be continued.'
punchline: The flattering honor of being picked for a Mars mission is really a pretext to get him to swallow a mysterious sedative and be sent away, suggesting someone is trying to get rid of him.
summary: A man is told he has been picked for a Mars voyage he never applied for, and the messenger hands him a sleeping pill to take for the journey.

title: Helpful Tails Genetic Conspiracy Theory

transcript.text: I'm starting to suspect management is somehow altering our genes to make us more productive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It can't be a coincidence that we all grew helpful tails at the same time.

situation: Dilbert and Wally walk outdoors, both sporting monkey-like tails. Dilbert suspects management has genetically altered employees to boost productivity, pointing to the sudden appearance of useful tails on everyone. Wally, holding a coffee cup, begs him not to spoil it.
punchline: Wally is so pleased with his new tail, which presumably lets him do even less work, that he'd rather stay ignorant of any sinister cause than risk losing it.
summary: A coworker voices alarm that the whole office suddenly grew handy tails, but his lazy colleague just wants to enjoy the perk.

title: Wally Trains Instead of Working

transcript.text: In fact, since my first day of work, I haven't accomplished a single thing. But I did gain a lot of technical skills.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I ever decide to do something useful, imagine how ready I'll be.

setting: Office break area or conference table with a coffee cup
situation: Wally sits across from a coworker and explains that he accomplished nothing this week because he was taking a training class. He then admits he has accomplished nothing since his first day of employment, though he has gained many technical skills. He sips his coffee and smugly notes how prepared he will be if he ever decides to do something useful.
punchline: Wally treats endless training as a substitute for work, boasting about being perfectly prepared for productive effort he has no intention of ever making.
summary: A lazy employee brags that a career of avoiding actual work has left him superbly trained for the day he finally chooses to do something.

title: Wally's Lazy Socialist Conversion

transcript.text: Shouldn't you be working?

Dilbert, still working at his computer, asks why Wally isn't working. Wally replies that work is optional under his system.
punchline: Wally's newfound socialism is just a convenient excuse to avoid working while he lectures others about generosity.
summary: A coworker who has suddenly embraced socialism scolds a hard-working colleague for being greedy, then reveals the ideology conveniently excuses him from doing any work.

title: You're Basically an Emoji

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Dick, I need a favor. Can you get me the latest usage stats?

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: No. A favor would require some kind of human connection between us, and I only know you as a digital image on my screen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We work for the same company.

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: You're basically an emoji to me.

setting: Dilbert's home office during a video call with a remote coworker
situation: Working remotely, Dilbert video-calls a coworker named Dick and asks him for the latest usage stats as a favor. Dick, eating a snack at his own desk, refuses because he only knows Dilbert as an image on a screen. When Dilbert points out they work for the same company, Dick says Dilbert is basically an emoji to him.
punchline: Remote work has made colleagues so impersonal that Dick treats Dilbert as a cartoon icon rather than a person, giving him an excuse to refuse even a routine work request.
summary: A remote worker declines to help a colleague because virtual contact has left him feeling no real connection to the person on his screen.

title: Therapist Admits Same Antisocial Habits

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Billing for your video therapy session begins now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm worried that all of my recent social isolation has changed me.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: How so?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, a year ago, I felt awkward and bored around people, and that was bad enough.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I hate them so much that I only pretend to wash my hands.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess I'm secretly hoping I'm a carrier for a deadly pathogen of some type.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Am I normal?

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: I sure hope so because I do the same thing.

setting: Dilbert's home office, during a video call
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer in a video therapy session and confesses that months of social isolation have left him hating people. He admits he only pretends to wash his hands, secretly hoping to spread a deadly pathogen, then asks if he is normal. The therapist on screen says he hopes so, since he does the same thing.
punchline: Instead of reassuring him, the therapist reveals he shares the same misanthropic, germ-spreading behavior, so 'normal' means equally antisocial.
summary: A man on a paid video therapy call confesses to resenting people and faking hygiene, only to find his therapist is just as bad.

title: Faking Attention on Zoom Calls

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some of you are only pretending to be paying attention to this Zoom call.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're still doing it! Stop it! Look into the camera!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Pretending to listen to your boss has never been easier.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Golden age!

setting: Remote work from home, during a Zoom video call
situation: The Boss, sitting at his laptop, accuses his video call attendees of only pretending to pay attention, then angrily demands they look into the camera. Dilbert and Dogbert, watching from home, remark on how easy it is to fake listening to a boss over video.
punchline: Video calls make it trivially easy for employees to look attentive while ignoring the boss, so the boss's angry demands only highlight how well the pretending works.
summary: A frustrated manager scolds his remote team for tuning out, while two of them note that video meetings have made feigned attention effortless.

title: Tired of Your Face, Pandemic Edition

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I am so tired of looking at your face.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I mean seriously, it's exhausting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, you should be.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pandemic: Year two

setting: A conference table, with coffee mugs, during the pandemic
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit across from each other at a table with coffee mugs. Dogbert complains that he is exhausted from looking at Dilbert's face all the time. Dilbert apologizes, and Dogbert says he should be sorry. A caption marks it as the second year of the pandemic.
punchline: After two years of pandemic isolation, people are so sick of seeing the same few faces that even a polite apology gets met with blame for simply existing in front of them.
summary: Two long-term pandemic companions are worn out from endless proximity, and one scolds the other for having a tiresome face.

title: Garbage Man Diagnoses Dilbert's Tail

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Looks like your employer meddled with your genes and caused you to grow a helpful tail.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: It has a weak base structure. Switch to decaf for a week, and it'll fall right off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And it only took a week.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Literally everything about your idea is bad.

setting: Outdoors by a garbage bin behind the office, then outside the office door
situation: Dilbert has grown a tail, and a garbage man examines it, explaining that his employer's genetic meddling made it weak and that switching to decaf for a week will make it fall off. In the last panel Dilbert, holding a coffee cup, recounts to a coworker how quickly the fix worked, and the coworker bluntly dismisses the whole idea as bad.
punchline: A garbage man's casual diagnosis of a bizarre workplace mutation is treated as ordinary, and the coworker's blunt reaction shows the whole employer-driven genetic scheme was ridiculous from the start.
summary: A sanitation worker offers a quick cure for a corporate-induced tail, and a colleague bluntly pans the entire concept afterward.

title: Never Admitting You're Wrong About Clouds

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You never admit you're wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me one example of that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well, for example, there was the time you said there were no such things as "cumulative" clouds.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: To this day, you have not admitted you were wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um. . .

setting: Conference room, then an exterior view of an office building
situation: Alice accuses Dilbert of never admitting he is wrong, and Dilbert challenges her to give an example. Alice cites the time he insisted that "cumulative" clouds don't exist and points out he has never conceded the point. Dilbert is left speechless, and the final panel shows the office building from outside with clouds in the sky.
punchline: Dilbert's challenge is answered with a perfectly valid example, and his stunned silence proves Alice's point that he never admits he's wrong.
summary: Asked for proof that he can't concede an argument, a man is handed a specific example he has no answer for.

title: Million-Dollar Bonus Was Only Recommended

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you finish by the deadline, I'll recommend you for a million-dollar bonus.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're lying.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm serious.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But you're also lying.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only one way to find out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd need to work around the clock for weeks to meet the deadline!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the spirit!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you're lying about the bonus, I'm going to be boiling mad.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Five weeks later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It nearly killed me, but I finished by the deadline.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where's my million-dollar bonus?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told you I'd recom-mend it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They said no.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss dangles a million-dollar bonus recommendation to get Dilbert to hit an aggressive deadline. Dilbert suspects he is being lied to but works around the clock for five weeks anyway. When he finishes and asks for the bonus, the Boss says he only promised to recommend it and that management turned it down.
punchline: The Boss never promised the bonus, only a recommendation, a technicality that let him extract weeks of overtime for nothing.
summary: A manager lures an employee into punishing overtime with a lavish reward that turns out to hinge on a hollow, technically true promise.

title: Zoom Meetings Fill Boss's Emptiness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're having another Zoom meeting at 4 p.m.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the topic?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's about how I fill the deep emptiness of my soul by scheduling Zoom meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you tried overeating? That seems to work for me.

setting: Dilbert's home office, on a video call
situation: The Boss appears on Dilbert's laptop screen and announces another Zoom meeting at 4 p.m. When Dilbert asks the topic, the Boss admits the meeting exists to fill the emptiness in his soul. Dilbert deadpans that overeating is a better way to cope.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically suggests overeating as a healthier-seeming substitute for the Boss's compulsive meeting scheduling, implying both are equally unfulfilling coping mechanisms.
summary: A manager confesses that his endless video calls are a way to cope with inner emptiness, and his employee offers comfort eating as an alternative.

title: No Correlation Between Effort and Success

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've been tracking my successes at work relative to my efforts, and I see no correlation.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So if you see me not working hard, you should assume everything is fine.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You've never had a success to track.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I was hoping you didn't know that.

situation: Wally, holding his phone, announces that he has analyzed his work successes against his effort and found no correlation. He concludes that if he looks like he's slacking, everyone should assume things are fine. A coworker points out he has never had a success to measure, and Wally admits he hoped that wasn't known.
punchline: Wally's data-driven excuse for laziness collapses because he has never actually succeeded at anything, so there is nothing to correlate.
summary: A habitually idle employee dresses up his laziness as a statistical finding, only to be reminded that his track record is empty.

title: Boss Needs Help Starting Podcast

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I decided to start my own podcast because, apparently, any idiot can figure out how to do one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All I need is a tiny bit of help with the technical stuff.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you plan to use a condenser microphone?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because if you do, you'll need phantom power to polarize its transducer element.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And make sure you use a de-esser so you don't sound like a snake.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know what any of that means.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do idiots figure out how to do all of that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They usually ask me for a tiny bit of help.

situation: The Boss announces he is starting a podcast because any idiot can do it, and says he only needs a little technical help. Dilbert rattles off audio-engineering jargon about condenser microphones, phantom power and de-essers, which the Boss cannot follow. The Boss asks how idiots manage it, and Dilbert reveals they come to him for help.
punchline: Dilbert implies the Boss is exactly the kind of idiot he claimed could easily do it, and that the 'any idiot can do it' idea only works because skilled people like Dilbert quietly do the technical work.
summary: A manager who thinks podcasting is trivial is confronted with technical jargon and learns that the so-called idiots who succeed are simply getting help from experts.

title: Spotting Non-Player Characters in Simulation

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you a player in this simulation or a non-player character?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I like beer and golf.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: High five!

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Air guitar!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have no further questions.

situation: Dogbert stops a man walking along a path and asks whether he is a real player in the simulation or a non-player character. The man answers with a stock phrase about liking beer and golf, then reacts to Dogbert's high five with an enthusiastic 'Air guitar!'. Dogbert concludes the man is a scripted non-player character.
punchline: The man's canned, stereotypical responses (beer, golf, high fives, air guitar) are so predictable that Dogbert concludes he is a scripted non-player character, implying he is shallow and generic.
summary: A talking dog tests a stranger's humanity by watching him respond with clichéd, automatic enthusiasm.

title: Engineer Deduces Marketing Employee Status

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your phone has no screen protector... and a cracked screen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you work in marketing?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Are you psychic?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Better. I'm an engineer.

setting: Office conference table, with a view of an office building
situation: Dilbert notices that a woman's phone has a cracked screen and no screen protector. From this he correctly guesses that she works in marketing. She thinks he must be psychic, but he explains he is simply an engineer.
punchline: Engineers see themselves as better than psychics because they deduce facts from evidence, and the joke also suggests marketing people are careless with their gadgets.
summary: An engineer works out a stranger's department just by looking at her battered phone, and takes pride in his reasoning.

title: Dilbert Diagnoses Boss With WebMD

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I consulted WebMD to figure out what personality disorder is driving your behavior.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I narrowed it down to either brain rot or Pointy-Haired Bossness.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're not a doctor!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would I need to be a doctor to know a headless torso doesn't need aspirin?

situation: Dilbert stands holding his phone in front of the boss's desk and announces that he used WebMD to diagnose the personality disorder behind the boss's behavior. When the boss objects that Dilbert is not a doctor, Dilbert replies with an analogy about not needing medical training to spot something obvious.
punchline: Dilbert implies the boss's problem is so glaringly obvious, and his thinking so absent, that no medical expertise is needed, comparing him to a headless torso that obviously needs no aspirin.
summary: Dilbert uses an internet symptom checker to diagnose his boss's behavior, then dismisses the objection that he lacks credentials by insulting the boss's missing brain.

title: Faking Credibility With Video Backgrounds

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Your video call background needs improvement.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I'll fill your shelves with sports trophies, plus photos of you shaking hands with Jesus.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who would believe I shook hands with Jesus?

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: The same people who will believe you won lots of sports trophies.

setting: Dilbert's home office desk during a video call
situation: A small egg-shaped consultant tells Dilbert that his video call background is lacking, and offers to fill his shelves with sports trophies and photos of him shaking hands with Jesus. Dilbert doubts anyone would believe the Jesus photo. The consultant replies that the same people would believe the trophies.
punchline: The consultant sarcastically implies that the whole fake background is equally unbelievable, and that Dilbert, a clearly unathletic engineer, would never be credited with sports trophies either.
summary: A consultant offers to dress up a remote worker's webcam backdrop with fabricated achievements and gets a dig in about how implausible they all are.

title: Intersectionality Card Game Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I made a deck of intersectionality playing cards.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: For example, Wally's card is worth five points because he's short, ugly, creepy, lazy, and bald.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Alice gets three points because she's a woman and...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop.

situation: Asok announces to Alice and Wally that he has made a deck of playing cards that assign points based on intersectionality. He cheerfully lists Wally's unflattering traits as the reason his card is worth five points. When he starts to explain Alice's card, she cuts him off.
punchline: Asok's game turns identity and disadvantage into a tally of insults, and he is about to do the same to Alice when she shuts him down.
summary: A well-meaning employee's scoring game for social disadvantage devolves into a string of insults aimed at his coworkers.

title: Private Emails Shown to Offended Parties

transcript.speaker: HR Representative
transcript.text: We found some private emails you sent during college that are deeply offensive to many people.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Did you show my private messages to the people who would be most offended, thus creating the very harm of which I am accused?

transcript.speaker: HR Representative
transcript.text: Yes. Why do you ask?

setting: Office, at an employee's desk with a laptop
situation: An HR representative holding a phone tells a seated employee that old private college emails were found and are deeply offensive to many people. The employee points out that by showing those private messages to the people most likely to be offended, HR itself created the harm the employee is being accused of. HR cheerfully admits to doing exactly that and asks why it matters.
punchline: HR is oblivious to the circularity of its own logic, creating the offense it is punishing and seeing nothing wrong with it.
summary: A worker exposes the flaw in being blamed for offense that was only caused when the company circulated their private messages, and the company shrugs it off.

title: Blackmailing Yourself Into a Promotion

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Is it my imagination, or is there a lack of diversity amongst senior engineers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll promote you to senior engineer if you promise to never mention this to the press.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Did you just blackmail yourself?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you'll have a private office.

setting: Office meeting table with coffee cups
situation: Asok, sitting with a coffee, observes that the senior engineers lack diversity. The Boss, glancing at his phone, responds by offering Asok a promotion to senior engineer if he promises never to tell the press about the issue. Asok points out that the Boss has effectively blackmailed himself, and the Boss sweetens the deal with a private office.
punchline: The Boss tries to silence a diversity complaint by buying off the complainer with a promotion, essentially bribing someone to keep quiet about his own company's problem, and sees nothing wrong with it.
summary: A young engineer raises a diversity concern and is immediately offered a promotion and an office in exchange for keeping it out of the news.

title: Illegal Elbonia Sale Makes Everyone Accomplices

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm happy to announce that we just made a huge sale in Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you aware that last week our government banned all sales to Elbonia?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Before you go blabbing that all over the place, remember that all of you are accomplices.

situation: The Boss proudly announces a big sale to Elbonia to his assembled employees. Dilbert points out that the government banned all sales to Elbonia just last week. The Boss responds by warning the staff not to tell anyone, since by hearing about it they are now all complicit.
punchline: Rather than admitting he broke the law, the Boss implicates his entire staff as accomplices to silence them.
summary: A manager celebrates a deal that turns out to be illegal, then pressures his listeners into silence by declaring them all complicit.

title: Trust Data, But Not Testers

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: We must base our decisions on data!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can we be sure the data is accurate?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: You have to do a deep dive on the data so you can see for yourself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean run my own tests?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: No, you fool! Just look at the data from the tests other people did.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do I know I can trust those other people?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: You have to use your best judgment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Instead of data?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I hate you so much right now.

situation: The boss insists that decisions must be data-driven. Dilbert asks how to verify the data is accurate, and the boss's answers go in a circle: first run your own tests, then trust other people's tests, then use your own judgment. Dilbert points out that judgment is the opposite of data, and the boss gets annoyed.
punchline: The boss's demand for data-driven decisions collapses into 'use your best judgment', which is exactly what data was supposed to replace, and he resents Dilbert for noticing.
summary: A manager's call for data-based decisions ends up back at gut feeling once Dilbert asks who can be trusted to supply the data.

title: Zoom Call Noise Hypocrisy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert! Can you keep down the noise while I'm on Zoom?!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm on a Zoom call too. Your call isn't more important than mine!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry, I can't stop the background noise.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Can you keep it down in there? I'm on a Zoom call!!!

setting: Dilbert's home, working remotely from desks in separate rooms
situation: Dilbert, on a video call at his laptop, shouts at Dogbert in the next room to keep the noise down. Dogbert, sitting in a chair at his own laptop, retorts that he is on a Zoom call too and that his call matters just as much. Dilbert apologizes that he can't stop the background noise, then Dogbert yells back asking him to keep it down.
punchline: Dilbert demands quiet from Dogbert for his own call, then is the one making the noise that disrupts Dogbert's call, so each is guilty of the very thing he complains about.
summary: Two people working from home on separate video meetings each scold the other for making noise, with neither noticing they are the source of the disruption.

title: Anonymous Sources Accuse Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anonymous sources tell me you have been stealing from the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Anonymous sources have no credibility.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's exactly what they told me you'd say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do you trust them over me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, for one thing, I hear you're a thief.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You heard that from the anonymous sources that have no credibility!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why would they lie to me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Same reason you lie to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, that makes sense.

situation: The Boss accuses Dilbert of stealing from the company based on tips from anonymous sources. Dilbert points out that anonymous sources lack credibility, but the Boss keeps defending them with circular logic. When Dilbert says they lie for the same reason the Boss lies to him, the Boss accepts this as reasonable.
punchline: The Boss is so unbothered by the idea of lying that he readily agrees that a source would deceive him for the same reasons he deceives others, undermining his own case without noticing.
summary: A manager's reliance on unnamed informants collapses into circular reasoning and an unintended admission of his own dishonesty.

title: Cancelling Subscriptions Is Deliberately Impossible

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to try to cancel some recurring online charges today. Wish me luck.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What resistance are you expecting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Obviously, they hide their contact information, so I allocated two hours to find the right phone number.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It should take about an hour to navigate their automated phone system that will keep sending me to the wrong place.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I reach a human, he'll try to divert me to their website to cancel, which I already know won't work because . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: . . . I won't be able to find my account in their system for reasons no one will ever be able to explain.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And, of course, their phone support person will be using a headset microphone that garbles his already-mumbled words.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But if you stick with it, you will eventually succeed?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know where you got that idea.

situation: Dilbert announces he is going to cancel recurring online charges and, while holding his phone, walks Dogbert through every obstacle he expects. These include hidden contact numbers, a maze-like automated phone system, a rep who redirects him to a useless website, a missing account, and a garbled headset. Dogbert asks if persistence at least pays off.
punchline: Dilbert has no faith that persistence will actually succeed, implying companies make cancelling so frustrating that it may be impossible.
summary: Dilbert lists in grim detail the predictable runaround awaiting him when he tries to end his online subscriptions, and admits success is far from guaranteed.

title: Sick Day Working From Home

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm not feeling well, so I'm going to take the day off from work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You work at home. And you'll be just as sick whether you work or not, so why not work?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I don't know if you know this about me, but I don't like working.

setting: A home office, seen over a video call
situation: A remote employee tells his boss over a laptop video call that he is too unwell to work and is taking the day off. The boss argues that since the employee already works from home, being sick makes no difference, so he should just work. The employee, leaning back barefoot in his chair, admits he simply doesn't like working.
punchline: The employee drops the pretense of illness and candidly admits the real reason he wants the day off is that he dislikes working.
summary: A telecommuter's sick-day request is challenged by his manager, prompting a blunt confession of his distaste for work.

title: Charles Barkley Filter Eliminates Racism

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now that we all work remotely, I built an app to eliminate racism.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a filter that turns every face on a video call into Charles Barkley.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I like him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: See?

setting: Dilbert's desk at home, working remotely
situation: Dilbert, working from home, tells Dogbert he has built an app to eliminate racism. The app is a video-call filter that turns every participant's face into Charles Barkley. Dogbert says he likes him, and Dilbert takes this as proof that the app works.
punchline: Dilbert's absurdly simplistic app 'proves' itself when Dogbert says he likes the face it produces, treating one liking for a famous person as evidence that prejudice has been solved.
summary: A remote-working engineer unveils a video-call filter that swaps everyone's face for a celebrity's and declares it a cure for prejudice once his dog approves.
themes: technology as a fix for social issues

title: Downgrading the Meeting, One Step at a Time

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll schedule a Zoom call with the whole team tomorrow to give the update.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or you could tell me tomorrow, and I'll tell the rest of the team on our noon Zoom call.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um, okay. I'll send you a Zoom link tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does our call need to be a video call? Can we do a voice call?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, yes, I guess we could just do a voice call.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do we need to talk, or can you just send me an email?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I suppose I could just send you an email.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, we're making progress. Now, have you heard of "texting"?

setting: Office, with Dilbert and the Boss talking by phone or video from separate locations
situation: The Boss proposes scheduling a Zoom call with the whole team to deliver an update. Dilbert gets him to cut it back step by step: first to a simple relay through Dilbert, then to a voice call, then to an email. Dilbert finally suggests texting as the next improvement.
punchline: Dilbert keeps trimming the Boss's unnecessary meeting until it becomes the briefest message possible, showing that the update never needed a call at all.
summary: An employee patiently talks his manager out of a big video meeting by pushing for ever lighter communication channels.

title: Auditor Told to Shoo

transcript.speaker: Auditor
transcript.text: I'll be performing an internal audit of your department.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: There are no audit problems here because I won't let you look for them. Shoo!

transcript.speaker: Auditor
transcript.text: That's good enough for me. Can you tell my boss I did a great job?

situation: An internal auditor arrives to audit a manager's department. The manager, seated at his desk, waves him off and claims there are no problems because he won't allow anyone to look for them. The auditor happily accepts this and asks the manager to vouch for his performance to his own boss.
punchline: The auditor accepts a blatant refusal to be audited as a clean result and wants credit for a job he never did, mocking lazy, box-ticking audits.
summary: An auditor is brushed off by the department head and cheerfully treats the brush-off as a successful audit worth praising.

title: Vacation Days Correlate With Stock Price

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I did a study on the relationship between my vacation days and our stock price.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As you can see, they rise over the years in a highly correlated way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you using misleading data to scam more vacation days?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So you're saying you don't care about our stockholder?

situation: Wally shows Dilbert a paper with a graph, claiming his accumulated vacation days rise in step with the company's stock price. Dilbert accuses him of using misleading data to get more time off. Wally responds by turning it around, implying Dilbert doesn't care about the stockholder.
punchline: Wally exploits a spurious correlation to justify more vacation, then deflects criticism by guilt-tripping Dilbert about caring for the stockholder.
summary: Wally presents a chart linking his time off to share prices, then shames his coworker when questioned about the dubious logic.

title: Hiring Trouble? Try Better Management

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're having trouble hiring qualified technical people. Have any suggestions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could stop managing the company incredibly incompetently and also pay everyone more.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That is not what I was looking for.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was it close?

setting: Office break area, both holding coffee cups
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert for suggestions on why the company can't hire qualified technical people. Dilbert bluntly answers that management should stop being incompetent and pay employees more. The Boss says that isn't the kind of answer he wanted, and Dilbert asks whether it was at least close.
punchline: The Boss wants hiring advice that doesn't require him to change anything, while Dilbert sarcastically offers the obvious, correct answer and asks whether it was close to what the Boss wanted.
summary: A manager laments his recruiting struggles and gets the honest answer he least wanted to hear.

title: Panda Filter Caught on Video Call

transcript.speaker: Voice from laptop
transcript.text: Your skin looks so perfect... are you using a digital filter of some sort?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, this is the real me.

transcript.speaker: Voice from laptop
transcript.text: And what about the panda ears and snout?

transcript.speaker: Panda-faced person (thought)
transcript.text: Awkward.

situation: Dilbert sits at his laptop on a video call while a colleague compliments his flawless skin and asks if he's using a digital filter. He insists he's not, and the colleague then asks about the panda ears and snout visible on his face. The final panel reveals the person on the other end is wearing a panda filter, and thinks it's awkward.
punchline: The person questioning Dilbert's use of a filter is the one actually wearing an obvious panda filter, so their accusation is hypocritical and embarrassing.
summary: A video chat participant suspects a colleague of using a beauty filter while unknowingly sporting an animal filter themselves.

title: Salesman Admits Emotional Manipulation Tactic

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Before I tell you about our newest product, I'd like to tell you a story about a traumatic experience I had as a child.

transcript.speaker: Bald Man
transcript.text: Is your story related to the topic, or is it just an excuse to yammer about something that happened to you?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I'm trying to manipulate your emotions to short-circuit your critical thinking.

transcript.speaker: Bald Man
transcript.text: Okay. Carry on.

setting: Conference room during a sales presentation
situation: A salesman begins his pitch by offering to tell a story about a traumatic childhood experience. A bald man in the meeting asks whether the story is relevant or just rambling. The salesman openly admits it is meant to manipulate emotions and bypass critical thinking, and the bald man shrugs and tells him to continue.
punchline: The salesman honestly admits his manipulative sales tactic, and the audience accepts it anyway, showing that disclosed manipulation still works or that nobody cares.
summary: A pitchman confesses that his sob story is a ploy to cloud his listeners' judgment, and they simply let him proceed.

title: Mask Demand On Video Call

transcript.speaker: Caller (offscreen)
transcript.text: I'd feel more comfortable if you wore a mask for this call.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm working at home. I can't possibly give you a virus over a video call.

transcript.speaker: Caller (offscreen)
transcript.text: Show me a study that proves that or else stop denying science.

setting: Dilbert's home office, on a video call
situation: Dilbert is working from home on a video call when the person on the other end asks him to wear a mask. He points out that a virus can't travel over a video call. The caller counters by demanding he produce a scientific study proving it, leaving him stumped.
punchline: Dilbert's common-sense claim is common sense but unsourced, so the caller turns the 'follow the science' argument against him and he can't produce a study for something too obvious for anyone to have researched.
summary: A remote worker is asked to mask up for a video call, and his sensible objection collapses when he's challenged to cite a study for it.

title: Dilbert Misreads Woman's Annoyed Growl

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can I tell if a woman likes me?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Say something to her and watch how pained she looks to take out her earbuds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Pained?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Yeah. Look for the degree of grimace, stink eye, and a low guttural sound.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like a growl?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Yes, but scarier.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Lisa, did you hear about the . . .

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: Wuuuut!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not good! Not good! Not good!

setting: Outdoors by a blue mailbox, then an office
situation: Dilbert asks a man in a gray cap how to tell whether a woman likes him. The man describes a pained grimace, stink eye and a guttural growl when she removes her earbuds. Dilbert tries it on his coworker Lisa, gets exactly that reaction, and runs away in panic.
punchline: The advice describes an obviously annoyed, hostile reaction, and Dilbert interprets it correctly as bad news, since it really signals the opposite of liking him.
summary: Following dubious dating advice, Dilbert interrupts a coworker's earbuds and flees when she snarls at him.

title: Ignoring Ted's Mentally Ill Email

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you respond to Ted's long email?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I judged it to be a manifestation of his mental issues and not something I need to address.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Nothing will ever get done around here unless you start pretending your co-workers are sane.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will do.

setting: Office, at Dilbert's desk, ending with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The boss asks Dilbert whether he answered a long email from his co-worker Ted. Dilbert replies that he considered the email a symptom of Ted's mental problems and so didn't respond. The boss tells him that work only gets done if he pretends co-workers are sane, and Dilbert agrees.
punchline: The boss's advice to pretend everyone is sane is itself an admission that the workplace is full of unstable people, and that dysfunction is simply accepted as the cost of getting anything done.
summary: A manager scolds an employee for dismissing a colleague's rambling message as madness, urging him to feign normalcy so the company can function.

title: Days Speeding Up: Software Upgrade

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It feels as if the days are going by faster lately.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because we're a computer simulation that just got a software upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: There's really nothing you can't ruin with that nonsense, is there?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear that a lot.

setting: Office, while on a coffee break
situation: A coworker with a big bowl of dark hair remarks over coffee that the days seem to be passing faster lately. Dilbert offers a deadpan explanation that they are living in a computer simulation that just received a software upgrade. The coworker complains that he can ruin anything with that kind of nonsense, and Dilbert says he hears that often.
punchline: Dilbert's pseudo-scientific simulation theory kills a casual small-talk moment, and he cheerfully admits that people frequently tell him he ruins conversations this way.
summary: A passing comment about time flying gets answered with a simulation-theory explanation that drains all the fun from the chat.

title: Bad Crypto Advice From Coworker

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm thinking of getting into cryptocurrency trading.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you know anything about it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then you should totally do it. That's how you learn.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll set up a crypto wallet and manage it for you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How much should I put in there?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: At least 90% of your net worth. That's called diversification.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then never look at it again.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Never?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Never, unless I die before you do. Then it's fine.

situation: The Boss tells a bespectacled coworker he wants to start trading cryptocurrency despite knowing nothing about it. The coworker cheerfully encourages him, offers to manage a wallet for him, and advises putting 90% of his net worth in it and never looking at it again, except if the coworker dies first.
punchline: The coworker's absurd, self-serving 'advice' is clearly a scam: the Boss should hand over most of his wealth and never check on it, with a dark joke that the wallet is only safe to look at if the coworker dies.
summary: A clueless boss is talked into handing most of his fortune to a coworker's crypto wallet under the pretense of diversification.

title: Employees Prefer Death Over Office

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How many of you would prefer going back to work in the office instead of working at home?

transcript.speaker: Employee (off-screen)
transcript.text: I'd rather be dead.

transcript.speaker: Employee (off-screen)
transcript.text: I quit.

transcript.speaker: Employee (off-screen)
transcript.text: Shoot me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I knew it was a mistake to let them taste happiness.

setting: The Boss's home, during a video call with his staff
situation: The Boss, working from home, asks his employees over a video call how many would prefer returning to the office. Voices coming from the laptop respond with extreme rejection, saying they would rather be dead, quit, or be shot. Afterwards he stands in his living room musing about the result.
punchline: The Boss blames the employees' violent aversion to the office on having been allowed to be happy working from home, rather than recognizing that the office itself is the problem.
summary: After a poll about returning to the office draws horrified replies, the boss concludes that letting staff enjoy remote work was his blunder.

title: Fired For Following Bad People

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I need to fire you for your social media activities.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did I share something offensive?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm getting reports that you follow bad people on Twitter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I follow people on both sides of every issue so I can see the full context.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That might sound good on paper, but half of the people you follow are monsters of one sort or another.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't it obvious that enforcing this kind of standard can only lead in a bad direction?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I don't see that at all. All I see is that you associate with people who are monsters.

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: I'm getting reports that you follow Dilbert on Twitter.

setting: Office, in the Boss's workspace at Dilbert's desk
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being fired because he follows bad people on Twitter. Dilbert explains that he follows people on all sides of issues for context and warns that such a standard leads somewhere bad, but the Boss insists that following monsters means associating with them. In the last panel a higher-up arrives and tells the Boss he follows Dilbert on Twitter.
punchline: The Boss's guilt-by-association standard immediately backfires on him, since his own superior applies the same logic to his following of Dilbert, who by the Boss's reasoning is now a monster.
summary: A manager sacks an employee for the company he keeps online, only to be caught out by the very same rule.

title: Weeding Out Gullible Creative Employees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want all of you to be creative and show initiative.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You fired all of the employees who thought you were serious the last time you said that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's how I weed out the dumb ones.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells his assembled employees to be creative and show initiative. Dilbert points out that the Boss previously fired everyone who took that request seriously. The Boss cheerfully admits it is his method of weeding out the dumb ones.
punchline: The Boss punishes employees who believe his motivational slogans, so only those who ignore him survive, and he considers that a clever filter for intelligence.
summary: A manager demands initiative from his team, then proudly admits he fires anyone naive enough to act on such demands.

title: Hired Social Media Troll Nemesis

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I hired Dick to be your workplace nemesis.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: You might know his work from social media.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This feels like a bad idea.

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: Doubt science much? Duhrr.

situation: A manager with hair buns introduces a new hire named Dick to Dilbert, announcing that Dick has been hired to be Dilbert's workplace nemesis. The manager adds that Dilbert may know Dick's work from social media. Dilbert says this feels like a bad idea, and Dick immediately responds with a snide, condescending jab.
