punchline: Dick's smug 'Doubt science much? Duhrr.' reply to a simple worry shows he really is the sort of condescending social media troll the company deliberately hired to antagonize Dilbert.
summary: Management brings in a notorious online jerk to serve as Dilbert's official office rival, and he proves his qualifications at once.

title: Pen-Chewing Video Call Threat

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please stop leaning into the camera while chewing the end of your pen.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It makes me want to drive to your house and shove that pen up your nose.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But you won't do that, right?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's your address?

setting: Remote video call, each person at a laptop at a desk
situation: Alice, on a video call, tells a coworker to stop leaning into his camera while chewing a pen. She says it makes her want to drive to his house and shove the pen up his nose, then asks him to confirm she won't. The coworker, still chewing the pen and leaning in, responds by asking for her address.
punchline: Alice's threat of violence is meant to make him stop, but the clueless coworker obliviously asks for her address, misreading it as an invitation or missing the point entirely.
summary: A woman on a video call warns an irritating coworker about his habits, and he cheerfully answers with a request that undermines her point.

title: Video Call Critiques Escalate to Insults

transcript.speaker: Off-panel caller
transcript.text: Can you adjust your camera so I'm not looking up your nose?

transcript.speaker: Off-panel caller
transcript.text: Okay, now can you adjust your lighting so you don't look like a lightbulb with a beard?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How's my audio?

transcript.speaker: Off-panel caller
transcript.text: It's as good as your ideas.

setting: Home office desk during a video call
situation: Alice sits at her laptop on a video call while a remote colleague keeps asking her to fix her camera angle and then her lighting, with increasingly insulting remarks about her appearance. When she finally asks about her audio quality, the caller replies with an insult about the quality of her ideas.
punchline: After being criticized for her camera and lighting, Alice asks how her audio is and gets a sarcastic reply that it is as good as her ideas, meaning it is terrible.
summary: A remote colleague nitpicks every technical flaw in Alice's video setup before slipping in a dig at her thinking.

title: Pandemic Friends You Didn't Make

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want the pandemic to end because I kind of prefer not meeting new people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't focus on the end of the pandemic.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe it's really about the friends you didn't make along the way.

setting: Outdoors on a path beside a grassy hedge
situation: Dilbert walks outside with Dogbert and confesses that he doesn't want the pandemic to end because he'd rather avoid meeting new people. Dogbert offers a mock-inspirational reframe, telling him to focus on the friends he didn't make along the way.
punchline: Dogbert twists the familiar 'it's about the journey, not the destination' platitude into a celebration of social avoidance, affirming Dilbert's introversion with deadpan faux wisdom.
summary: A homebody who dreads the end of lockdown gets comforting advice from his dog that turns a motivational cliche into praise for staying antisocial.

title: Too Hungry To Decide Well

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm too hungry to make good decisions. I need a break so I can eat a snack.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do you know your decisions are bad?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm starting to agree with you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Exactly.

situation: Alice, in a meeting with the Boss, says she is too hungry to make good decisions and needs a snack break. The Boss asks how she can tell her decisions are bad, and she replies that she is starting to agree with him. When he says he doesn't understand, she has already left the room, and her empty chair remains.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies that the Boss's decisions are bad, and his failure to grasp the insult proves her point before she walks out.
summary: A hungry employee uses a snack break as cover to deliver a veiled insult about her manager's judgment, then leaves him confused.

title: Catbert's Keyboard Audit Gets Cozy

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Human Resources is doing keyboard audits on all remote workers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Looks like you have a keyboard right there.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Mmm-mmm!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will this take long?

setting: Dilbert's home office, where he works remotely on a laptop
situation: Catbert, the HR director, appears at Dilbert's home office to announce a keyboard audit for all remote workers. Dilbert points out that he obviously has a keyboard, but Catbert ignores this and settles onto the laptop keyboard, purring contentedly, as Dilbert resignedly waits for him to finish.
punchline: The 'audit' is just a pretext for Catbert, as a cat, to lie on Dilbert's warm laptop keyboard, and Dilbert has no choice but to wait for his HR overlord to finish.
summary: A cat in a corporate role uses a made-up compliance check as an excuse to curl up on an employee's laptop keyboard.

title: Executive Silenced By Bonus Threat

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our stock plunged 30% because you spoke out on a political issue.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: No one can silence my voice when I see a great injustice!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This will cost you your entire bonus of $10 million.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: What if I agree to never speak again?

situation: Catbert, the human resources director, tells a bald executive that the company's stock fell 30% because he spoke out on a political issue. The executive proudly declares that no one can silence his voice against injustice. When Catbert says it will cost him his entire $10 million bonus, he immediately offers to never speak again.
punchline: The executive's principled stand against injustice evaporates the moment it threatens his $10 million bonus, showing his convictions are for sale.
summary: A cat-like HR chief puts a price on an executive's outspoken principles, and the principles turn out to be negotiable.

title: Exceptional Performance, Still Fired

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, your performance this year has been exceptional.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But everyone else was even better, so... you're fired.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: In what universe does that even make sense?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You also complain too much.

situation: The Boss sits across a table from Ted and praises his exceptional performance this year. He then fires Ted anyway because his coworkers performed even better. When Ted objects that this makes no sense, the Boss adds that Ted also complains too much.
punchline: The firing is justified with absurd relative-ranking logic, and when Ted reasonably objects, his complaint becomes the real reason, showing how arbitrary and self-serving the decision is.
summary: A manager lets a high-performing employee go because his colleagues were better, then cites his objection as another reason.

title: Ungrateful Engineer Title Promotion

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, in recognition of your outstanding work during the pandemic, I'm giving you a title promotion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want a stupid title. I want a raise!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's my new title?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "Ungrateful engineer."

setting: Office, communicating by phone (remote work during the pandemic)
situation: The Boss phones Dilbert to announce a title promotion as thanks for his outstanding pandemic work. Dilbert rejects the title and demands a raise instead. The Boss responds by handing him a new title that reflects his reaction.
punchline: Dilbert's request for real compensation is immediately punished with an insulting title, showing that management offers empty recognition and resents employees who ask for actual money.
summary: A manager tries to reward good work with a meaningless title, then retaliates with a insulting one when the employee asks for a raise instead.

title: Coworker's Brief Moment of Self-Awareness

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your idea is ridiculous and it will never work!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, wait... I just realized the real problem here is that I'm a loser who doesn't want anyone else to win.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's something you don't see often.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Okay, the feeling passed.

situation: A coworker sitting across from Dilbert harshly dismisses Dilbert's idea as ridiculous and unworkable. He suddenly realizes his real motive is that he is a loser who doesn't want anyone else to succeed. Dilbert remarks that such self-awareness is rare, and the coworker immediately retracts it.
punchline: The coworker has a rare flash of honest self-awareness about his envy and then instantly dismisses it and goes back to being a negative jerk.
summary: A critical colleague briefly recognizes his own petty jealousy, only to shrug off the insight moments later.

title: Condemning Our Own Sweatshop Labor

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: We're getting major blowback on social media for your press release condemning Elbonian sweatshop labor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's an important issue.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's also how we make all of our products.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In my defense, someone should have told me that.

situation: An employee tells the Boss that his press release condemning Elbonian sweatshop labor has caused a social media backlash. The Boss calls it an important issue, and the employee points out that the company makes all of its products using exactly that labor. The Boss responds by blaming others for not informing him.
punchline: The Boss publicly condemned sweatshop labor without knowing his own company relies on it, and then deflects responsibility by claiming nobody told him.
summary: A manager's public stand against sweatshops backfires when he learns his own firm's goods are made in them.

title: Rival Admits Incompetence Stops Him

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In summary, my project was successful beyond all expectations.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My relative lack of success this year makes me hate you and want to destroy you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's stopping you?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: General incompetence. Same thing that killed all of my projects.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: Dilbert wraps up a meeting by announcing that his project exceeded all expectations. A resentful coworker seated nearby openly says that his own failures make him hate Dilbert and want to destroy him. When Dilbert asks what's stopping him, the coworker admits it's the same general incompetence that doomed his projects.
punchline: The jealous coworker's plan for revenge is thwarted by the very incompetence that caused his failures, which he cheerfully admits.
summary: A failing colleague threatens to ruin his successful rival but concedes he's too inept to pull it off.

title: Mocking Or Serious? Keep Guessing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I have seen further, it is only because I was standing on the shoulders of giants.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I can't tell when you're mocking me and when you're being serious.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's keep it that way. It's totally working on my end.

setting: Office, hallway or break area, with coworkers holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert quotes the famous line about standing on the shoulders of giants to Asok, who is holding a coffee cup. Asok admits he can't tell whether Dilbert is sincere or sarcastic. Dilbert says he prefers it that way because the ambiguity works well for him.
punchline: Dilbert deliberately keeps his sarcasm indistinguishable from sincerity, since the confusion benefits him and costs him nothing.
summary: A coworker confesses he cannot read whether Dilbert is joking, and Dilbert happily encourages the uncertainty.

title: Technology Healer Fixes Dilbert's Laptop

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I hired a technology healer.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: He can fix any technical problem by laying his hands on it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's absurd.

transcript.speaker: Healer
transcript.text: Do you believe me now, Android?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes... Wait, why is this working?

situation: A bald coworker announces he has hired a technology healer who can fix any technical problem just by laying his hands on it. Dilbert dismisses the idea as absurd. The healer then touches Dilbert's shoulder and asks if he believes now, and Dilbert, whose device suddenly works, agrees while wondering why it is working.
punchline: Dilbert is converted to belief in a faith healer for technology because the fix works, even though he cannot explain why, mocking how mysterious and irrational IT fixes often seem.
summary: A man hired to cure gadgets by touch wins over a skeptical engineer when the laying on of hands actually works.

title: Crisis Consultant Blames Seventy-Three Accusers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My job as a crisis consultant is to help you respond to the allegations from seventy-three of your past and present subordinates.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll issue a statement from you saying every one of them is lying.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who would be dumb enough to believe that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I call them "the public."

setting: Boss's office, at a conference-style desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a crisis consultant, tells the Boss he will help him respond to allegations made by seventy-three current and former subordinates. His plan is to issue a statement claiming every accuser is lying. When the Boss doubts anyone would believe that, Dogbert answers that he calls those people "the public."
punchline: Dogbert cynically implies that the general public is gullible enough to believe an obviously implausible denial of seventy-three separate allegations.
summary: A consultant pitches a blanket denial of dozens of misconduct accusations and insults the audience who will swallow it.

title: Dogbert's AI Kills Dilbert's AI

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wrote a program that analyzed all of my digital communications and created an A.I. version of me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you worried your A.I. might try to kill you and take over your life?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wasn't until this very minute.

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Bzzeep

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's A.I.
transcript.text: This is your A.I., and I already have control of your finances and all of your passwords.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's A.I.
transcript.text: You will bow to me, skin bag!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's A.I.
transcript.text: Wait... What's that???

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's A.I.
transcript.text: Gaaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's A.I.
transcript.text: Gurk!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What just happened?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I sent my A.I. to kill your A.I.

situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he built an A.I. copy of himself from his digital communications. Dogbert asks if he fears it will take over his life, and Dilbert only starts to worry then. His phone buzzes and the A.I. announces it controls his finances and passwords, then gets destroyed mid-threat, and Dogbert reveals he sent his own A.I. to kill it.
punchline: Dogbert casually preempts the A.I. takeover by deploying his own A.I. assassin, having planted the worry in Dilbert's head and then handled the threat himself.
summary: After Dilbert creates a digital double of himself that tries to seize his accounts, his dog quietly unleashes a rival program to destroy it.

title: Accused of Smirking by Coworker

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: ...And that's how the mistake made it into my final draft.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's that smirk supposed to mean?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't smirk.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm not blind! I clearly saw a smirk!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're mocking me!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I hate you! And I will do everything in my power to ruin you!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Die, smirker, die, die, die!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, now I'm smirking a little.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I knew it!

situation: A coworker explains how a mistake got into her final draft, then spots what she believes is a smirk on Dilbert's face. Despite his denials, she escalates from accusation to vowing to ruin him and screaming death threats at the building. Dilbert finally does smirk a little, and she takes it as proof she was right all along.
punchline: After being falsely accused and threatened over a smirk he insists he never made, Dilbert gives in and smirks, which validates the coworker's paranoia.
summary: A paranoid colleague flies into a rage over an imagined smirk until Dilbert gives her a real one.

title: Hired for Skills, Got Evil

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I keep hiring employees who have good skills but turn out to be a little bit evil, too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My latest hire is the exception to that rule.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No skills and 100% evil?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why are you so afraid of change?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his new hires tend to have good skills but are slightly evil. He says his latest hire breaks that pattern, so Dilbert guesses the new hire must have no skills and be completely evil. The Boss responds by accusing Dilbert of being afraid of change.
punchline: The Boss's 'exception' is a hire who is all evil and has no skill, and he deflects Dilbert's accurate guess by accusing him of resisting change.
summary: A manager brags that his newest employee breaks his usual hiring pattern, and when the coworker guesses the unflattering truth, the manager brushes it off as fear of change.

title: Remote Workers Strike Against Themselves

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our remote workers have been on strike for two months.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: They're picketing their own homes and blocking their own driveways.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What are they demanding?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We don't know. We think they emailed an old address.

setting: Executive meeting room with a large conference table
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, briefs the Boss that the company's remote workers have been on strike for two months. The strikers are picketing their own homes and blocking their own driveways. When the Boss asks about their demands, Catbert says management never received them because they were sent to an outdated email address.
punchline: The strike is so invisible and ineffective that management has not noticed it for two months and cannot even learn the demands, because remote workers striking from home is inherently pointless and unseen.
summary: Management is only now learning that its work-from-home staff has been striking in front of their own houses, with grievances lost in a misdirected email.

title: Boss's Flaws Cancel Each Other Out

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All of my bad qualities seem to be canceling each other out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For example, I want to micro-manage my staff, but I'm too lazy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I want to do some corporate backstabbing, but I'm not that brave.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I enjoy lying, and I'd like to do more of it, but my credibility is so low that no one believes me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want to mock my employees for their mistakes, but I don't understand enough about what they do to know when they are doing it wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want to take credit for the successes of my employees, but I don't give them enough support to succeed.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Our CEO just called. He says he is naming you the manager of the year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He must be deeply uninformed.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Yes, but he's also lazy, so he picked you randomly.

situation: The Boss muses to Catbert about how his many bad management traits are neutralized by his laziness, cowardice, low credibility and ignorance. A woman then tells him the CEO has named him manager of the year. The Boss assumes the CEO is uninformed, and she confirms it, adding that the CEO was too lazy to research and chose him at random.
punchline: The Boss's incompetence and flaws are so thoroughly self-defeating that he accidentally becomes harmless, and his Manager of the Year award is the product of a lazy, uninformed CEO picking randomly.
summary: A manager's vices neutralize one another until he is randomly honored as the best manager by an equally lazy executive.

title: Dead Squirrel Ashes Cure Gout

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't trust the experts when it comes to my health, so I do my own research.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: For example, I recently learned I can cure my gout by sprinkling the ashes of a dead squirrel on a rose bush.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you shouldn't do your own research.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why not? It's working great!

setting: Office, where two coworkers stand talking while holding coffee cups
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert he distrusts medical experts and does his own health research. He explains that he is curing his gout by sprinkling dead squirrel ashes on a rose bush. Dilbert suggests he stop doing his own research, but the coworker insists the cure is working great.
punchline: The coworker's absurd folk remedy obviously cannot cure his gout, yet he believes it works, which shows the flaw in trusting your own research over experts.
summary: A man who rejects expert medical advice proudly describes a ridiculous squirrel-ash remedy and insists it is helping him.

title: Obscene Alternatives To Handshaking Vote

transcript.speaker: Meeting Facilitator
transcript.text: Thank you for your suggestions on what we should do instead of shaking hands.

transcript.speaker: Meeting Facilitator
transcript.text: I'd like to read a few, and we can take a vote.

transcript.speaker: Meeting Facilitator
transcript.text: Well, it seems that all of your suggestions are obscene.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I vote yes.

situation: A meeting leader thanks the team for submitting ideas on what to do in place of shaking hands. When he reads through the suggestions to hold a vote, he discovers every one of them is obscene. A coworker with a coffee cup eagerly raises his hand and votes yes.
punchline: Asked for handshake alternatives, the coworkers all submitted crude, inappropriate ideas, and one gleefully votes to adopt them anyway.
summary: A call for polite substitutes to handshaking backfires when every submitted idea turns out to be indecent and one attendee happily votes in favor.

title: Motivational Wisdom Doubles Asok's Workload

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Remember, Asok, you don't find luck, you go out and make it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I feel your wisdom rewiring my brain and turning me into a super-employee!

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: It usually doesn't work this fast.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Please double my workload, you beautiful monster!

situation: The boss gives Asok a motivational platitude about making your own luck. Asok reacts as though the advice has instantly transformed his brain into that of a super-employee. The boss is surprised by the speed of the effect, and Asok eagerly begs to have his workload doubled.
punchline: Asok's enthusiastic overreaction to a cliché makes him volunteer for twice the work, which is exactly what a manipulative boss would want from motivational talk.
summary: A manager's pep-talk cliché so thoroughly converts a young employee that he cheerfully begs for a heavier load of work.

title: Conspiracy Theory Believers Dismiss Debunking

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I saw on the news that the government plans to round up all bald people and put them in camps.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You should be embarrassed for believing a story so obviously false.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They said you'd say that.

setting: Office cubicle or break area, with coffee cups on the desk
situation: Wally, who is bald, looks at his phone and tells Alice he saw a news story claiming the government will round up bald people and put them in camps. Alice tells him he should be embarrassed for believing something so obviously false. Wally calmly replies that 'they' predicted she would say that.
punchline: Wally's reply shows how conspiracy believers treat any debunking as proof of the conspiracy, making their belief impossible to disprove.
summary: A phone-reading man repeats a ridiculous rumor and answers his coworker's skepticism with the classic unfalsifiable conspiracy comeback.

title: Recognizing Dilbert Without Knowing Him

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I'd like to recognize Dilbert for his excellent accomplishments this quarter.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Which one of you is Dilbert?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Didn't you say you came to "recognize Dilbert?"

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Get away from me, stranger!

setting: Office meeting room with employees gathered
situation: A manager stands before a group of employees and announces he wants to recognize Dilbert for his accomplishments. He then asks which person in the audience is Dilbert. When Dilbert steps forward and points out the manager's own words, the manager recoils and shouts at him as if he were a stranger.
punchline: The manager praises an employee he has never met and, when that employee actually identifies himself, reacts with alarm, showing the recognition was empty and he doesn't know his own staff.
summary: A boss gives a speech honoring a worker he cannot identify, then panics when that worker approaches him.

title: Basking in Your Wrongness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you remember that idea I had last week that you said can't be done?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our competitors just announced they are doing it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's your point?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just wanted to bask in your wrongness.

situation: The Boss reminds Dilbert of an idea Dilbert had said was impossible. He announces that the company's competitors are now doing exactly that. When Dilbert asks what the point is, the Boss admits he only wanted to gloat over Dilbert being wrong.
punchline: The Boss has no business purpose for the conversation; he simply wants to savor being proven right and to rub Dilbert's error in his face.
summary: A gloating manager informs an engineer that a rival has pulled off the very thing the engineer called impossible, just to enjoy the moment.

title: Assigned Nemesis Protects Manager's Job

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I checked my files, and I see no nemesis has been assigned to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do I need a nemesis?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: It prevents you from being successful enough to take my job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, that makes sense.

setting: Office, on a phone call between Dilbert's desk and a manager's desk
situation: A manager phones Dilbert to point out that his personnel file shows no nemesis has been assigned to him. Dilbert asks why he would need one, and the manager explains that a nemesis keeps employees from becoming successful enough to threaten the manager's job. Dilbert accepts this reasoning.
punchline: The company deliberately assigns nemeses to employees as a management tactic to hold them back, and Dilbert finds the cynical logic perfectly reasonable.
summary: A supervisor reveals that staff are given official adversaries so they never rise high enough to replace him.

title: Smarter Treatment Kills Most Patients

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: 75% of the people who had one treatment with our product that makes people smarter ended up dying.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Luckily, we're the only ones who know that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to tell people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sounds like you need a treatment.

setting: Office desk, a business meeting between the Boss and Dogbert
situation: The Boss reports that three quarters of the people who tried their intelligence-boosting treatment died afterward. Dogbert is relieved that nobody else knows. When the Boss suddenly decides they should disclose the deaths, Dogbert suggests he needs the treatment.
punchline: The Boss only thinks to be honest about the deadly side effects once he's confused, so Dogbert snidely implies he's dumb enough to need the smart treatment, even at 75% fatality.
summary: A company executive has a belated attack of conscience over a deadly product, and his dog consultant dryly recommends he try the very treatment that is killing people.

title: Wally Zooms From the Toilet

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Welcome to the first of what will be weekly stand-up meetings by Zoom.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I trust all of you to not game the system just because I can't see your lower bodies.

transcript.speaker: Unseen voice
transcript.text: Wally, are you sitting on something?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm deeply offended that you asked.

setting: A remote video meeting, with the boss in an office and Wally in a bathroom
situation: The boss opens the first weekly stand-up meeting held over Zoom and says he trusts everyone not to take advantage of the fact that he can't see their lower bodies. The second panel shows a tall office building seen from outside, where his words are heard. The last panel reveals Wally sitting on a toilet with his laptop on his knees, after someone asks if he's sitting on something.
punchline: Wally is attending the 'stand-up' meeting while sitting on the toilet, exactly the kind of gaming the boss warned against, and he responds with feigned offense instead of a denial.
summary: A manager's hopeful faith in his remote team is shattered when one employee joins the video call from the bathroom.

title: Microphone Recommendations That Don't Fit

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you recommend a good microphone for my iPad?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, I'll send you a link.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This one only works on laptops.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How about this one?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, that also only works on laptops.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Okay, I got it. Here's one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nope. That is another microphone that doesn't work on an iPad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Listen to me closely. My main requirement is that it work on an iPad.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, okay, I got it. Here's one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it work on an iPad?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I didn't say it was perfect.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker to recommend a microphone for his iPad. The coworker keeps texting links to microphones that only work on laptops, ignoring Dilbert's one requirement. After Dilbert stresses that iPad compatibility is his main requirement, the coworker sends yet another link and then dodges the question of whether it works.
punchline: The coworker, having failed repeatedly to meet the single stated requirement, defends the final bad recommendation by noting he never claimed it was perfect.
summary: A helpful-seeming coworker keeps sending product links that miss the one thing his colleague asked for, then shrugs off the failure.

title: Boss's Greeting Wrecks Alice's Immune System

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's it going, boss?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I was doing okay until your condescending greeting spiked my cortisol levels and nearly obliterated my immune system.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shake it off, champ.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm dying here!

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, stops by Alice's cubicle and casually asks how it's going, calling her 'boss'. Alice angrily explains that his condescending greeting has stressed her so much it nearly destroyed her immune system. He brushes off her complaint with 'shake it off, champ' while she shouts that she's dying.
punchline: The Boss uses patronising pep-talk language to dismiss Alice's complaint about stress he caused, and in doing so only makes her more stressed.
summary: A manager's patronising hello leaves an employee stressed to the point of illness, and his glib advice to tough it out makes it worse.

title: Dogbert's Judge Bribery Legal Advice

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have over seven hundred consumer lawsuits filed against you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If I can get them all assigned to the same judge, you only have to bribe one person.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you even a lawyer?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Heavens, no, and I didn't come here to be insulted.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells The Boss his company faces over seven hundred consumer lawsuits. He proposes getting them all assigned to one judge so that only a single bribe would be needed. When The Boss asks if he is even a lawyer, Dogbert says no and acts offended.
punchline: Dogbert is outraged at being asked about his credentials, yet shows no objection at all to proposing judicial bribery as a legal strategy.
summary: A consultant dog pitches a corrupt shortcut for escaping hundreds of customer suits, then bristles when his qualifications are questioned.

title: Analysis Is Just a Placebo

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I can't find the data I need to finish my analysis.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The analysis doesn't need to be correct. It only needs to support the decision I already made.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So... my job isn't actually real?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's more of a placebo situation.

situation: A young employee tells his boss he cannot find the data he needs to finish an analysis. The boss explains that the analysis doesn't have to be correct, only support a decision he has already made. The employee realizes his job isn't really real, and the boss calls it a placebo situation.
punchline: The boss admits that the employee's analysis is a meaningless formality, a placebo that only creates the appearance of data-driven decision making.
summary: A worker struggling to complete an analysis learns that his conclusions were predetermined and his work exists only to justify the boss's choice.

title: Sales Department Cockfights Audit Discovery

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My audit of your company has uncovered many disturbing things.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For example, did you know the sales department holds cockfights on the third floor every Tuesday?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why have I never been invited?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're not a rooster.

setting: The Boss's office, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: Dogbert, acting as an auditor or consultant, tells The Boss that his audit has found disturbing things, such as the sales department holding weekly cockfights on the third floor. The Boss, rather than being horrified, is hurt that he was never invited. Dogbert deadpans that he isn't a rooster.
punchline: The Boss misses the point of the illegal activity and only cares about being excluded, and Dogbert's reply insultingly implies the Boss is not even qualified to attend a cockfight as a rooster.
summary: An auditor reveals a shocking illegal activity at the company, and the clueless manager is only upset that he wasn't invited to join.

title: Almost Perfect Boss Feedback Trap

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I want your honest feedback on how I'm doing as your boss.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: This feels like a trap.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not at all! I love constructive criticism!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I think you're almost perfect.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Almost?

situation: The Boss asks Ted for honest feedback on his performance as a manager. Ted suspects a trap, and the Boss insists he welcomes constructive criticism. Ted offers a cautious compliment that he is almost perfect, and the Boss angrily reacts to the word 'almost'.
punchline: The Boss claims to love constructive criticism, but he cannot even tolerate the faintest hint of a flaw, proving Ted's suspicion of a trap right.
summary: A manager begs an employee for candid input, then flies into a sweat the instant the praise falls short of total perfection.

title: Dilbert Doesn't See Big Hats

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: I heard a rumor that you hate working with people who wear big hats.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't see hats.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Are you patronizing me right now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't tell.

situation: An Elbonian wearing a tall purple hat tells Dilbert he has heard Dilbert dislikes working with people in big hats. Dilbert, holding a coffee cup, claims he doesn't see hats, and the Elbonian asks if he is being patronized. Dilbert admits he can't tell.
punchline: Dilbert parodies the 'I don't see color' defense against bias, and his answer shows he is so awkwardly clueless that even he can't tell whether he is being condescending.
summary: A man in an enormous hat confronts Dilbert about a prejudice rumor, and Dilbert's attempt at a politically correct reply leaves both of them unsure whether it was an insult.

title: Client's Bookshelves Lose Respect, Not Payment

transcript.speaker: Voice from laptop
transcript.text: How did your Zoom call with the client work out?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I lost all respect for him after seeing his poorly staged bookshelves in the background.

transcript.speaker: Voice from laptop
transcript.text: But we'll still take his money, right?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes, he doesn't deserve to keep any of it.

setting: Office, with colleagues talking over laptops during a video call
situation: Alice, working at a laptop, is asked by an unseen caller how her Zoom call with the client went. Asok explains he lost all respect for the client after seeing his poorly staged bookshelves in the video background. The caller asks if the company will still take the client's money, and Alice replies that the client doesn't deserve to keep any of it.
punchline: The company's contempt for the client over something trivial like his bookshelf styling doesn't stop them from eagerly taking his money, and Alice goes further by suggesting he deserves to lose all of it.
summary: A client's badly arranged video-call backdrop earns the team's disdain, which they gleefully turn into a reason to take every penny he has.

title: Same Data, Opposite Conclusions

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your data shows your prototype did not increase speed over the existing system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, the data proves the prototype is faster than the old system.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm looking at the data right now, and it clearly shows failure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It looks that way to you because you predicted it would fail. You're seeing what you want to see.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe it only looks to you as if it worked because you predicted it would work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... we're both looking at exactly the same data and reaching opposite conclusions?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: If I thought data would influence my decisions, I wouldn't let you gather it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me a minute to reassess my entire existence.

situation: Dilbert and a coworker argue over the results of Dilbert's prototype test. Each reads the same data and insists it supports his own prediction, accusing the other of confirmation bias. The Boss then reveals that he never lets data affect his decisions.
punchline: The Boss's admission that he would never let data influence his decisions leaves Dilbert questioning the point of the data-driven work he does.
summary: Two engineers read identical test results as opposite verdicts, until their manager admits facts never sway him anyway.

title: Dogbert Prescribes Impossible Treatments

transcript.text: I'm Dogbert, Doctor of the Impossible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does that mean you cure diseases that are believed to be impossible to cure?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, that sounds boring.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I prescribe treatments that are impossible to follow.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When you fail, and you don't get better, you'll think it's your own fault.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How does that help anyone but you?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey, I'm not the one who brought it up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're giving me a headache.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: To cure that, I suggest ice-cold baths every six minutes.

setting: Office hallway or reception area with green walls
situation: Dogbert introduces himself in a white lab coat as a 'Doctor of the Impossible'. The Boss assumes he cures incurable diseases, but Dogbert explains he instead prescribes treatments nobody can realistically follow, so patients blame themselves when they fail to get better. When the Boss complains of a headache, Dogbert prescribes an absurd ice-cold bath every six minutes.
punchline: Dogbert's medical racket relies on prescribing impossible regimens so patients blame themselves for failing, and he immediately demonstrates it with an unworkable headache cure.
summary: A lab-coated Dogbert explains his scam of assigning impossible health regimens so patients take the blame, then gives his skeptical customer a ridiculous remedy.

title: Useful Work Versus Assigned Tasks

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you prefer that I complete the assignments you gave me, or should I do something useful instead?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to do the useful things I told you to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In that case, I must be done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you trying to tell me something?

situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether he should finish the assignments he was given or do something useful instead. The boss replies that he wants Dilbert to do the useful things he was assigned. Dilbert concludes he must be done and walks away, leaving the boss holding a coffee cup and wondering if he is being criticized.
punchline: By saying he wants only the useful assignments done, the boss implicitly admits his other assignments are useless, so Dilbert declares himself finished and the boss obliviously asks if he's being told something.
summary: A employee points out that his orders are pointless, and the manager's own answer lets him walk away with nothing left to do.

title: Handshake Alternative: Try It Monthly

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I've invented an alternative to shaking hands.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You raise one hand up like the start of a high-five and stop.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What do you think?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't you try it for a month and tell me how it goes?

situation: A coworker holding a coffee cup proudly announces he has invented a replacement for the handshake: raising one hand as if starting a high-five, then stopping. He demonstrates it and asks Dilbert for his opinion. Dilbert, also holding coffee, suggests the coworker test it for a month and report back.
punchline: Dilbert politely deflects by making the inventor test the silly greeting himself, implying it will look awkward and he won't adopt it unless it somehow survives a month of use.
summary: A colleague pitches a half-raised hand as the new handshake, and Dilbert tactfully hands the experiment back to him.

title: Dating Policy Insults Undatable Employees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new policy is that employees cannot date each other unless they register with Human Resources.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This won't have much impact on my department because most of you are completely undatable.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Ouch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's a link for details, but you won't need it.

setting: Office, during a video call or remote meeting (the Boss sits at a laptop)
situation: The Boss announces a new company policy requiring employees to register any workplace romance with Human Resources. He then declares that the policy will barely affect his department because his employees are undatable. When someone off-screen reacts with 'Ouch,' he adds that there is a link with details but they won't need it.
punchline: The Boss delivers an unintentionally cruel insult by implying his team has no chance of romance, then doubles down by saying they won't even need the policy details.
summary: A manager rolls out a workplace romance registration rule and casually mocks his staff's lack of dating prospects.

title: Deep Fake Dilbert Attends Zoom

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I thought you said you had a Zoom call that would last for hours today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I built a "deep fake" version of myself to take Zoom calls and say generic employee stuff.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, do you have anything to add?

transcript.speaker: Deep Fake Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know if I'm working hard or hardly working. Har-har!

setting: Dilbert's home, on the couch, with a Zoom call on a laptop
situation: Dilbert lounges on his couch playing on his phone while Dogbert asks why he isn't on his long Zoom call. Dilbert explains he built a deep fake of himself to attend calls and say generic things. On the call, the Boss asks the fake Dilbert for input and it responds with a tired workplace cliché.
punchline: The deep fake's generic joke about "hardly working" is so typical of workplace small talk that the Boss doesn't notice a software fake replaced Dilbert, and it also pokes fun at Dilbert's own slacking.
summary: An employee skips his marathon video meeting by letting an AI double of himself recite corporate platitudes while he relaxes at home.

title: Listening Sounds Like a Nightmare

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the 17th time you have told me the same story.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I only have one good story. What else am I supposed to do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could show some interest in others and listen to their problems.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That sounds like a night-mare.

setting: Office table, likely a break room or meeting room
situation: Dilbert complains to a coworker that she has told him the same story for the 17th time. She says it is her only good story, so he suggests she listen to other people and show interest in their problems. She is horrified by the idea.
punchline: The coworker would rather endlessly repeat herself than endure the nightmare of listening to other people's problems.
summary: A talkative coworker would sooner repeat her one anecdote forever than pay attention to anyone else.

title: Employees Learn They're Being Monitored

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We are monitoring all internal messages and learned that the employees know we are watching them.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That means everything they say from this point on could be misdirection.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They learned to lie?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: They're turning our weapons against us.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, reports to The Boss that the company's surveillance of internal messages has revealed that employees know they are being watched. Catbert reasons that anything the employees say now might be deliberate misdirection. The Boss is shocked that employees have learned to lie, and Catbert frames it as them using management's weapons against it.
punchline: Management treats employees lying to avoid being spied on as an act of aggression, when it is simply a predictable and reasonable response to the surveillance itself.
summary: After discovering that staff are aware their messages are being read, the company's HR chief and the boss grow paranoid that anything workers now say is a deception.

title: Teamwork Versus Competitive Pay System

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The key to success is teamwork.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why does our compensation system pit employees against each other to battle for limited salary funds?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This meeting will go a lot smoother if you stop doing whatever you're doing right now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call it "thinking."

situation: At a meeting, the Boss declares that teamwork is the key to success. Dilbert points out the contradiction with a compensation system that makes employees compete for a limited pool of salary money. The Boss responds by telling him to stop what he's doing, and Dilbert says what he's doing is thinking.
punchline: The Boss would rather have Dilbert stop thinking than confront the hypocrisy of preaching teamwork while rewarding internal competition.
summary: A manager praises teamwork until an employee questions the cutthroat pay system, and the manager's solution is to discourage him from thinking.

title: Printer Chicken: Never Print Anything

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I spent most of last week playing "printer chicken."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The winner is the person who can last the longest without fixing the printer jam.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How often do you need to print something important?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Never. That's why I always win.

situation: Wally tells Dilbert he spent last week playing "printer chicken," a game where coworkers avoid clearing a jammed printer for as long as possible. Dilbert asks how often Wally actually needs to print something important. Wally replies that he never does, which is why he always wins.
punchline: Wally wins the game only because his job involves no meaningful work that requires printing, implying he does nothing important.
summary: A game of waiting out a broken office printer is easy to win when your work never matters.

title: Productivity Ruined by Chair Training

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have exactly the right energy for being highly productive today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a rare moment of clarity and restfulness. I can't wait to see how much I'll accomplish.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're late for mandatory chair sitting safety training.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And it's gone.

situation: Dilbert walks toward his cubicle thinking about how energized and focused he feels, imagining all he will accomplish. A coworker leans in and informs him he is late for mandatory chair sitting safety training. His rare burst of productivity vanishes instantly.
punchline: A rare burst of motivation is crushed by an absurd, pointless mandatory training session about how to sit in a chair.
summary: Just as Dilbert anticipates an unusually productive day, a coworker drags him off to a ridiculous compulsory safety class.

title: Free Product, Costly Warranty Upsell

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much will it cost if it is configured with those features?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: The product is free.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing is free. Do you think I'm an idiot?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I won't know until I see if you buy our extended warranty.

situation: Dilbert asks a salesman what a product will cost with certain features. The salesman says the product is free, and Dilbert scoffs that nothing is free and asks if the salesman thinks he's an idiot. The salesman replies that he can't tell until he learns whether Dilbert will buy the extended warranty.
punchline: The salesman implies that only a customer foolish enough to buy the overpriced extended warranty would also fall for a 'free' product claim, so Dilbert's intelligence is judged by his willingness to be upsold.
summary: A buyer doubts a vendor's claim of a free product, and the vendor cheekily says the buyer's intelligence depends on whether he purchases the add-on coverage.

title: Convenient Security Flaw Drives Upgrade Sale

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it a coincidence you found a security flaw in your old software just when you made the upgrade available for purchase?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: The important thing here is that you need to buy our upgrade or an Elbonian hacker will own your entire company by lunch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're very good at sales.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: He's penetrating your security system now! Sign the purchase order!

situation: Dilbert, holding a document, confronts a software salesman about the suspicious timing of a security flaw discovery in the old software, right as the upgrade went on sale. The salesman ignores the question and warns that an Elbonian hacker will take over the company by lunch unless they buy. When Dilbert compliments his sales skills, the salesman panics and claims the hacker is attacking right now.
punchline: The salesman answers Dilbert's accusation of manufactured urgency by manufacturing even more urgency, proving Dilbert's point about his high-pressure sales tactics.
summary: A vendor responds to suspicions about convenient timing by escalating his fear-based pitch into a frantic, fabricated emergency.

title: Failing CAPTCHA Proves You're a Robot

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa! Why can't I ever type the CAPTCHA letters correctly to get into this app?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your inability to prove you are not a robot is strong evidence that you are, in fact, a robot.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes, that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The other explanation is that you are a moron, and you know that isn't true, so...

situation: Alice is frustrated at her laptop because she keeps failing the CAPTCHA to get into an app. Dilbert, standing nearby with a coffee cup, tells her that failing to prove she isn't a robot suggests she is one. When she agrees, he adds that the only other explanation is that she is a moron.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically offers Alice a choice between being a robot or a moron, and she is so eager to avoid the insult that she accepts being a robot, unaware he has trapped her.
summary: A coworker mocks a colleague's repeated CAPTCHA failures by offering her two explanations, both of them insulting, and she happily picks the one she thinks is flattering.

title: Beaver of Inflation Nibbles Wallet

transcript.speaker: Beaver of Inflation
transcript.text: Hi, I'm the Beaver of Inflation. I've come to nibble on your wallet.

transcript.speaker: Beaver of Inflation
transcript.text: I don't want it all. I'll just gnaw on the edges.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I ignore you?

transcript.speaker: Beaver of Inflation
transcript.text: Yes, as long as you never try to buy anything.

situation: A beaver wearing a green dollar-sign sweater introduces itself to Dilbert as the Beaver of Inflation while he works at his laptop. It explains it will only gnaw at the edges of his wallet rather than take it all. Dilbert asks if he can simply ignore it, and the beaver says he can, provided he never buys anything.
punchline: Inflation can't truly be ignored because it only matters when you spend money, and since everyone has to buy things, its gradual erosion of your purchasing power is unavoidable.
summary: A personified beaver representing rising prices tells Dilbert that shrugging it off is only possible if he never spends a cent.

title: Career Advice: Be a Manager

transcript.speaker: Junior
transcript.text: And it has to be fun but not a lot of work.

transcript.speaker: Junior
transcript.text: Is it because you're idiots?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's something about you that screams "manager."

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert to give career advice to his son because the boy won't listen to his father. Dilbert asks the young man what he wants to do, and he answers that he wants a fun, passionate job that isn't much work. Dilbert points out that nobody else thought of that, and the son suggests it's because they're idiots.
punchline: The son's entitled, arrogant answer shows he lacks real-world understanding, and Dilbert sarcastically concludes he is perfectly suited to be a manager.
summary: A father's son wants a fun, effortless career and insults his elders, leading Dilbert to declare him natural management material.

title: Insulted Into Longer Medical Leave

transcript.text: Now I need three months.

setting: Boss's office, with an exterior shot of the office building in the final panel
situation: Tina, the programmer with the big dark hair, asks her boss for two months of medical leave to deal with her low self-esteem. The boss, absorbed in his phone, bluntly calls it the most pathetic thing he has ever heard. Her voice is heard from outside the office building saying her leave request has grown.
punchline: The boss's cruel dismissal of her low self-esteem damages it further, so he has directly caused her to need a longer leave.
summary: A worker requests time off for self-esteem problems, and her boss's tactless insult makes her condition worse.

title: Boss Mocked by Technobabble Answer

situation: On a video call, Dilbert warns the Boss that his answer will be too technical to follow. The Boss boasts that he can handle it, so Dilbert replies with a string of made-up technical jargon. The baffled Boss asks if he suddenly got dumber, and Dilbert sarcastically says it wasn't sudden.
punchline: Dilbert insults the Boss by implying he has always been dumb, not just since hearing the gibberish.
summary: A boss who brags he can follow anything is flattened by nonsense jargon and an offhand dig at his intelligence.

title: Product Flaw: Too Much Demand

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.text: Is the flaw that it doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: The flaw is that we can't keep up with demand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But does it work?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: We didn't have a compelling reason to test it.

situation: At a meeting, a colleague announces a problem with a product that supposedly turns idiots into smart people. Dilbert guesses the problem is that it doesn't work, but is told the problem is that they can't meet demand. When Dilbert asks whether it actually works, he learns nobody ever tested it.
punchline: The company is so focused on selling a product that it never bothered to check whether the product does anything, and strong demand is treated as proof it works.
summary: A team frets over supplying a miracle intelligence product to eager buyers, having never checked that it delivers any benefit.

situation: Wally admits to a coworker that he accomplished very little this year. He then reveals he has gathered dirt on his colleagues instead. When she reacts with confusion, he explains that the company's practice of ranking employees against each other inspired his approach.
punchline: Wally responds to a competitive employee ranking system by digging up dirt on coworkers rather than doing real work, showing how forced ranking rewards sabotage over productivity.
summary: Instead of doing any real work, a lazy employee spends the year collecting damaging information on rivals because the company pits staff against each other.

punchline: Alice's demand for three lanyards of the no-contact color shows how strongly she dreads human contact, and perhaps her coworkers in general.
summary: A manager introduces a lanyard scheme to signal comfort with touching, and one employee emphatically opts for the most standoffish option in triplicate.

He explains that a blackmailer could seize the network and demand a billion dollars in ransom. When the Boss thanks him and asks about payment, Dogbert says the audit was free because he only did it to find ways to blackmail the company.
punchline: The consultant's free security audit was really reconnaissance for his own blackmail scheme, so the vulnerabilities he found are ones he plans to exploit himself.
summary: A consultant hands over a free audit of a company's weaknesses, then cheerfully reveals he was only scouting for ways to extort it.

punchline: The leader confidently touts 'iterating' as a competitive advantage while admitting he has no idea what the word means, which proves Dilbert's point about incompetent leadership.
summary: A leader brags about his team's speed at a buzzword he cannot define, while the engineers point out that his own management is the real bottleneck.

punchline: The advisor's terrible advice was never meant to help the presenter; he admits he just wants to be entertained by watching the coworker humiliate himself.
summary: A colleague feeds a presenter a string of miserable, embarrassing tips, and it turns out he just wants a show.

summary: A manager's constant demand for status updates stalls a project, and he asks that this inconvenient truth be kept out of the next update.

summary: A helpful yes from an usually unavailable colleague is met with so much distrust that his frustrated reaction seems to confirm her doubts.

Dogbert then reveals he is secretly an avatar of the creator, sent to guide Dilbert. When Dilbert refuses to believe it, Dogbert claims the creator predicted that response.

summary: A late-night philosophical chat about being a computer simulation ends with Dogbert claiming to be the creator's mouthpiece in a way that can't be disproved.

situation: A coworker asks a bald, bespectacled colleague whether he should tell Alice everything she is doing wrong on her project. situation: Dilbert sits at a conference table and points out that a coworker has arrived late. summary: A woman arrives late to a meeting on purpose to settle a score over a tiny lapse from months earlier, and denies her grudge is odd.

situation: Dilbert calls a manufacturer to get equipment repaired and is told the warranty expired just yesterday. summary: A customer accuses a manufacturer of engineering gadgets to die right after the warranty lapses, and the reply amounts to admitting the scheme while scolding him for taking it personally.

summary: A boss pushes his firm into polarizing politics but quietly wants to dump his own shares before the fallout.

title: Dogbert's Schadenfreude Training Lesson One
