transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I feel like a loser.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Which delights me. That was your first lesson.

setting: A hallway leading to Dogbert's training room, then Dogbert's desk
situation: Dilbert walks toward a sign advertising Dogbert's Schadenfreude Training and asks how much the class costs. Dogbert replies that anyone who has to ask can't afford it, which makes Dilbert feel like a loser. Dogbert says his delight at that reaction was the first lesson.
punchline: Dogbert demonstrates schadenfreude, taking pleasure in someone else's misfortune, by humiliating Dilbert and then declaring the humiliation to be the course's first lesson.
summary: A prospective student asks about tuition for a course on enjoying others' misery and gets an instant, humiliating demonstration.

title: DNA Predicts Wally's Supply Theft

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, according to your DNA, the odds of you stealing office supplies later this week are nearly 100%.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That sounds like junk science.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: He refuses to listen to experts.

situation: Catbert, acting as an expert, tells Wally that his DNA shows he is nearly certain to steal office supplies this week. Wally dismisses the prediction as junk science. Catbert then turns to a coworker and complains that Wally won't listen to experts.
punchline: Wally rejects the expert's finding as junk science, which the expert treats as proof that Wally ignores experts, so the denial itself becomes part of the accusation.
summary: A scheming red cat announces a genetic forecast of Wally's petty theft, and Wally's dismissal of it gets turned into a complaint about his stubbornness.

title: Dilbert Considers Marriage Over Vacation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have two weeks of vacation I need to use by year end.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I take an inconvenient and expensive trip to someplace I've already seen in photos and videos?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or should I hang around at home feeling useless and bored?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could volunteer to help the less fortunate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate the less fortunate because they're all happier than I am.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe you need a wife to make you do things you don't want to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not a bad idea. Are there any other benefits of marriage?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes. For example, you'll never need to wonder if you have any major character flaws.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy path and hillside during a walk
situation: Dilbert walks with Dogbert while pondering how to spend two weeks of leftover vacation, rejecting travel, staying home, and volunteering. Dogbert suggests he get a wife to force him into doing things he doesn't want to do. Dilbert warms to the idea and asks about other benefits of marriage.
punchline: Dogbert's sarcastic 'benefit' of marriage is that a spouse will constantly point out your major character flaws, so you'll never have to wonder about them.
summary: While deciding what to do with unused time off, Dilbert is steered by Dogbert toward marriage, sold on the perk of having his faults endlessly pointed out.

title: Dogbert's Zoom Camera Warning

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's tips for Zoom calls

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Never assume your camera is turned off.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As Mark Twain once advised, dance like no one is watching, but Zoom like seven hundred nuns with smartphones are watching.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Twain was way ahead of his time.

setting: Dogbert's desk, with an office building shown in the middle panel
situation: Dogbert sits at a desk and delivers a tip for video calls: never assume your camera is off. He then twists a Mark Twain-style quote into a warning to behave as though a crowd of nuns with smartphones is watching every Zoom call. He closes by remarking that Twain was far ahead of his time.
punchline: Dogbert absurdly credits Mark Twain with anticipating Zoom etiquette, while the imagined audience of seven hundred nuns with smartphones underlines how easily a call can expose you.
summary: Dogbert gives remote workers a mock-wise piece of advice about videoconferencing, borrowing a famous author's quote to say they should always act as if watched.

title: Making the Boss Dumber On Purpose

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I'd be more effective at work if my boss were either smarter, so he'd understand me...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...or dumber, so he'd know it's better to let me make all of the technical decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I can't make him any smarter, so my plan is to make him dumber.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It seems I've been a bad influence.

setting: A couch, apparently during a conversation with Dogbert
situation: Dilbert sits on a couch and explains to Dogbert that he would be more effective if his boss were either smarter or dumber. Since he cannot make the boss smarter, he announces he will make him dumber instead. Dogbert reacts by noting that he must have been a bad influence on Dilbert.
punchline: Dilbert's plan to deliberately dumb down his boss is so devious that Dogbert, usually the schemer, concludes he has corrupted Dilbert.
summary: Dilbert lays out a scheme to sabotage his manager's intelligence, leaving his scheming dog companion feeling responsible for the bad idea.

title: Walking Back Things Never Said

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's this I hear about you wanting to replace our network with a knotted rope?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's dumb. I've never said anything like that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll tell everyone you're walking it back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tell them I never said it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll tell them you moved the goalposts.

situation: A coworker confronts Dilbert about a rumor that he wants to replace the company network with a knotted rope. Dilbert denies ever saying it, but the coworker says she will tell everyone he is walking it back. When Dilbert asks her to tell them he never said it, she replies she will say he moved the goalposts.
punchline: Whatever Dilbert says, even a flat denial, gets spun as backpedaling or goalpost-moving, so he can never win against a rumor.
summary: A coworker twists every denial of an absurd rumor into proof of backpedaling, leaving the accused with no way to clear his name.

title: No Way To Win Against Bigotry

transcript.speaker: Asok's Coworker
transcript.text: I hear you're marrying an Elbonian man to avoid being called a bigot.

transcript.speaker: Asok's Coworker
transcript.text: But it doesn't work that way. You can still be a bigot in your mind, no matter what you do in the real world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... there's no way to win?

transcript.speaker: Asok's Coworker
transcript.text: Did I forget to tell you that when I hired you?

setting: Office cubicle, with an office building shown in the final panel
situation: A coworker in an orange sweater with a topknot hairstyle talks to Dilbert, who sits at his desk. The coworker says that marrying an Elbonian man to avoid being called a bigot won't work, because you can still be a bigot in your mind regardless of your actions. Dilbert concludes there is no way to win, and the speaker admits he should have mentioned that when he hired him.
punchline: The no-win bigotry trap is presented as a hidden condition of the job, as if being unable to ever win was part of the hiring terms that nobody mentioned.
summary: A manager explains that outward actions can never clear you of bigotry in your own head, leaving his employee with a no-win situation he apparently signed up for unknowingly.

title: Faking Empathy For Crazy Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert doesn't believe me when I tell him I need more alone time for my mental health.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why would he listen to you when you're obviously crazy?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate talking to you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Should I fake more empathy?

situation: Dilbert walks with a bald, green-shirted coworker holding a coffee and complains that Dogbert won't believe he needs more alone time for his mental health. The coworker bluntly replies that nobody would listen to someone so obviously crazy. Dilbert says he hates talking to him, and the coworker asks if he should fake more empathy.
punchline: The coworker's insulting reply is followed by an offer to fake empathy, showing he is utterly tactless and that his sympathy would only ever be an act.
summary: A man seeking sympathy about his need for solitude gets insulted by a blunt colleague who then offers to pretend to care.

title: Salesperson Admits Lying In Person

transcript.speaker: Salesperson (phone)
transcript.text: Can we meet for lunch so I can show you our new line of products?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Show it to me by email.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson (phone)
transcript.text: I can't do that because no one buys our products unless we lie in person.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson (phone)
transcript.text: How about I send our most attractive salesperson to have lunch with you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That'll work.

setting: Dilbert's desk in an office, on a call with a salesperson via laptop
situation: A vendor's salesperson calls Dilbert and asks to meet for lunch to pitch a new product line. Dilbert asks for the information by email, and the salesperson candidly admits their products only sell when they lie in person. The salesperson then offers to send their most attractive colleague, and Dilbert happily accepts.
punchline: Dilbert is told outright that the pitch relies on in-person lying, yet he agrees to it as soon as an attractive salesperson is offered, showing how easily buyers are swayed by looks rather than facts.
summary: A vendor confesses that its goods only sell through face-to-face deception, and the buyer cheerfully agrees to a lunch once a good-looking rep is promised.

title: Engineer Distrusts Data Before Network Upgrade

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll need more data before making a decision on the network upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that because you are the last person on Earth who still trusts data to be accurate and also properly contextualized?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do you make everything sound like a bad idea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm an engineer.

situation: The Boss says he needs more data before deciding on a network upgrade. Dilbert responds by sarcastically asking if he is the last person who trusts data to be accurate and properly contextualized. The Boss complains that Dilbert makes everything sound like a bad idea, and Dilbert explains it's because he's an engineer.
punchline: Engineers are so deeply skeptical about data quality and context that they make any plan sound doomed, and Dilbert treats this pessimism as simply part of his job.
summary: A manager wanting more information for a decision gets a cynical rebuttal about data reliability, which the engineer blames on his profession.

title: Boss Orders Databases Deleted Before Audit

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Internal auditors just showed up unannounced.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Delete all of our databases and make it look like an accident!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They'd know I did it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But they wouldn't know I ordered it.

situation: Dilbert warns his boss that internal auditors have arrived without notice. In a panic, the boss orders Dilbert to delete all the company databases and disguise it as an accident. When Dilbert points out that he would be traced as the culprit, the boss is unbothered because he himself would not be blamed.
punchline: The boss is only concerned with shielding himself, happily letting his employee take the fall for destroying the data.
summary: Panicking over a surprise audit, a manager tells his employee to wipe out the company's data and take the blame so the manager stays in the clear.

title: Dead Last: Barrel of Squirrels Review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A trade publication ranked us dead last on their list of "best places to work."

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The review says, "Employees say working there is like eating a barrel of dead squirrels."

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting
transcript.text: Could have been worse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Only for the squirrels.

setting: Conference room and exterior of the company office building
situation: At a meeting, the boss announces that a trade publication ranked the company dead last among best places to work. A caption quotes the review, which compares working there to eating a barrel of dead squirrels. A colleague says it could have been worse, and another points out it would only be worse for the squirrels.
punchline: The workplace is so awful that the insulting comparison to eating dead squirrels is dismissed as no big deal, since the only one who'd really suffer is the squirrels.
summary: Management shrugs off a scathing employer ranking while employees trade dark quips about how bad the company really is.

title: Hiring Handsome Future CEO

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a good-looking guy with no discernable talents.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He doesn't have any skills whatsoever, but he sure looks as if he would, and that has to count for something.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I plan to be nice to him. I think he's destined to be our next CEO.

setting: Office desk, a meeting with Catbert
situation: The Boss, seated across a desk from Catbert, explains that he hired a good-looking man who has no discernible skills. He reasons that the man's appearance suggests competence and decides to be nice to him. He predicts the new hire is destined to become the next CEO.
punchline: The joke satirizes how corporate leadership is often awarded on appearance rather than ability, implying that having no talent but looking the part is the best qualification for the top job.
summary: A manager brags about hiring an attractive but unskilled employee and expects him to rise straight to chief executive.

title: Leader Must Praise First

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You never give me any positive reinforcement.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: First you have to do something worth praising.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You can't call yourself a leader if you make me go first.

situation: Phil, holding a phone, complains to Wally that he never gets any positive reinforcement. Wally replies that Phil must first do something worth praising. Phil counters that a real leader wouldn't make him go first.
punchline: Wally's dismissal of Phil as unworthy of praise is met with Phil's claim that true leaders offer praise up front, so each tries to shift responsibility to the other.
summary: Two coworkers trade barbs over who should earn or give approval first, each accusing the other of failing at it.

title: Marrying an Elbonian to Keep Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People at work accused me of being bigoted against Elbonian men, so I'm marrying one to prove them wrong and keep my job.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's his name?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think it's something like Gluppfril or Breemf.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sounds like a solid plan.

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting on a blue couch
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch eating snacks and tells Dogbert that coworkers accused him of bigotry against Elbonian men, so he plans to marry one to clear his name and save his job. Dogbert asks the fiance's name, and Dilbert admits he only vaguely knows it. Dogbert approves of the plan anyway.
punchline: Dilbert is entering a marriage to a man whose name he doesn't even know purely as a workplace defense, and Dogbert's deadpan approval sarcastically highlights how absurd the plan is.
summary: To fend off a workplace discrimination charge, Dilbert decides to wed a stranger from Elbonia whose name he can't recall, and his dog calmly endorses the scheme.

title: Wally Becomes a Socialist, Alice Objects

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I decided to become more of a socialist.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: With any luck, I'll benefit from your hard work without adding any value myself.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That feels immoral.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Get back to work. I have bills to pay.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee cup, announces to Alice that he has decided to become more of a socialist. He explains that his hope is to live off her hard work without contributing anything himself. Alice says that feels immoral, and Wally tells her to get back to work because he has bills to pay.
punchline: Wally's version of socialism is simply freeloading on coworkers' labor, and he cheerfully demands that Alice keep working so he can profit from it.
summary: Wally frames his lifelong laziness as a political philosophy, expecting a coworker's labor to cover his expenses.

title: Flip-Flopper Loses the Meeting

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You're recommending the opposite of what you recommended a year ago!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You're a flip-flopper.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How can we trust anything you say if it changes in a year?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Your credibility is shot, bruh. What an embarrassment you have become.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When the data changes, sometimes I change my opinion. How do you play it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you keep your same dumb opinions, or do you sometimes update them?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You have exposed me for the fool I have always been. I quit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the first time I ever won a meeting. It feels good.

situation: In a meeting, a coworker (Asok) attacks Dilbert for recommending the opposite of what he recommended a year ago, calling him a flip-flopper with no credibility. Dilbert calmly replies that he changes his opinion when the data changes, and asks whether Asok ever updates his own. Asok is crushed, admits he is a fool, and quits.
punchline: Dilbert wins an argument for the first time ever by pointing out that changing your mind when the facts change is sensible, and his accuser is so fragile that he quits on the spot.
summary: A colleague mocks Dilbert for reversing his stance, but Dilbert's calm reply about updating opinions with new data devastates the accuser and gives him a rare meeting victory.

title: Authorization Loop Blocks Contract Access

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I see a copy of our network maintenance contract?

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: You're not authorized to see contracts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a legitimate business need.

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: It doesn't matter because you're not authorized.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, who is in charge of authorizing access?

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: That would be me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... give me access.

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: You need an access request form.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where do I get one of those?

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: Fill out an online request.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the URL?

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: I'm not authorized to tell you.

setting: Office cubicle of a records clerk
situation: Dilbert asks a clerk for a copy of the network maintenance contract and is told he isn't authorized to see contracts. He learns the clerk himself controls access, but is told to fill out an online request form. When Dilbert asks for the URL of that form, the clerk says he isn't authorized to tell him.
punchline: The bureaucratic gatekeeper's rules form a circular trap, where even the information on how to request access is itself restricted.
summary: A gatekeeper stonewalls an employee with circular authorization rules that make it impossible to ever get approved.

title: Engineer Blames Salesperson For Audio

transcript.speaker: Voice from laptop
transcript.text: I can't hear you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well, I'm an engineer, and you're in sales, so that narrows it down to some dumb thing you're doing.

transcript.speaker: Voice from laptop
transcript.text: I... can't... hear... you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This is going to be a long meeting.

setting: Alice's desk, on a video call from home
situation: Alice is on a remote meeting when a salesperson on the other end says they can't hear her. Alice immediately blames the salesperson, reasoning that as an engineer she must be competent and they must be at fault. The salesperson keeps repeating the same complaint, and Alice resigns herself to a long call.
punchline: Alice's snide assumption that the salesperson must be the problem proves unhelpful, since the audio is still broken and the meeting will drag on.
summary: A technical glitch on a video call turns into an engineer insulting a sales colleague, who only keeps repeating that the audio is still dead.

title: Dogbert Threatens Dilbert's Zoom Calls

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Can you please stop talking so loudly on your Zoom calls??!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sorry, but I pay the mortgage, and I have a right to make as much noise as I want in my own house.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh, wow. Did you really play the "mortgage card" on me?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is war!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wait until you see what I do in the background of your next Zoom call.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't want to ruin the surprise, but think of the number-one worst thing you can imagine me doing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you picturing it in your mind?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's bad, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now imagine at the same time I also start doing the second-worst thing you can imagine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Noooo!!!!

situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert to stop talking so loudly on his Zoom calls, and Dilbert replies that he pays the mortgage and can make all the noise he wants. Dogbert declares war and threatens to do something terrible in the background of Dilbert's next video call. He has Dilbert imagine the worst thing he could do, then adds the second-worst thing on top, and Dilbert is horrified.
punchline: Dogbert turns Dilbert's own imagination against him, letting him picture the worst possible background antics so that no actual stunt is needed to win the war.
summary: After being scolded by his homeowner, a small dog vows revenge and torments the man by making him envision the awful things he might do behind him on camera.

title: Everyone Is an Idiot Except Me

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sometimes, Asok, I think everyone in the world is an idiot except for you and me.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I can't tell if you are serious.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I guess it's down to just me.

situation: Alice and Asok sit side by side at their laptops. Alice says she thinks everyone in the world is an idiot except the two of them. When Asok says he can't tell whether she's serious, she reveals that she now counts only herself as non-idiotic.
punchline: By saying Asok can't tell if she is serious, he proves himself an idiot too, so Alice concludes she is the only sensible person left.
summary: A coworker's compliment about being smart is withdrawn the moment he shows he missed her sarcasm.

title: Proving Innocence by Marrying Elbonian

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm getting reports that you are bigoted against Elbonian men.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That is irrelevant. There is only one way to prove your innocence.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Yes, I'll marry you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought it would be a tougher sale.

situation: Catbert, acting as the HR director, tells Dilbert that he has received reports of Dilbert being bigoted against Elbonian men. When Dilbert denies it, Catbert declares the denial irrelevant and says there is only one way to prove innocence. In the last panel Dilbert holds a flower and proposes to an Elbonian, who immediately accepts.
punchline: Dilbert is coerced into proposing marriage to an Elbonian to clear himself of an accusation, and is only surprised that the proposal was accepted so easily.
summary: Faced with an HR accusation he can't refute, Dilbert ends up offering a flower and a proposal to an Elbonian who says yes without hesitation.

title: Skunk Fight Meets Orthopedic Socks

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our latest product is getting a bad reception on social media.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A Twitter user describes our user interface as "a cross between a skunk fight and orthopedic socks."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't make sense.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Apparently, neither does our user interface.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with an office building shown in the middle panel
situation: In a meeting, a coworker reports that the new product is getting poor feedback on social media. A Twitter user compared the user interface to a skunk fight crossed with orthopedic socks. Dilbert says the comparison makes no sense, and a coworker replies that the same is true of the interface.
punchline: The nonsensical insult is a fitting description because the product's user interface is itself confusing and makes no sense.
summary: A baffling online insult about a product's interface turns out to be a perfectly accurate review of its baffling design.

title: Keyboard Conscience Cannot Stop Mean Email

transcript.speaker: Keyboard
transcript.text: Hello, human. I'm your keyboard's conscience. You should reconsider sending such a mean email.

transcript.speaker: Keyboard
transcript.text: Working remotely has caused you to devolve into an empathy-free monster who cares nothing for the feelings of others.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Send.

transcript.speaker: Keyboard
transcript.text: Now you're just being a jerk.

setting: Dilbert's home office desk while working remotely
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer about to send a harsh email when his keyboard speaks up as a conscience, urging him to reconsider. It lectures him that remote work has turned him into an empathy-free monster. Dilbert ignores the warning and simply says 'Send', and the keyboard notes he is now just being a jerk.
punchline: Even a talking keyboard conscience can't talk Dilbert out of sending a nasty email, and its own scolding makes him dig in, so the final verdict is simply that he's being a jerk.
summary: A chatty keyboard conscience tries to stop a remote worker from firing off a nasty message, but he hits the button anyway.

title: Firing Remote Employees By Text

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The best part of having a remote workforce is firing them by text.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, you're fired.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tap tap tap

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's done?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I also need to give a thumbs-up to his crying face emoji.

situation: The Boss, holding his phone, tells Catbert (the evil HR director) that the best part of a remote workforce is firing people by text message. He types out a termination text to Ted. When Catbert asks if it's done, the Boss says he still has to respond to Ted's crying emoji with a thumbs-up.
punchline: The Boss callously caps off the impersonal text firing by replying to the fired employee's distress with a flippant thumbs-up emoji, showing how little empathy remote management requires.
summary: A manager happily terminates a distant employee by smartphone and then mockingly acknowledges the man's tearful reaction with a cheerful emoji.

title: Dogbert's Secret Bitcoin Billionaire Plan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This pandemic has been hard for all of us.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not me. I became a Bitcoin billionaire and made progress on my covert plan of ruling over the planet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why am I just hearing of this?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because I'm good at it.

setting: Office conference table with coffee and a donut
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit at a table with coffee, and Dilbert comments that the pandemic has been hard on everyone. Dogbert replies that he instead became a Bitcoin billionaire and advanced his secret plan to rule the world. When Dilbert asks why he is only now learning this, Dogbert says it is because he is good at keeping it hidden.
punchline: Dogbert's plan for world domination is so successful precisely because it has been kept secret, so Dilbert not knowing about it proves how competent Dogbert is.
summary: While his friend laments the hardships of the pandemic, Dogbert casually reveals that he has quietly gotten rich on cryptocurrency and is closing in on global conquest.

title: Fake Death Sentence Before Weekend Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, you've been exposed to lethal workplace chemicals, and you will be dead by the weekend.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What??!! No!!! I'm too young! This can't be happening!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It isn't. But now you won't feel so bad when I tell you to work all weekend.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, with an exterior view of the office building in the middle panel
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, tells Dilbert he has been exposed to lethal chemicals and will die by the weekend. Dilbert panics and protests that he is too young. The Boss then admits it was a lie, told so that Dilbert will feel relieved and accept being ordered to work all weekend.
punchline: The Boss deliberately frightens Dilbert with a fake death sentence so that being told to work all weekend feels like good news by comparison.
summary: A manager invents a deadly exposure scare purely to make an unpaid weekend shift seem like a relief.
